CTO Julie Eng presented Coherent's VCSEL-based NPOs. The VCSEL NPO shown at OFC integrates the VCSEL, photodiodes, drivers, TIAs and coupling optics into a single deployable NPO. The NPO built on the 2D VCSEL array integrates the substrates, drivers and TIAs, 2D VCSELs, 2D photodiode arrays, a heat spreader and a lens array, and has been demonstrated at 1.2 picojoules per bit, which she said is, as far as she knows, the lowest CPO or NPO power consumption including the laser. A second NPO built on the high-density VCSEL and photodiode, integrated with TIAs and drivers, can take the light out the top or out the side (adding a turning mirror, lenses and a lensed fiber array).
1.2 picojoules per bit, including the laser

CTO Julie Eng laid out the CPO vs NPO trade-off: CPO puts the optical engine literally on the package of the switch or XPU chip and offers the lowest power consumption and, in many cases, the highest density, while NPO moves the optics off the package onto the board right next to it - easier to deploy and more serviceable, but moving it away from the chip costs power and the socket impacts signal integrity. NPO is also an architectural platform: a common form factor and socket can accommodate either silicon photonics or VCSELs, and Coherent is a founder of the Open CPX MSA, helping develop an open ecosystem for a common connector among vendors to give customers architectural flexibility.

→ NVIDIA: CTO Julie Eng identified the anchor customer long-term agreement (LTA) secured for Coherent's CPO solution as 'our NVIDIA agreement, which is a public agreement' - the only customer named at the PhotonLink launch - among over 10 active customer engagements in CPO. She expects CPO scale-out in Q4 of 2026 and scale-up in the second half of next year.

ECOC 2026 product demonstration (official press release, not a call): Lumentum announced its plan to demonstrate an eight-wavelength dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) laser module in an External Laser Small Form Factor Pluggable (ELSFP). The module's optical interface is designed to meet the applicable requirements of the Optical Compute Interconnect Multi-Source Agreement (OCI MSA), and it is intended for external laser source applications in co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-packaged optics (NPO) architectures. It provides eight simultaneous DWDM wavelengths across two four-channel bands centered near 1311 nm and 1331 nm; the design targets wavelength accuracy of +/-0.2 nm and demonstrates up to 24 dBm (~250 mW) of optical output power per wavelength at the fiber, with all eight channels operating simultaneously from a single pluggable module at approximately 12 W of power consumption. The module uses Lumentum's Ultra High Power (UHP) laser platform, already in production, in an eight-channel configuration. Lumentum expects initial availability of the DWDM ELSFP module with an OCI MSA optical interface in the first half of calendar year 2027. Sri Venkat (SVP and GM, Components) called CPO and NPO 'defining architectures for AI scale-up' and external laser sources 'a critical building block of that shift', and said the demonstration positions Lumentum to serve customers as the CPO/NPO market scales.

eight DWDM wavelengths in two four-channel bands near 1311 nm and 1331 nm; wavelength accuracy target +/-0.2 nm; up to 24 dBm (~250 mW) per wavelength at the fiber; approximately 12 W module power; initial availability expected in the first half of calendar year 2027

ECOC 2026 joint demonstration (official press release, not a call): Lumentum announced plans for a joint board-level demonstration with Qualcomm Technologies and Corning of a high-density die-to-die (D2D) optical interconnect for AI scale-up architectures, combining a D2D interface IP subsystem from Qualcomm Technologies with Lumentum's VCSEL-based optical interconnect platform and Corning multimode fiber connectivity. The massively parallel optical D2D architecture is designed for future co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-packaged optics (NPO) implementations supporting emerging D2D interfaces such as UCIe, extending high-density D2D connectivity over multimode-fiber optical links spanning tens of meters while maintaining low latency and power consumption. The proof-of-concept configuration uses optical channels operating at 32 Gb/s NRZ; the architecture is designed to support approximately 1 Tb/s/mm of shoreline bandwidth density today, with line of sight to approximately 4 Tb/s/mm through higher lane rates and increased channel density. This is a proof-of-concept demonstration; the release gives no product availability date, customer or commercial terms.
32 Gb/s NRZ optical channels (proof-of-concept); approximately 1 Tb/s/mm shoreline bandwidth density today, line of sight to approximately 4 Tb/s/mm

XPO / NPO / CPO ROADMAP WITH DATES: SVP Cloud and AI Networking Tyson Lamoreaux said 'XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that is where we start to see some of that CPO ramp occur'. The sequence is copper as long as possible, then NPO/XPO (XPO is the NPO-based architecture) for the multi-rack density copper cannot reach, then CPO once it can be built at scale - early CPO adoption expected, but a completely different manufacturing technology whose yields will be very challenging early on. Arista builds CPO or NPO switches when customers ask; XPO timing is partly aligned with scale-up form factor and bandwidth density needs.

FIRST HARD SIZING OF THE CPO TEST MARKET, PLUS WHO WINS WHICH INSERTION (CEO Greg Smith): the test-equipment TAM for silicon photonics co-packaged optics is about $100 million in 2026 and is expected to be between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, reaching about a billion dollars of test equipment by 2030 (optical alignment, interface hardware and material handling are a separate TAM). Today it is 'a very concentrated market' - one customer and a very small number of devices drive most of the 2026 capital intensity. A CPO device has four major optical test insertions: (1) the photonics wafer, (2) the silicon photonics wafer with the electronic ICs bonded to it, (3) the singulated optical engine dielets with the mounting plate for FAU alignment, (4) the assembled CPO device. On this first device at this first customer, 'Advantest is strongest in insertion one, Teradyne is strongest in insertion two, a Taiwanese supplier is strongest in insertion three, and Teradyne is strongest in insertion four.' Management flags scaling pain as the reason for 'increasing excitement about copper networking for scale-up' and for NPO, which avoids the yield risk of a full CPO device.
CPO/SiPho test equipment TAM about $100 million in 2026, between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, about a billion dollars by 2030

OPTICAL TIMELINE TIGHTENED - CONNECTOR REVENUE 2027, NPO REVENUE IN 2H 2027, CPO AT 400G PER LANE: Mohan said optical revenue starts in 2027 with component-level sales of the glass coupler/connector from the aiXscale Photonics acquisition closed 'in December of last year', which customers are qualifying for their own CPU scale-out applications and which 'might very well end up becoming the first revenue that we see in 2027'. Next is NPO, which Astera considers the right answer at '200 gig per lane data rates' because it does not stress the supply chain while delivering the distance and density scale-up needs; 'we will start to see initial revenues in the back half of 2027 from our NPO efforts. Then full year ahead in 2028.' At '400 gig per lane data rates and even higher densities' CPO takes over, with Astera supplying the full optical engine - its own electrical IC, its own photonics IC (PIC) and the fiber-to-silicon-photonics packaging - landing both on an optically enabled Scorpio SKU and on the XPU side, so a link that previously had no such component gains two. He also corrected a pricing assumption for multi-rack scale-up: as cluster sizes go from 72 to 144, 288 and 576 GPUs the switch radix rises and 'contrary to popular belief that price per lane goes down, it actually goes up with radix'.
initial revenues in the back half of 2027; 200 gig per lane; 400 gig per lane

CPO REVENUE RAISED AGAIN AND THE CUSTOMER BASE IS BROADENING. CEO Mike Slessor: 'we started the year with a view of maybe $10 million-$20 million in revenue. Have now successfully upgraded that to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter' — i.e. the top of the original full-year range is now hit by the end of Q3. More important than the dollars, the concentration is changing: 'one of the exciting things that we're now seeing in the second part of the year is broader production adoption of this TRITON high-volume manufacturing platform at multiple foundries with multiple fabless customers'. Today it is 'pretty concentrated, with one major foundry fabless partnership', but FormFactor is 'building backlog and building the breadth of the backlog where this diversifies a little bit beyond that one customer set'. Installed base: 'hundreds of systems installed worldwide' at close to as many customers, with 'installed now tens of systems' specifically ramping in CPO production. The 2025 acquisition of Keystone Photonics is described as 'really an enabling technology for optical probing'. On the NPO-versus-CPO debate, Slessor said FormFactor has built one fundamental optical probing technology applicable across CPO, NPO and pluggables, and that NPO is not yet pulling in at the scale CPO is affecting 2026 revenue, though there is 'lots of activity' across the customer base. He also embraced the bottleneck label: photonics test is where the industry is constrained, and FormFactor is resolving technical and operational challenges in real time on installed systems.

CPO revenue view upgraded from $10 million-$20 million for the year to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter; hundreds of systems installed worldwide; tens of systems in CPO production

Content economics of the 1.6T transition, with ASPs: 'if you look at 800G, most of the market data will say ASPs are running, I don't know, $35 to $50 probably, versus a 1.6T, which is probably $80 to $100 plus the cost of the TIA, which pushes it above $100.' Rushmore is in customer qualification and is 'expected to go to market mid-next year,' with full scale production 'in the following year,' sold alongside the Washington TIA. Looking further out, architectures disaggregate: at 3.2T expect a standalone TIA, a standalone driver and the SerDes 'incorporated differently. Maybe it is not in a DSP'; in a CPO or NPO application the driver (today integrated into the DSP) becomes standalone and the SerDes 'ends up being in a chiplet', so versus the DSP and a TIA today 'the content is higher in a CPO or an NPO application.' Pricing is expected to hold: 'I don't anticipate pricing coming down much, between now and the end of next year.'
800G ASPs $35 to $50 versus 1.6T $80 to $100, above $100 with the TIA; Rushmore to market mid-next year, full scale production the year after

Semtech introduced a family of 224G linear TIA and driver solutions designed for Near-Packaged Optics (NPO) and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) architectures for AI/ML clusters and hyperscale data centers: the GN1838L and GN42T380 linear octal TIAs (which Semtech calls the industry's first linear octal TIAs) and the GN42M380 linear octal Mach-Zehnder Modulator (MZM) driver, optimized for 1.6T, 3.2T, 6.4T and 12.8T optical engines and for CEI-224G-Linear and Open CPX interfaces. The GN1838L offers a 500µm channel pitch and the GN42T380 a 375µm channel pitch; the TIAs can be placed side-by-side with the photonics integrated circuit (PIC) or directly on top of it. The GN42M380 driver (375µm channel pitch) supports silicon photonics, indium phosphide MZM and thin-film lithium niobate modulators. No availability date is stated (the release says to contact Semtech for availability). Amit Thakar, VP signal integrity product marketing: the TIAs and drivers are 'purpose-built to give NPO and CPO developers the building blocks to scale optical I/O while addressing the power and density challenges of next-generation AI systems.'
224G per lane; octal TIAs at 500µm and 375µm channel pitch; for 1.6T, 3.2T, 6.4T and 12.8T optical engines
Semtech press release: Semtech Sets Bar for 224G Optical Connectivity (09-09-2026)

He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.

AGENTIC WORKLOADS ARE THE CPU DEMAND DRIVER, AND IRELAND IS THE SUPPLY ANSWER: CFO David Zinsner quantified the workload shift for the first time - comparing a regular training data center with an agentic-like activity, 'it's like a 4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements'. Server CPU units, which used to decline low single digits, are now growing double digits with core counts growing at multiples of that, and ASP per core - which fell almost 20% in some years - has at least stabilized and in some like-for-like cases is going up, so core-count growth now flows straight through to revenue. The constraint is supply, not competitive performance: 'as we look at this year, next year, probably even into 2028, this is going to be less about competitive performance of CPUs and more about can you get the CPUs to the customer', and share will follow whoever can supply. Granite Rapids, the data-center flagship, is built in Ireland on Intel 3; part of next year's CapEx is to ramp Ireland where Intel wants to 'more than double the output there next year'. Even so Intel will 'under-supply for sure this year', 'probably under-supply next year', and hopes to be in a good position by 2028.
4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements; more than double the output there next year

MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

eVoS / eVerest / NavX ARE DESIGNED INTO SUB-2 NANOMETER LOGIC, BUT REVENUE IS A 2027-2028 EVENT. Kelley: 'Today we are being designed into sub-2 nanometer applications, logic for instance. On the mix of what is ramping now: 'As you see the ramp this year, that is almost all older technologies. They are existing wins from many years ago where our customers are ramping the volume. WFE VIEW RAISED: asked about the mid-teens 2026 WFE framework the moderator attributed to Nova from May, CFO Guy Kizner said the numbers have moved up - external estimates have been revised up every two months, driven by AI, and on Nova's read of WFE 'it will be above 20%', though he would not name a number (Nova does not forecast WFE internally and refers to market consensus). He noted the market range is still unusually wide four months from year end: 'Gartner talking about 20% growth, TechInsights in the high 20s', with other analysts at 30, 35, 38 - even with the big players' backlog and shipment plans already visible.
it will be above 20%; Gartner talking about 20% growth, TechInsights in the high 20s

WHY NOVA IS NOT OUTPERFORMING WFE AS USUAL IN 2026 (the '2x WFE' framing was the moderator's, not management's): Kizner said Nova historically outperforms WFE significantly ('2024, we grew by 30%', '2025, we grew by 31%' while WFE did not grow much) but 2026 breaks the pattern because of investment MIX. Three reasons: (1) NAND contributes to WFE but nothing to Nova because the spend is upgrades, not greenfield capacity; (2) heavy DRAM investment, where metrology intensity is lower than logic; (3) most important, the AI customers did NOT transition to Gate-All-Around - they are 'still using the N-1, 3 nm and 5 nm' and are spending on 3 nm capacity expansions in both the U.S. and Taiwan, so the metrology intensity of 2026 spending went down on mix.
2024, we grew by 30%; 2025, we grew by 31%; still using the N-1, 3 nm and 5 nm

2027 SETUP BY END MARKET: Kizner expects the mix to swing back in Nova's favour in 2027 - NAND capacity additions would be 'coming from zero to business' for Nova since it is positioned with all the key NAND customers (he called this the longest NAND down cycle, with upgrades-only spend that Nova does not benefit from, and hopes for greenfield in 2027); DRAM stays a significant driver on capacity expansion but with NO metrology-intensity increase until the industry moves to 4F², which he placed in '2028 and going forward'; and logic mix shifts 'much more towards the 2 nm and the Gate-All-Around, and less on the 3 nm', pushing metrology intensity up.
it will happen in 2028 and going forward

CHINA GUIDANCE REVISED UP: Kizner said China is 'around 30% of our revenues' today and 25% to 30% of overall WFE spending, and that although Nova said at the start of the year China would be slightly down to flat, the visibility it now has means 'it will be another growth year for China for us on a nominal basis' (still declining as a percentage because other regions grow faster). He treats domestic Chinese metrology vendors as a real risk rather than dismissing them - they have the talent, funds and government support, there is still a capability gap today, and Nova's answer is to keep spending a significant portion of revenue on R&D to keep the gap open.
it is around 30% of our revenues; 25% to 30% over all WFE spending; it will be another growth year for China for us on a nominal basis

First cost and gating condition put on the EUV plan the Q3 call described only as partnerships: 'we have a plan to go to EUV, but a full EUV program would cost us about $300 million. Mask-set ASP ladder and share, quantified: citing a Morgan Stanley Japan initiation report on a competitor, Moreau said a 90 nanometer design is about 25 masks per set and roughly '$50,000 of revenue for that one chip design'; at 14 nanometers the set goes to close to 80 masks and 'we're talking about $1 million in revenue contribution'; at five nanometers 'you're talking about $10 million to $20 million for that one semiconductor chip design, for the photomask set' - 'a very parabolic move'. Photronics holds about 10% of the total photomask market including captives, captives are about two-thirds of the market and gained share in 2025 purely on ASP (conceivably going to 70%), while display share is about 28% and has held steady for five years. On units, Photronics estimates it manufactures about as much volume as TSMC does in-house, but that TSMC's fully captive mask output would be worth 'at least five or six times' Photronics' roughly $620 million of semiconductor photomask revenue last year if it carried an external price.

Node-capability roadmap by site, more granular than the Q3 call. Boise is the U.S. high-end facility and 'can produce masks down to seven nanometers' today, with little revenue at 7 nanometers so far, and 'with the same equipment, we are advancing our capabilities to actually go down to four' - not ready and no revenue presented today. Allen, Texas is being taken from 180 nanometers and 130 nanometers up to 65 nanometers and 'we should be up and running in the next month or two'; production then shifts out of Boise to Texas, freeing Boise to capture more 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometer business. Korea is the other upgrade: the bulk of that facility's business today is about 40 nanometers, the expansion to 8 nanometers is expected 'in about a year from now', and Photronics expects significantly greater 8 and 10 nanometer business there 'largely because of customers that are very close to that facility'. The U.S. is 17%-19% of revenue today and is expected to be a higher share of total revenue in fiscal 2027.

CEO split the GaN roadmap into two supply models. Lateral GaN (GaN-on-Silicon) is sourced through partners: 'We have announced a partnership with Innoscience and a partnership with GlobalFoundries... Technology position (DART half-year report): GENI-SYS anneals at 250 ~ 450 degrees C and 1 ~ 25 ATM with 100% hydrogen or deuterium, against 600 ~ 1,100 degrees C and under 5% hydrogen for conventional furnace anneal, and the company says it is applied on 2nm to 16nm processes while conventional anneal cannot be used below 16nm; it calls GENI-SYS the only high-pressure hydrogen anneal tool certified to global pressure-vessel standards (PED, ASME, KGS) and says no competing tool is in volume production. It releases tools with new functions every 2-3 years, has a GENI-SYS installed at imec for logic, NAND and DRAM research, and holds a technical-advisory contract with POSTECH through 2027. AI / HBM / ADVANCED PACKAGING framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the company says the surge in AI semiconductor demand has raised the importance of HBM and advanced-packaging processes, pushing up the technical barrier for high-purity chemicals and precision polishing materials; the global semiconductor market is growing at an unprecedented pace on AI data-center memory and on-device AI, and the introduction of sub-2nm GAA processes and volume production of 300+ layer V-NAND are driving continued demand for high-performance etchants and next-generation precursors. Seasonality has flattened because AI and cloud enterprise demand now leads, producing a longer up-cycle. Product positioning: special etchants for sub-2nm GAA, next-generation CMP slurry and precursors for HBM4 stacking; ultra-high-purity chemicals supplied at near-exclusive levels to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix from the leading-edge ramp and ultra-high-layer V-NAND development stage; a completed portfolio of TSV formation and planarisation materials for HBM4 and chiplet structures to lift high-value-added revenue; display unit expanding into glass-substrate processing materials for next-generation packaging; customers' processes moving to GAA and to HBM / 400+ layer NAND, with joint development from the process-design stage. US entities Soulbrain TX LLC (2022) and Soulbrain RASA TX LLC (2024) respond in real time to customers' new fab lines in Texas and North America; the Xi'an entity supports China memory lines. Semiconductor material ASPs +5% vs FY2025 while raw-material costs rose +14%; semiconductor materials 85% of H1 revenue, +31% company-wide revenue growth.
HBM4 CMP slurry / precursors / TSV materials portfolio; sub-2nm GAA etchants; 300-400+ layer V-NAND; glass-substrate materials; Texas entities for US fab ramps

AI / HBM framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the memory market is leading semiconductor growth on AI and big-data demand, and the equipment market is expected to keep growing over the medium-to-long term on the aggressive DRAM-centric investment memory makers are making to break the HBM SHORTAGE caused by the explosive expansion of AI end-markets. 2022-2024 is described as a harsh down-cycle (memory price collapse, utilisation drop); 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase driven by generative-AI infrastructure build-out, led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than commodity products. The AI-accelerator and HBM demand surge is forcing the equipment market onto a single high-end track where marginal technology or adequate tools have no place; foreign vendors from the US, Japan and Netherlands still hold the largest shares but Korean localisation is rising and the company's tools are now in mass-production lines of major customers at home and abroad, with overseas sales rising (China semiconductor revenue KRW 63,346M in H1 2026 vs KRW 42,017M in H1 2025). Company cannot estimate market share because device makers' total orders are not observable.
HBM shortage-driven DRAM capex cited as multi-year equipment driver; 2025-2030 structural growth phase (HBM, sub-2nm foundry)

Management states (FY2026 annual securities report) that, on the rapid spread of generative AI, investment in advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging led the semiconductor market, and new and expanded fabs progressed worldwide for economic security and supply-chain resilience. GUC announced that its HBM4E PHY and Controller IP is design-ready and has been adopted in customer AI ASICs (customers not named). Implemented on TSMC's N2P process, the HBM4E PHY has taped out on TSMC CoWoS-L advanced packaging. Building on GUC's silicon-proven 12 Gbps HBM4 IP on TSMC N3P, the HBM4E IP pushes data transfer speeds up to 16 Gbps across all signed-off operating conditions (GUC claims industry-leading power efficiency and a compact area), with its proprietary interposer layout optimized for SI/PI across TSMC CoWoS packaging configurations. A face-up variant is engineered as a bottom die in TSMC SoIC-X, with dedicated TSVs for signal pull-out and feedthrough power delivery to top dies; the IP incorporates proteanTecs interconnect monitoring. CTO Igor Elkanovich said uniting face-up HBM, face-up UCIe and GLink-3D IPs gives GUC a complete interface IP portfolio for 3D SoIC architectures.

On the roughly '70% growth on a year-over-year basis' in HBM in the first half, Slessor attributed it to three things: share gains from 'adding a second HBM customer'; industry bit growth as HBM3 moved to HBM4; and ASP uplift that came not from price increases but from delivering a higher-value configuration 'able to test at the 11 gigabit per second spec of HBM4 and test hundreds of die at once'. FormFactor's largest customer is the HBM leader, where it is the strong incumbent. At the third DRAM maker the major competitor is the entrenched incumbent and FormFactor sees less adoption of its high-speed stack-die configuration — but 'there is a very active conversation with that customer about what to plan for in 2027 and into 2028, as we have more capacity available to serve them'. On the HBM de-spec debate, Slessor called it 'much ado about nothing': fewer/simpler stacks would be offset by more HBM units and by more networking infrastructure to transact data across those units, leaving it 'net net... neutral'. He framed the whole test tailwind as a chiplet problem — in an HBM stack 'one of the 16 die actually causes the entire stack to be essentially scrapped and lost' without known-good-die certainty.

DE-SPECCING DOES NOT DENT HBM PROCESS-CONTROL INTENSITY: asked about customer de-speccing (the analyst's framing - AI servers putting in less memory and stepping from 12 high to 8 high), Higgins argues 'the roadmap dynamics I talked about earlier, those are generally unchanged in the HBM environment' - redundancy, IO count, die size and performance specs still hold, and 'You cannot bin an HBM device'. He reads the behaviour as a reaction to today's memory pricing and supply-demand imbalance rather than a roadmap change, and says KLA does not like paying today's memory prices either. HIGH BANDWIDTH COMPUTE (HBC) IS AN EXPLICIT ALTERNATIVE TO HBM, WITH SPECS AND A SHIP DATE. Durga Malladi (EVP Tech Planning, Edge & Data Center): HBC puts compute right next to memory and was 'a direct take on an alternative way of doing things as opposed to HBM'. Claimed '6x improvement compared to HBM in terms of tokens per second per watt'; where 'HBM today is about give or take 21, 22 terabytes per second. We are, like, in hundreds of terabytes per second'. Against SRAM the argument is TCO/area (more racks for the same work). Proof points: the silicon is taped out and 'back in the lab ... coming along very well', with silicon validation and engineering plus commercial samples on track. Generation 1 is 'slated to be commercial and shipping in 2027'; generation 2 lands in 2028 and is benchmarked against HBM4E, where Malladi says the relative gain looks even better because more arithmetic is moving into the logic die under the DRAM stack.

6x improvement compared to HBM in terms of tokens per second per watt; HBM today about 21, 22 terabytes per second vs hundreds of terabytes per second; gen 1 commercial and shipping in 2027, gen 2 in 2028 vs HBM4E

HBC SUPPLY CHAIN AND DIVISION OF LABOUR: Qualcomm is not a memory vendor - 'We're not doing the DRAM stacking ourselves. What we prescribe is this is how things should be done. These are the TSVs that need to occur.' The compute die comes from Qualcomm, and 'We still have to work with the likes of TSMC to tape it all together'; Qualcomm positions itself as the overall system integrator and the single front end to the hyperscaler customer. On supply: right after Investor Day Malladi was 'in Korea with two memory vendors' and, instead of pushing back on the HBM comparison, they asked how to work more closely - 'we have been working with them because we need to make sure that we have the right supply as we do the commercialization', with additional inbound interest from the wider memory community. Hyperscaler engagement is modular across three independent tracks (standalone HBC, HBC plus Qualcomm CPU, or the full stack), and a hyperscaler taking HBC brings 'certain volume commitment, some sort of a demand signal'.

Asked whether High Bandwidth Flash (the moderator named SK hynix and SanDisk) could undercut High Bandwidth Compute on TCO, Durga Malladi gave his own view after in-depth talks with memory vendors: 'HBF is trying to solve a slightly different problem. It is not quite exactly the same problem.' HBF uses flash in addition to DRAM for something else, which 'is not the same thing as increasing the memory bandwidth to the point that the decode performance becomes really good', though 'it has its own use case' and more work remains. He sees HBF as a stack 'kind of independent of this', while the HBM vendors are opening 'a parallel track' because they cannot offer anything like HBC through HBM for the foreseeable future ('Maybe 5 years down the stream, it is going to be a different story').

Product pipeline as described in the half-year report: (1) CUBE PROBER - HBM test equipment that fully inspects HBM at the individual-stack level with sub-5-micrometre vision precision, skipping the loader/unloader/COK tray steps by transferring wafers directly to the chuck; first Samsung HBM Cube Prober order won 2025-01 and a KRW 9,720M HBM test equipment supply contract with Samsung disclosed 2026-05-19; filing says the HBM market is led by SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron and that stacked-die (TSV) inspection difficulty is driving double-digit annual growth in memory ATE. (2) Probe stations TWP300 (in mass-production lines) and second-generation-vision TWP300H targeting localisation of a market dominated by Tokyo Electron and other Japanese vendors. (3) Burn-in chambers and sorters - started with overseas SSD burn-in, expanding to DRAM and non-memory; eSSD / PCIe 5.0-6.0 burn-in demand tied to AI data-center build-outs. (4) Memory, non-memory (SoC) and module/SSD test handlers plus change-over kits and interface boards sold as a handler-plus-board total solution. Filing frames test and inspection equipment as the fastest-growing equipment segment because HBM-style advanced packaging requires 100% inspection at each process step, raising both ASP and unit counts. Corporate: new Taiwan branch manager approved 2026-07-07; subsidiary CK Electronic Technology Nanjing liquidated in H1; charter amended 2026-03-24 to rename outside directors as independent directors and extend directors' duty of loyalty to shareholders; KRW 15,000M of capital surplus transferred to retained earnings.
Cube Prober (sub-5um vision, per-stack HBM full inspection) + TWP300/TWP300H probe stations + SSD/DRAM burn-in expanding; first Samsung Cube Prober order 2025-01

AI / HBM framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the memory market is leading semiconductor growth on AI and big-data demand, and the equipment market is expected to keep growing over the medium-to-long term on the aggressive DRAM-centric investment memory makers are making to break the HBM SHORTAGE caused by the explosive expansion of AI end-markets. 2022-2024 is described as a harsh down-cycle (memory price collapse, utilisation drop); 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase driven by generative-AI infrastructure build-out, led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than commodity products. The AI-accelerator and HBM demand surge is forcing the equipment market onto a single high-end track where marginal technology or adequate tools have no place; foreign vendors from the US, Japan and Netherlands still hold the largest shares but Korean localisation is rising and the company's tools are now in mass-production lines of major customers at home and abroad, with overseas sales rising (China semiconductor revenue KRW 63,346M in H1 2026 vs KRW 42,017M in H1 2025). Company cannot estimate market share because device makers' total orders are not observable.
HBM shortage-driven DRAM capex cited as multi-year equipment driver; 2025-2030 structural growth phase (HBM, sub-2nm foundry)

HBM-related products in the report: Ring Frame cleaning equipment used in next-generation packaging for HBM production (de-bonding the device wafer from the carrier, residue cleaning and chip cutting on ultra-thin wafers), commercialised for 300mm and 400mm cleaning tools (product ATOM); the company expects continued benefit from HBM market growth. It has developed Temporary Bonding / De-bonding (TBDB) equipment for HBM chip stacking and bumping, offering mechanical, laser and photonic debond (the photonic method has no mass-production record yet), under government projects for HBM ultra-thin wafer bonding and debonding (2022.04 to 2025.12) and a UV laser debonding system for 2.5D packaging (2024.04 to 2026.12); these tools are currently dependent on foreign suppliers and Zeus aims to localise them. Also developing PEP (Pressurized Etch Process) wet etch equipment and a 12-chamber ION 12 cleaner (more than twice the throughput of 8-chamber tools). R&D spend KRW 23,290,765 thousand in H1 2026 (17.0% of revenue).

Order intake has accelerated sharply: MORE THAN $600 MILLION of orders received year to date, with deliveries scheduled through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027, materially improving visibility well into 2027. >$600M orders year to date; ~80% advanced packaging; OSATs >50% of intake; HBM >20%; photonics ~5%

Advanced packaging mix is stepping up through the year: it was approximately 75% of Q2 revenue and is expected to reach around 80% by Q4. Advanced packaging ~75% of Q2 revenue rising to ~80% by Q4; AP +45% H2 vs H1; Q4 AP ~70% above Q1; HPC/AI ~55% of revenue rising toward ~60%

Electroplating momentum on both front-end and back-end: in logic, larger die sizes and steadily higher interconnect layer counts; in memory, HBM packaging demands higher levels of DRAM stacking and thus more copper process steps. ACM shipped its 2,000th electroplating chamber in the quarter (500th in 2022, 1,500th in 2025); the copper plating market is now almost $1.5 billion, with backside power and HBM DRAM stacking driving more plating tool demand.
2,000th electroplating chamber shipped; copper plating market almost $1.5 billion

Memory is expected to show strong year-over-year growth in 2026 with momentum into 2027 as customers accelerate clean room investments to support growing DRAM and high-bandwidth memory demand driven by AI; 2026 is a significant improvement over the low 2025 base with significant DRAM memory revenue, and second-half memory revenue probably looks similar to the first half because customers are solving bottlenecks in existing fabs until new clean room space comes online.

Memory customer portfolio is expanding: a recent order for multiple high current systems in the current quarter, and additional orders from the leading North American memory manufacturer (referenced last quarter) after the successful completion of its system evaluation, to support new fab investments. 2027 memory: too early to size, indications are another year of growth but at a much lower percentage growth rate than 2026 given the low 2025 base; customers have ambitious capacity plans and Axcelis is expanding beyond its traditional position into other areas of the memory market and other customers. no specific figure (analyst estimate ~$120 million annual memory run rate)

Memory: despite the anticipated sequential decline from a strong Q1, customer engagement remains robust; strong year-over-year growth expected in 2026 with momentum into 2027 as customers accelerate clean room investments to support DRAM and high-bandwidth memory demand driven by AI. Recent order for multiple high current systems in the current quarter, and additional orders from the leading North American memory manufacturer after its system evaluation, to support new fab investments.

ADVANCED PACKAGING set a record and contributed nearly one-quarter - 'nearing 25%' - of overall product revenue in Q2, driven by the dimensional metrology portfolio and fuelled by customers' continued investment in advanced packaging and HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY capacity to support AI-related device demand. Advanced packaging a record at nearly 25% of Q2 product revenue, inching toward 25% for the full year (initially guided 20-25%)

The Nova WMC dimensional-metrology platform won a recent TOOL OF RECORD SELECTION BY A LEADING FOUNDRY CUSTOMER (not named on the call) for MULTIPLE LAYERS MEASUREMENT in advanced-packaging production flows. Memory and others was 27% of Q2 product revenue and Nova projects MEMORY AT ABOUT 30% for full-year 2026, a slight increase on the 70/30 logic-to-memory ratio of 2025, against a long-term model of about 60/40 in favour of logic because process-control intensity in logic is higher. The MAJORITY OF NOVA'S MEMORY EXPOSURE IS DRAM, where demand is strong, while 3D NAND remains 'somehow muted' this year because its growth is driven by UPGRADES rather than capacity expansion - even though metrology intensity between DRAM and NAND is 'more or less similar.' A new generation of the Nova PRISM platform is targeted at advanced memory structures.
Memory 27% of Q2 product revenue and ~30% expected for 2026 (2025 was 70/30); long-term model 60/40 logic/memory; DRAM strong, 3D NAND muted and upgrade-driven

HBM / ACOUSTIC METROLOGY QUALIFICATION: CEO says the majority of the qualification processes discussed earlier are finalized and PVA TePla is in the volume business with those customers; it is qualified / in final agreements with half of the big logic and memory players and is working on the other half (his answer when asked about the second Korean memory player). half of the big logic / memory players qualified or in final agreements; relevant for 16-high HBM stacks

NPO = tens-of-% of SiPho shipments by H2-2027; integrated InP lasers = tens of $M in 2027; pluggables already displaced copper for scale-out

memory output +20% per year vs demand +200% per year

CEO view on hybrid-bonding adoption: hybrid bonding has become a critical enabler of next-generation chip architectures (density, performance, thermal management). AMD started shipping hybrid-bonded logic devices in 2022; Apple, Intel and Broadcom all have products ramping into production using hybrid bonding. He believes hybrid bonding will be a requirement in HBM with 20 or more layers, if not sooner, and in NAND as layer counts approach 400, with the big three memory players all ramping to get there. Leading foundries, memory companies and OSATs are planning to spend approximately $125 billion in the near term on advanced packaging including hybrid bonding — 'we know broad adoption of hybrid bonding is coming because the capital equipment required is being ordered.' Hyperscalers 'are semiconductor companies now', differentiating with their own chips, which he expects to create additional opportunity. He puts the semiconductor market at over $1.5 trillion this year.
HBM with 20 or more layers; NAND approaching 400 layers; ~$125 billion near-term advanced-packaging spend; semiconductor market over $1.5 trillion

For 2026 Ichor expects revenue growth in alignment with the high end of WFE expectations, an increase of at least 30% from full year 2025; the steepening customer demand ramp indicates sequential revenue growth exceeding 10% in each of the next two quarters and second half revenue volumes at least 25% higher than the first half. 2026 revenue growth at least 30% vs 2025; H2 at least 25% above H1; >10% sequential growth in each of Q3 and Q4

AI data center applications drive the WFE market: sales to AI data center are expected to grow by five times or more in the five years from calendar 2023 through calendar 2027, spanning not only GPU and HBM but also DDR, CPU and 3D NAND. Technology transitions expected within two years: logic scaling from the 3 nanometer mainstream toward 2 nanometer with backside PDN adoption, DRAM evolving to the 1D node (1C to 1D transition), HBM stacked DRAM count rising from 12 to 16, and NAND evolving to 300 layers and further to 400 layers. Agentic AI is the driver of the overall WFE market; CY2026 WFE application mix is about 60% logic and 40% memory, versus 65%/35% last year.
AI data center WFE sales to grow five times or more CY2023-CY2027; HBM stacks from 12 to 16; NAND to 300 then 400 layers; logic mainstream 3 nanometer moving to 2 nanometer

HBM3/HBM4/HBM4E final-inspection shipments to a US IDM; roadmap to HBM5; Neon qualified at a Taiwan OSAT

HBM: continued repeat orders from HBM manufacturers; installed tools at one customer now deployed to HBM4 in high volume manufacturing, plus low volume manufacturing with multiple memory makers for HBM4; entered an exclusive joint evaluation program with a key memory player for HBM5 advanced memory packaging. HBM stack height possibly from 775 micron to beyond 900

Record June quarter: revenue $6.72B (+15% QoQ, +30% YoY), non-GAAP EPS $1.82; September-quarter guide $8.1B (+>20% QoQ). DRAM = 23% of systems revenue. DRAM technology drivers: leveraging foundry-logic capabilities into DRAM PITCH SCALING — VECTOR hard-mask and diffusion-barrier tools 'critical for next-generation requirements'; Argos surface-treatment expanding into a growing set of DRAM applications; Equipment Intelligence / Dextro self-maintaining-tool solutions now expanding from NAND INTO DRAM. Optical Engine small-volume production from end-2026 (OBO, OSFP); CPO switch shipments from H2 2027; AI-chip integration ~2028; TSV-based DDR-5 DRAM volume production from Q4 2026

Tier-1 US hyperscaler NEXT-GEN HBM IP design win (license; proliferates with the architecture); PCIe7 license revenue near-term; CXMT licensed

On NAND supply: 'we still able to get supply, but unfortunately supply not enough to what we need... We have supply, but supply still not enough what we need.' Phison met every NAND supplier at FMS last week and pitched that its purchases feed its own AI data-platform systems, not just module resale; it will not disclose how many LTAs it holds so competitors cannot ask for the same amounts. CEO expects the NAND shortage to continue into next year and beyond ('many year'); a top NAND-maker executive told him a new fab takes 4 years from investment to production, not 2. Downgrade-grade NAND supply is also shrinking structurally: 3D NAND yields now run 90-plus percent, with some wafers at 95% good die, so the cheap downgrade bin that used to feed consumer products is disappearing.
new NAND fab: 4 years investment-to-production; 3D NAND yields 90%+ (some wafers 95%)

NAND pricing/margin view: back in March the CEO said NAND makers' gross margin reaching a floor of 80% was easy and 85% might happen; now he says 90% gross margin may happen in 2026, but warns that is unhealthy for the industry ('if you ask component for 90% gross margin, industry potentially will be killed - you can see the IoT, you can see the consumer die'). Demand is too strong, so price will keep rising but at a decelerating rate toward saturation, at which point suppliers start choosing whom to ship. On demand structure: systems have cut DRAM content ('a lot of systems, they cut half of the DRAM') but nobody cuts storage - inference needs storage, 'storage is money' - and aiDAPTIV uses flash to complement DRAM.
NAND-maker gross margin: 80% floor easy, 85% may happen, 90% possible in 2026 (CEO view)

6 new AI-networking design wins; 2 new neocloud design wins

For AI-on-device, Phison partners with Intel and MediaTek (versus AMD working with Longsys): a POC with MediaTek uses Phison's UFS4 controller to cut a phone's required LPDDR5 from 24GB to 12GB while keeping AI-model performance, targeted at the market next year. utilization: advanced logic mid-80%, mainstream logic low 80%, DRAM high 80%, NAND low 80%

CEO view on hybrid-bonding adoption: hybrid bonding has become a critical enabler of next-generation chip architectures (density, performance, thermal management). AMD started shipping hybrid-bonded logic devices in 2022; Apple, Intel and Broadcom all have products ramping into production using hybrid bonding. He believes hybrid bonding will be a requirement in HBM with 20 or more layers, if not sooner, and in NAND as layer counts approach 400, with the big three memory players all ramping to get there. Leading foundries, memory companies and OSATs are planning to spend approximately $125 billion in the near term on advanced packaging including hybrid bonding — 'we know broad adoption of hybrid bonding is coming because the capital equipment required is being ordered.' Hyperscalers 'are semiconductor companies now', differentiating with their own chips, which he expects to create additional opportunity. He puts the semiconductor market at over $1.5 trillion this year.
HBM with 20 or more layers; NAND approaching 400 layers; ~$125 billion near-term advanced-packaging spend; semiconductor market over $1.5 trillion
CEO: 3D NAND leader SanDisk is an Adeia customer and began using hybrid bonding for NAND in 2023.
CEO: 3D NAND leader Kioxia is an Adeia customer and began using hybrid bonding for NAND in 2023.

Magnetic sales JPY 81.6 billion +49.6%; HDD head shipments +36%, suspensions +31% YoY on AI data center demand

Product momentum in FY2027: coater developer (share of more than 90% across EUV to immersion lithography) won PORs in multiple processes in advanced logic and DRAM with the new Resive Pro Dice; full-year etch system sales of JPY 1 trillion are coming within reach; cryogenic etch systems for 400-layer NAND start deploying in customers' mass production lines from calendar 2027; a POR was won for a new low resistance metal deposition system in a new application area. In advanced packaging, prober sales show outstanding growth with full-year sales likely to go significantly beyond JPY 100 billion, and the Prexa SDP device prober for advanced logic launched in April; bonder/debonder and 3D-IC are growth areas combining leading-edge front-end and bonding technology.

Coater developer share more than 90%; etch sales JPY 1 trillion full-year within reach; DRAM interconnect etch five-year cumulative sales near JPY 1 trillion vs JPY 500 billion original guidance; prober sales significantly beyond JPY 100 billion; cryogenic etch for 400 layers in mass production from calendar 2027

AI data center applications drive the WFE market: sales to AI data center are expected to grow by five times or more in the five years from calendar 2023 through calendar 2027, spanning not only GPU and HBM but also DDR, CPU and 3D NAND. Technology transitions expected within two years: logic scaling from the 3 nanometer mainstream toward 2 nanometer with backside PDN adoption, DRAM evolving to the 1D node (1C to 1D transition), HBM stacked DRAM count rising from 12 to 16, and NAND evolving to 300 layers and further to 400 layers. Agentic AI is the driver of the overall WFE market; CY2026 WFE application mix is about 60% logic and 40% memory, versus 65%/35% last year.
AI data center WFE sales to grow five times or more CY2023-CY2027; HBM stacks from 12 to 16; NAND to 300 then 400 layers; logic mainstream 3 nanometer moving to 2 nanometer

CALL — TRAINIUM MERCHANT-SILICON DOOR OPENS; OWN FRONTIER MODEL: 'An increasing number of customers are interested in us providing the Trainium chips to them, SEPARATE FROM OUR CLOUD, and we're actively having those conversations... I expect there's a REAL CHANCE we'll do that in the future' (Jassy). Trainium adopter list broadened beyond the Anthropic + OpenAI multi-year multi-gigawatt anchors: unicorns Neurorobotics and Odyssey join Twelve Labs, Descartes Labs, Poolside AI, Karakuri, Metagenomi, NetoAI and Splash Music, plus Uber and Pinterest. Amazon IS pursuing its OWN FRONTIER MODEL — for cost control, training-priority control and speed — while keeping Bedrock model-agnostic: 'within the next few years you're going to have at least a half dozen models comparably good to each other... one of them will be ours.' Amazon Leo: ~400 satellites in orbit, initial internet service THIS YEAR with 'meaningful revenue commitments' from enterprises/governments. Memory/HDD/SSD inflation: existing contracts keep agreed prices for their duration; NEW deals price in current component costs.
Trainium sales OUTSIDE the cloud 'a real chance'; own frontier model coming ('one of the half dozen will be ours'); Kiro 3x QoQ

CALL — HBM PROCESS-CONTROL INTENSITY 'RIVALS ADVANCED LOGIC': CFO Bren Higgins said HBM is 'a unique animal' for KLA — base-die CUSTOMIZATION, the integration of each DRAM in the stack, the ultimate device value and tighter performance specs are driving process-control intensity levels 'RIVALING WHAT WE SEE IN ADVANCED LOGIC' across some products; conventional DRAM intensity has improved but is NOT the same as HBM. 2027 memory setup: DRAM investment broad across conventional AND HBM with GREENFIELD FABS (whole new toolsets, not just upgrades) — 'given where prices are and how that translates into margins, the VALUE OF YIELD is pretty high,' plus rising EUV adoption in DRAM; even NAND gets some greenfield. Mix: September quarter memory = 27% of semi-PC systems (DRAM 90% / NAND 10%); memory share RISES in the December quarter and stays elevated through H1 2027. HBM PC intensity rivals advanced logic; DRAM greenfield + EUV in 2027; memory GM headwind ~100bps+ through 2027 then tailwind

Macronix says eMMC for automotive will be shipped in 2027; the automotive sector continues to maintain stable demand, and high-density NOR for automotive is shifting toward SLC NAND.

Memory market: AI servers keep driving HBM demand and high-end memory packaging demand stays very strong; DRAM and NAND market demand and prices are rising together, with customers maximising output of committed capacity - customer revenue gains are mostly price-driven as supply is limited, but PTI's packaging volumes are still growing and utilisation keeps improving. Packaging material costs keep rising and PTI is passing them through to customers gradually (its customers are large long-term partners, so price adjustments are made carefully each quarter). AI-server eSSD demand keeps rising with shipments expanding QoQ and YoY.

WFE is expected to grow about 20% in calendar 2026 and a similar level in calendar 2027. Updated CY2026 growth by application: advanced logic foundry over 20%, DRAM over 25% (raised), NAND about 20% (raised from a bit less than 15%), power devices a bit less than 10%. Foundry AI-driven leading edge investment is the primary WFE driver; advanced DRAM and HBM are in shortage and even existing DDR is in shortage, so CapEx is going into both HBM and general DDR, with strong NAND investment also expected as data center demand recovers. Memory device makers are asking for accelerated delivery - demand is now stronger than SCREEN's current capacity. Average equipment lead time is about 4.2 months. Chinese demand for advanced AI-related tools is at record-high inquiry levels.
WFE about 20% growth in calendar 2026 and 2027; DRAM over 25%, NAND about 20%, advanced logic foundry over 20%; lead time 4.2 months; demand stronger than capacity

CALL-ONLY / DEMAND-SIDE READ ON THE MEMORY SHORTAGE: at the OSAT level the DRAM squeeze is now measurable in handset volumes - Amkor's ANDROID revenue fell 20% SEQUENTIALLY 'reflecting the impact of MEMORY SUPPLY DYNAMICS', and Q3 communications is guided down high-single-digits sequentially (against normal seasonality) partly on 'ongoing MEMORY SUPPLY CONSTRAINTS', with memory PRICING also expected to weigh on phone unit volumes this year. Android -20% QoQ on memory supply; Vietnam adding SiP + NAND memory capacity

Arizona Phase I FULLY COMMITTED; capex $2.5-3.0B (65-70% facilities); Gwangju cleanroom for 2028+

Cloud & AI segment revenue $7.7B (+23%); traditional server orders grew triple-digits on agentic-AI inferencing; DRAM/NAND inflation + supply constraints lifting server ASPs (working with silicon/memory partners on long-term supply).

Sequential revenue +15% reflects higher server ASPs from DRAM/NAND inflationary costs; networking products constrained by DDR4/DDR5 and wafer capacity ('supply chain is the name of the game in networking' — purchase commitments +40% sequentially). FY2026 guide assumes NO incremental supply; component costs expected elevated into 2027 until new fabs yield. FY2027 framework: revenue +8-12% with AI-systems revenue accelerating.
DRAM/NAND-driven ASPs; no incremental 2026 supply; FY27 +8-12%

Data-center optics ramp: on the receiver side both 100G and 200G products are in mass production and shipping, with 100G (i.e. 800G transceivers) the mainstay this year and 1.6T expected to be a breakout next year. On the transmit side, 400G lasers entered mass production in Q2 2026 (first design win back in March 2023), with volumes expected to multiply next year, and CW laser customers have been in mass production since Q4 2024. New applications: solar-cell substrates for drones and low-earth-orbit satellites (including radiation-resistant flexible solar panels, with an LEO satellite project this year), and VCSELs used as the heating source in HAMR HDDs - in development for two years, with a meaningful contribution expected next year and the year after.

receiver-side 100G and 200G in mass production; 800G the mainstay this year with a 1.6T breakout expected next year; transmit-side 400G in mass production from Q2; CW lasers in production since Q4 2024

1.6T test w/ 20+ leaders at OFC; first UEC interop demo w/ Broadcom; 3.2T R&D rising

Portfolio extensions: 6-SIDE INSPECTION (pre/post-TC-bond HBM yield control), world-first two-in-one BOC+COB bonder (stacked GDDR, enterprise eSSD), entry into 2.5D PACKAGING (TC/FC/die bonders for interposer integration of HBM + base die + CPU/GPU), MSVP 8.0 saw/vision placement (world #1 since mid-2000s, boosted by larger PLP/chiplet panels), EMI Shield 2.0 X (#1 share). WIDE TC bonder launch imminent (hybrid-bonder delay = TC extension); 2.5D packaging entry; Micron now a disclosed customer

Cube Prober = per-stack HBM full-inspection; probe-station localization vs TEL

Memory: Aehr achieved the correlation a key memory supplier asked for and is discussing system specs for its next-generation flash and high bandwidth flash; it hopes to close in the next few months on a development agreement, followed by a 12- to 18-month development of memory-optimized blades for FOX-XP/NP. 12- to 18-month development; orders possible in fiscal '27, ramps in fiscal '28

3D NAND: ACM's proprietary N2 bubbling wet etch is positioned for 3D NAND silicon nitride etching, where larger bubble size and uniformity control become more critical at 300 layer and above; the CEO said it covers today's 300-layer demand and addresses uniformity issues as the industry moves to 400 or even 500 layer, with demand seen both in China and globally.
300 layer and above; 400 or even 500 layer

Data storage fully booked for 2026; slider fab orders for 2027 shipment

Technology drivers (CEO): industry projections suggest semiconductors could reach $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2027, possibly earlier. Leading-edge fabs are deploying new materials like molybdenum and new structures such as gate-all-around and high-bandwidth memory, raising deposition/etch capex intensity. UCT expects strength around etch and deposition, especially ALD and high-precision etch, to support gate-all-around and backside power distribution logic transitions as well as high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging and greater than 300-layer NAND. A multiyear WFE upturn should follow once wafer fabs address their near-term clean room constraints.
semiconductor market $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2027 (industry projection); greater than 300-layer NAND

Memory cycle (CEO): some of UCT's customers' customers say the shortage will last until 2028; Micron, Samsung and SK are investing in greenfield fabs while converting existing fabs to address immediate demand, a multiyear upturn for memory. HBM will compromise the nameplate capacity in DRAM factories, so more WFE investment is needed to compensate while makers still address the unbalanced supply and demand in regular DRAM. NAND upgrades from 2xx to 3xx and 4xx layers continue; the CEO cited Lam's talk of $40 billion over multiple years of NAND upgrade investment, and said customers see a 22% CAGR for AI-specific memory (2 to 3x the regular memory market).
memory shortage until 2028 (per customers' customers); $40 billion multiyear NAND upgrade (Lam, as cited by the CEO); AI-specific memory 22% CAGR (per customers)

Q4 2025 segments: Materials Solutions sales were $362 million, flat year over year and up 4% sequentially. Advanced deposition materials drove most of the sequential growth, helped by demand for moly deposition in NAND. The segment's adjusted operating margin was 20.9%. Advanced Purity Solutions sales were $465 million, down 5% year over year and up 1% sequentially. Fluid Handling and FOUPs drove the year-over-year decline, partly offset by strong growth in liquid filtration, which had another record quarter. The APS adjusted operating margin was 24.8%. The CFO said the year-over-year margin decline came from costs related to ramping the Taiwan and Colorado manufacturing sites and lower production volumes, and the sequential decrease from unfavorable product mix and the timing of operating expenses.

Materials Solutions $362 million (flat YoY, up 4% sequentially), adjusted operating margin 20.9%; Advanced Purity Solutions $465 million (down 5% YoY, up 1% sequentially), adjusted operating margin 24.8%

NAND: the move from roughly 250 layers to approximately 300 layers is under way. Management expects more than 20% NAND bit growth in 2026, driven mainly by higher-layer, higher-capacity NAND rather than a big increase in wafer starts. Entegris expects a double-digit increase in its NAND content per wafer as customers move to higher layer counts and adopt new materials such as moly and selective etch. It has won strong POR positions in NAND deposition materials, CMP and selective etch. NAND utilization is around 85%, and layer-count increases are absorbing most of the remaining 15% of capacity, with fewer new wafer starts. If demand stays strong, flash makers will likely need to add significant fab capacity, setting up higher NAND MSI growth in 2027. The CEO said Entegris gains from both layer growth and wafer growth, with slightly more from a full wafer start.
more than 20% NAND bit growth expected in 2026; double-digit increase in NAND content per wafer; NAND utilization around 85%

1.5 port to one XPU OCS attach rate; $8 billion OCS TAM seen with upside; 576 XPUs in a cluster; late 2028, early 2029 timeframe

64x64 OCS sample developed; 128x128 OCS in early development

He noted OCS demand is not only from module vendors: 'there's also some hyperscalers who do it directly'. The driver is power - 'there's not enough power in the world to power all these data centers' - pushing architectures from electrical to optical. Because the cost of one bad port pair is a bad switch, customers 'test everything to the nth degree', and for a '100 terabit switch, I don't think anybody's going to skip any tests'.

K&S made a notable structural claim about wire bonding in AI infrastructure: it estimates the DATA CENTER MARKET RELIES ON WIRE BONDING TECHNOLOGY AT LEAST AS MUCH AS, IF NOT MORE THAN, traditional semiconductor markets such as smartphones and PCs, because the majority of data center chips are still traditionally wire bonded - general infrastructure, networking, communication, power management and storage. Ball bonding is the more prevalent technology for data center power management, while wedge bonding remains more focused on automotive and high-current applications. Data center expansion therefore drives demand for BOTH the thermocompression and the wire bonding lines.

SCOPE OF THE RECORD DATA-CENTER ORDER DISCLOSED: CFO Michael Metcalf says the $400 million-plus order booked in fiscal Q3 was 'the entire outside electrical kit for a two gigawatt phase one data center' and that Powell 'won 100% of the outside' - unusual, because 'Usually, they'll split it up. CAPACITY IS BEING ADDED AND MORE IS QUEUED: Powell is 'just finishing up a 335,000 square foot expansion at our fabrication yard that'll give us the ability to lay down 10 to 12 additional substations to work on per year', with 'Each substation is $10 million to $15 million' - that yard is bespoke for large one-piece buildings for core industrial (LNG, refineries). DATA-CENTER VOLTAGE STEP-UP IN ONE YEAR - CONTENT MIX MOVING TO POWELL'S HIGH END: 'If I was sitting here last year talking specifically about data centers, it was 5,000 and 15,000 volt. Now it's 38,000 volt. They need more power.' 38,000 volts is the top of Powell's medium-voltage range ('that's where we stop') and Metcalf says 'We can't build it fast enough.' He adds 'I think the power equation hasn't yet been solved ... these things need so much power, and there's not enough power to feed all of them.' Powell remains outside the data center only ('we do not do anything on the inside'), supplying switchgear inside power control rooms / e-houses that step power into the site. On cycle length, management's working assumption is three to five years of this demand with no let-up visible today, and revamps of today's data centers in about five years are viewed as a future services opportunity.
data-center orders moved from 5,000 and 15,000 volt last year to 38,000 volt today

NEW ROUTE TO MARKET - NEOSCALERS: 'we booked a large order last quarter with a neoscaler, a new term to us'. Powell initially worked with the hyperscalers and the colos, but 'the terms and conditions on some of these hyperscaler colo operations are really tough', so it now goes direct with neoscalers and predominantly through distribution with hyperscalers and colos. Metcalf describes neoscalers as real-estate-origin operators who build out infrastructure and lease it back to a Google or a Microsoft, and says they are easier to contract with; the hyperscaler terms Powell refuses include consequential damages of 'millions and millions of dollars' for five minutes of downtime caused by its equipment, terms 'you'd never see ... in a utility contract'. Powell also notes the data-center customers found Powell after COVID when Schneider, ABB and Eaton ran out of capacity.

CEO Abinand Rangesh: Tecogen's data-center strategy has shifted from smaller data centers toward hyperscale and big brand developers. Specific projects and delivery dates were discussed, and the company is beginning to build inventory of its dual power source chiller and power gen modules to cut lead times. CEO Abinand Rangesh on Vertiv: the data-center demonstrations were arranged through Tecogen's own sales and marketing, a path parallel to its Vertiv relationship ('there are places where it may make sense to collaborate'). CEO Abinand Rangesh on the product case: the dual power source chiller is closed loop (no water evaporation), runs in noise-sensitive urban settings, has very low NOx and carbon monoxide emissions, can move cooling load to natural gas when a utility asks large loads to drop load (avoiding diesel generator use) and can keep cooling during a power outage. He sees demand in new builds, phases of campus expansions, existing cloud data centers that are running out of power (often adding Tecogen chillers while keeping the electric chiller as backup) and smaller data centers using it as primary cooling; InVerde modules can shed some standby loads at peak times.

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. A RARE DOWNWARD REVISION TO A DATA-CENTER PIPELINE — AND WHY IT MATTERS: Exelon's data-center growth pipeline now shows a combined 36 GIGAWATTS, DOWN ROUGHLY 11 GW FROM THE 43 GW previously cited. CFO Jeanne Jones attributes the cut not to demand weakness but to Exelon's own screening discipline: it developed TRANSMISSION SECURITY AGREEMENTS (TSAs) that 'never existed in our regions', and its cluster process now requires a customer to sign a TSA and, importantly, 'PUT UP COLLATERAL BEHIND THAT'. The result: 'what this update reflects is we have now WEEDED OUT SPECULATIVE PROJECTS, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real.' Exelon says it has deliberately kept capex increases consistent with historical levels and only committed capital that was 'certain and durable', alongside its stance on CO-LOCATION and fair cost allocation to shield existing customers from infrastructure costs. This is a useful reality-check datapoint on how much of the headline AI interconnection queue is firm versus speculative.
Data-centre pipeline cut 43 GW -> 36 GW after TSA + COLLATERAL requirements weeded out speculative projects

VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.

Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.
Technology = 15% to 20% of the business; Quanta can self-perform 80% to 90% of a data-center build

WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

CONTRACTED AI/DATA-CENTER LOAD CROSSES 17 GW. Four large-load projects were signed in the quarter alone: three projects in Alabama where Alabama Power added approximately 3 GW, plus a Georgia Power 3.2 GW, 25-year electric service contract with OpenAI at its newly announced site near Savannah, Georgia. Combined, those four projects represent 6 GW of newly contracted customer load, and together with agreements previously signed they bring total contracted large load agreements across Southern's electric subsidiaries to over 17 GW by the mid-2030s. CEO Christopher Womack framed the vertically integrated, state-regulated model (one-stop shop across generation, transmission and distribution) as the differentiator winning hyperscaler and data-center developer business in the Southeast.
6 GW newly contracted in Q2 (Alabama ~3 GW + Georgia Power/OpenAI 3.2 GW); total contracted large load over 17 GW by mid-2030s

Beyond the 17 GW already contracted there are an additional 8 GW of projects in late stages, including 3 GW projected to be finalized in the near term; CFO David Poroch said those contracts are likely to go into 2028 and beyond, with a couple of them initiating their ramp-up in 2028 and running into the next decade. DATA-CENTER LOAD ACTUALLY ON THE SYSTEM IS COMPOUNDING FAST. System-wide data-center load now exceeds 1.2 GW, an increase of more than 500 megawatts over the prior year, and Poroch noted the company 'crossed over the 1,000 MW line this particular quarter.' Data-center usage was 55% higher than Q2 2025 and is up 49% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from large-load customers. That pulled weather-normal commercial sales up 7.4% in Q2 (+6% year to date) and total weather-normal retail electricity sales up 2.3% in the first half - the highest retail sales growth through June in nearly two decades. Q2 adjusted EPS was $1.13, up $0.21 versus Q2 2025 and $0.13 above the company's own estimate; first-half adjusted EPS was $2.46.

GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.

HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.
About $21 billion of collateral in aggregate at full ramp across the 17 GW contracted portfolio; minimum bills cover 100% of incremental cost to serve

FIRST FLEXIBLE-DEMAND DATA CENTER: 1 GW OF DEMAND RESPONSE AT THE OPENAI SITE. The Savannah site features 1 GW of flexible demand response, and Womack confirmed this is the first time Southern has done that for a data center. Poroch said demand-response flexibility 'does enter into all those conversations' and is possible because the three electric jurisdictions are not limited to a tariff and can negotiate bilateral contracts that price hyperscaler flexibility. Womack said technical requirements - how a hyperscaler's operations affect the system and the grid, and whether it can be more than 'just a taker' - are raised very early in every hyperscaler conversation, and that peak shaving from this resource benefits the whole system.
1 GW of flexible demand response at the OpenAI Savannah site - Southern's first for a data center

NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'

SOUTHERN POWER TOLLING AGREEMENTS ROLLING OFF ARE BEING RE-AIMED AT HYPERSCALERS. As existing tolling agreements expire, Womack said the team is in the midst of recontracting conversations with a host of counterparties, screened for creditworthiness, and sees upside in pricing versus where the contracts were originally struck - contributing to the durability and length of the long-term plan. Poroch added that conversations with both current and new Southern Power counterparties are 'proving to be very fruitful', covering repricing of expiring contracts into the next decade plus the previously announced uprate/brownfield opportunities, with an update expected later in the year; the business will not 'build something and see who shows up.'

Applied Digital says its standardized AI factory design lets it consolidate purchasing around a common set of qualified partners - including ABB for electrical equipment, BASX for mechanical and cooling systems, and Caterpillar for backup generation - and place bulk orders against a multi-gigawatt development pipeline; with prefabricated skids, modular construction and early procurement of long-lead equipment this supports build cycles of approximately 12 to 18 months per 100 to 150 MW facility.
build cycles of approximately 12 to 18 months per 100 to 150 MW facility

2H26 outlook: IT (consumer) product revenue expected lower than 1H on notebook price increases and memory shortages; non-IT products see strong BBU (backup battery module) demand driven by AI data-center construction; 2H26 revenue expected to grow double digits over 1H, and non-IT is expected to exceed 50% of full-year revenue
2H26 revenue double-digit growth over 1H; non-IT >50% of 2026 revenue
