Data center revenue will land in the HIGH TEENS AS A PERCENTAGE OF REVENUE for fiscal 2026 and is growing much faster than the rest of the portfolio - very healthy double digits, higher in some subsegments. Over the next THREE TO FIVE YEARS management expects data centers to become ONE THIRD OF THE COMPANY by revenue, and describes the mix as extremely accretive to the enterprise. As the installed base expands on double-digit systems growth, service attachment rates should improve and generate strong service growth, fuelling the data center mix profitably. CEO Joakim Weidemanis framed the era directly: 'this is the age of thermal management.'
Data center ~high teens % of FY2026 revenue, expected to reach one third of company revenue in three to five years

Johnson Controls introduced an AI FACTORY ABSORPTION CHILLER REFERENCE DESIGN GUIDE, which it says demonstrates how advanced thermal management can REDUCE COOLING ELECTRICAL DEMAND BY APPROXIMATELY 44% by converting waste heat into productive cooling. Because those savings free power for compute without increasing on-site generation, management claims the potential for BILLIONS OF DOLLARS OF ADDITIONAL REVENUE OVER THE LIFE OF A 1 GIGAWATT FACILITY for the customer. The approach builds on more than 65 years of YORK absorption innovation. Management noted thermal management can represent ABOUT A THIRD OF POWER in a data center, so multiple percentage points of thermal efficiency are very meaningful - and that what JCI is working on 'goes well beyond a couple of percentage points.' Efficiency now matters more because power availability constrains where data centers can be sited.
Absorption chiller reference design cuts cooling electrical demand by ~44%; thermal management is ~1/3 of data center power

The CDU (coolant distribution unit) business reaches revenue: Johnson Controls WILL START SHIPPING CDUs THIS QUARTER, with most testing and validation complete and some hyperscaler validation still in progress, and it has RECENTLY RECEIVED NVIDIA CERTIFICATION. The CDU pipeline is 'well beyond the hundreds of millions and has now reached $1 BILLION,' built on JCI's Alloy investment plus pilots and early orders. Management frames CDUs as expanding total addressable market per megawatt within a broader thermal management solution set.
CDU shipments start this quarter; CDU pipeline reached $1B; NVIDIA certification received

On the chiller-versus-liquid-cooling debate, management pushed back directly: as rack densities increase and new chips are used, the heat generated in data centers keeps rising and thermal management becomes more critical, so speculation about reduced demand for chillers is 'a very nominal impact if any.' Air handling demand continues with the Silent-Aire franchise increasing, CDUs become more important as liquid cooling is implemented, and controls matter as well. The strategy is explicitly to keep increasing DOLLARS PER MEGAWATT across the whole thermal management chain - including the Armada modular container, which is 'loaded with everything we make.'

Capacity and supply chain: Johnson Controls says it is more vertically integrated than others in its industry, controlling the manufacturing and cost of goods of all FIVE SUBSYSTEMS that make up an HVAC chiller, which gives it more control of its own supply chain; bottlenecks occur occasionally in a high-growth environment. Meaningful physical plant investments made about two years ago are ramping slightly AHEAD of expectations. At the Airside Center of Excellence, applying the business system MORE THAN QUADRUPLED CAPACITY on the computer room air handler line WITHOUT SIGNIFICANT CAPITAL INVESTMENT, while achieving 100% on-time delivery, halving customer lead times, shrinking manufacturing floor space by more than 30% and cutting inventory by 50%. Management expects to need some new physical capacity at this growth rate but believes the business system buys time to ramp it. JCI operates approximately 40 manufacturing facilities worldwide.
Computer room air handler line capacity more than quadrupled without significant capital investment; lead times halved; inventory cut 50%

Edge and modular: Johnson Controls collaborates with and holds an investment in ARMADA, building modular solutions described as 'data centers in a shipping container' in JCI factories and including everything Johnson Controls makes. Management believes not all future data centers will be mega sites like 1 gigawatt facilities and expects decentralized, close-to-the-edge deployments to keep growing; the TAM is described as significant but still in formation, with more detail promised over the next couple of quarters. Balance sheet: approximately $600 million of cash on hand, net debt down to 1.9x - below the long-term target range - and year-to-date adjusted free cash flow of $2.1 billion. Fire and Security revenue was flat against a flat underlying global market, with management targeting mid-to-high single-digit growth there over time.
~$600M cash; net debt 1.9x (below target range); year-to-date adjusted FCF $2.1B

high-voltage data center architectures expected probably in 2027 and beyond; very low volume proof-of-concept shipments today

data center design wins more than doubled YoY; high-voltage content two to four times low-voltage; 25% to 30% data center CAGR over five years

BlackRock 1GW El Paso JV; compute offers at 'significant premium'; demand-constrained incl core; maximize 26/27 capacity; FCF $784M

CALL — BUILD RATE, THE $175B CY2026 NUMBER, AND RPO QUALITY: Microsoft added 31 NEW DATA CENTERS this quarter (88 in the fiscal year) across five continents, added ANOTHER GIGAWATT of capacity, cut GPU dock-to-live times ~50% over the year, and remains on track to ROUGHLY DOUBLE overall capacity in two years. Azure FQ1 guide ~+45% cc with H1 growth ACCELERATING. Also disclosed: a $3.2 BILLION GAIN ON MICROSOFT'S ANTHROPIC INVESTMENT.
31 DCs in qtr / 88 in FY; +1 GW; CY2026 capex ~$175B (lease-adjusted, DC life 15->25yr); FQ1 capex >$50B; RPO +25% ex-OpenAI; Azure FQ1 ~+45%

AI represented about 16% of total revenue in Q2, up roughly another point QoQ (management cautions AI revenue measurement requires assumptions and keeps refining the model). AI ~16% of Q2 revenue; computing/enterprise share 24.9% -> 27.3%; mix ~80% premium / 20% commodity

Capacity is tight: Q3 utilization rates will be raised above 90% for BOTH commodity and specialty (from about 85% blended / 80% commodity in Q2) to meet demand and rebuild healthy inventory. Capacity is being expanded across the board - Kaohsiung (the large purpose-built MLCC fab, running tight), Vietnam, Suzhou and Mexico - led by tantalum and MLCC; only less than NT$3 billion of capex was spent in H1 with larger increments planned for H2, and equipment lead times are long so expansion is planned ahead, adding capacity quarter by quarter. Q3 utilization >90% (commodity and specialty), up from ~85%/80%; H1 capex <NT$3B; Greater China channel ~2 months on hand

Management endorsed as 'a fair characterization' the view that high-capacitance MLCC demand ramping alongside next-generation AI servers will force conversion of mid/low-end capacity and put shortage pressure on the rest of the portfolio - part of its customer conversations already cover securing that non-AI piece too, with peers also raising MLCC utilization. Adjacent driver: the whole AI power chain 'from the grid down to the rack of the server' has many voltage step-down/conversion stages needing filtering and ripple-current management, driving strong growth in film capacitors and aluminum electrolytic capacitors plus the magnetics (inductors) and connector lines - embedded across computing, industrial and telecom segments. In notebooks, new tantalum packaging offering higher capacitance in a smaller package positions a laptop recovery as more of a 2027 story.

data center orders up 4x YoY; total orders +40%; backlog over $8 billion (+40% YoY, +20% QoQ), 40% of Commercial backlog is data centers

2026 data center sales ~$2 billion (prior $1.5 billion); 1H $500 million / 2H $1.5 billion; 2026 sales ~$23 billion, adj. EPS ~$2.90

data center exit run-rate ~$2.5 billion; Charlotte capacity +50%

new U.S. site online by end of Q1 2027; 2026 CapEx ~$600 million (+$100 million for the site)

1.3 MW CDU shipping; 2.5 MW / 2.6 MW CDU launching in Q3; 5 MW CDU around end of 2026

share ~10% moving to 15%-20%; CSA Commercial margins mid to high teens

Semiconductor Solutions organic +31%; wafer plating and power electronics volume +high teens

no specific figure (capacity by YE2027 raised materially)

data center sales +65% in Q2; ~50% data center growth expected for full-year 2026; Electrical Solutions sales $686M (+25%)

Utility Solutions net sales $1.026B (+10%); grid infrastructure +7% organic; H1 Utility book-to-bill ~1.2x

High-voltage transmission for data-center interconnections: 'We see it where load growth and data centers are going in. That's where the request for interconnections are the highest. Transmission/substation project quotes have about doubled in the last couple of years; the $1.5 billion opportunity over 10 years is worth about a point of additional growth over the next several years.
$1.5B high-voltage transmission opportunity over 10 years; first 765 kV shipments in 2027; 550 kV shipping in H2 2026

2026 CapEx $175M-$190M (vs $155M in 2025); ~$25M of new capacity brought online per quarter; CapEx 2.5%-3% of sales

Product content for higher-capacity data centers: 'We're adapting some of our products for those applications ... our new Pin & Sleeve devices that are going to higher amperage to the 800 volt infrastructure.' new Pin & Sleeve devices for 800 V data-center infrastructure

400V/800V HVDC power transition; AI data-center growth >50%

data-center demand above >50% outlook and constrained by supply

isolation solutions for 800-volt HVDC power architectures added to the AI data-center design win pipeline

CEO: heat exchangers delivered their best quarter ever, with particularly strong demand tied to liquid cooling for data centers; Dover is actively working to double capacity for these products over the next 12 months, coming on sequentially over 2H 2026 into 2027; Q2 growth would have been higher with that capacity. short cycle 61% / long cycle 39% of revenue

T&D capacity +~100% vs 2023-2024; Betim +10-15% mid-2026 (25% of announced capacity); remaining 75% beginning of next year (Mexico, Colombia)

Data centers (Salgueiro): WEG's data-center exposure is mainly Marathon alternators for energy backup, transformers used in the connection of data centers or grids, and growing demand for pumps and ventilation for cooling refrigeration systems; WEG does not sell directly to data centers but sees very positive demand. → Liberty Energy: Liberty's 10-Q: during the three months ended June 30, 2026 Liberty entered into supply contracts with various global suppliers, including Bergen Engines AS and Wärtsilä North America, Inc., for the purchase of power generation equipment, including engines and certain balance of plant equipment, for its prospective data center and other distributed power projects.

data center doubled YoY; 800 volts to 48 volts to 12 volts conversion stages

Record order book of SEK 53.5 billion — SEK 29.1 billion currently planned for 2026 delivery and SEK 24.5 billion already booked for 2027 — supporting continued invoicing growth, assessed in line with current input cost levels. PhotonLink formally launched at ECOC (pre-announced on the August earnings call). CMO Sanjai Parthasarathi introduced it as 'our integrated optics platform, purpose-built for AI data center connectivity', and CEO Jim Anderson set out its scope and rationale: it is a single integrated platform that is 'architecture agnostic, that works across CPO, NPO, chip-to-chip as well', and it exists because a number of customers 'came to us and asked' for 'the complete optical solution, the complete assembly' rather than components, since pulling together laser sources, fiber optic cable, complex optical assemblies and passive optics is the hard part of moving to optics. Anderson framed the transition it targets: telecom, scale-across and scale-out networks were long ago converted from electrical to optical, and over the coming years 'the only remaining electrical portions of the network' - the scale-up network and even chip-to-chip links - will become photonic. His end-to-end example for a switch or compute chip fed by an external laser source: Coherent supplies the complete ELS, the complete optical assembly from the ELS to the chip, and the complete optical assembly back out to the faceplate for photonic I/O. He argued only Coherent has the whole generate/shape/guide/detect technology set in-house, and cited 'hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies' delivered as evidence it can ramp at data-center scale.
architecture agnostic across CPO, NPO and chip-to-chip; hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies delivered

EVP Beck Mason previewed the high-density 2D VCSEL for NPO (the 'ultra-dense VCSEL arrays' of his summary), which Coherent was demonstrating in its booth on the ECOC floor: the VCSELs are so tightly spaced that the whole array couples into a single multi-core fiber. Coherent makes 'fibers with up to 37 separate cores' and has 'a VCSEL array and a PD array with 37 elements', flip-chipped with backside lenses - 'the most dense solution we have out there', giving very high capacity in a single fiber. It suits both PAM4 and NRZ ('slow and wide' as well as 'fairly fast and narrow'). 'These will be in production in the second half of calendar 2027.'

The technology reaches 30 meters, extending Credo from a 7-meter AEC reach to 30 meters 'with an equal level of reliability and power efficiency,' and the cable is 75% SMALLER BY TOTAL VOLUME than today's bulky 7-meter AECs at 200G per lane. THREE-TIER DEAL MODEL made explicit. (1) MID-TERM core AI cloud contracts of one to three years — four landmark deals closed in Q2 with REFLECTION, COHERE, an unnamed scale U.S. Neolab and a large U.S.-based quant trading firm, averaging MORE THAN $1B EACH at a yield of $20-25M PER MEGAWATT, upfront payments covering 50-60% of associated capex and payback under two years. → AMD: Commercial partnership with AMD for up to 2.5 GW of data center capacity. The initial agreement represents more than $14 billion of base contracted revenue across 15-year agreements with 2.5% annual escalators, with Core Scientific delivering 530 MW across five sites: approximately 380 MW directly to AMD under a triple-net lease across Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee, and the remaining approximately 150 MW across Auburn and Dalton supporting an unnamed neocloud under a modified gross lease for which AMD provides full credit support for the full 15-year term. The credit support carries no equity step-in rights, protecting Core Scientific's equity in the projects. Core Scientific issued AMD a warrant struck at current market levels, vesting subject to certain commercial conditions. The platform is an integrated colocation platform engineered to support AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with a close-coupled design framework aligned to AMD's GPU and CPU technology roadmap. Pecos is the lead site with initial megawatt delivery in the first half of 2027; about half the contract delivers in 2027 and half in 2028. The build requires approximately $6 billion of capital at $11 million-$12 million per megawatt, to be financed through project-level bonds. AMD additionally holds an exclusive reservation right on as much as two additional gigawatts at Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee.

Fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) for AI: chairman confirms PTI is an AMD AI-chip supply-chain partner providing fan-out PLP solutions and is actively pursuing more AMD AI-chip applications; despite equipment-delivery delays, installation issues and doing new-product qualification in parallel, the program is on schedule and PTI is confident of volume production before the middle of next year, which would make it the world's first company to mass-produce fan-out PLP for AI applications. The former-AUO fab conversion is going smoothly: floor 1 for middle-end/RDL processing, floor 2 for chip-on-panel and mounting packages onto ABF substrates; the G7 panel equipment supporting the AMD program is fully installed and in qualification, with automation being added. PTI showed an engineering sample of a 5x-reticle-size AI package (one reticle = 26x33mm) - it says only TSMC otherwise has this capability - and notes a G7 panel fits about 45 such large AI packages versus 8 to 9 on a wafer, positioning panel output as a complement to foundry wafer-based advanced packaging. FOPLP equipment lead times run about a year plus installation; management estimates a new entrant would need roughly three years from ordering to customer qualification (PTI started fan-out panel work in 2015). In high-end flip-chip BGA, PTI already mass-produces large FC-BGA/MCM and will move a large one-reticle-size chip package into volume production in Q3.
AMD fan-out PLP volume production before mid-2027 (target: world's first FOPLP for AI); 5x reticle-size panel packages, ~45 per G7 panel vs 8-9 per wafer; FOPLP equipment lead time ~1 year

Capacitor R&D (annual securities report; group R&D JPY 7,279 million, of which Capacitor JPY 2,357 million and NECST JPY 4,921 million): launched the chip-type conductive-polymer aluminum solid electrolytic capacitor 'PCY series' with a 125°C 12,000-hour guarantee (company: industry-top level) for information and communications equipment such as AI servers and telecom base stations, where higher data-processing volumes raise power consumption and internal temperatures; developed the conductive-polymer hybrid 'GYG series' with capacitance three ranks above the standard 'GYA series' and up to 1.8 times the ripple current, for high-current automotive uses such as electric power steering (EPS), electric water pumps and electric oil pumps; developed the lead-type aluminum electrolytic 'UTF series' with up to 51.1% higher allowable ripple current, for on-board chargers (OBC) in EVs and PHEVs; developed and launched the 'UBR series' (125°C 5,000-hour guarantee, 2.5 times the life of the previous series) for telecom base-station power supplies. EVP of Semiconductor Devices Beck Mason said the 'generate' part of PhotonLink rests on four light-source platforms: ultra-high-power CW lasers, high-power CW lasers, VCSEL arrays and high-density VCSEL arrays. The ultra-high-power CW laser, where Coherent has 'really strong traction from a number of customers', sits remote from the transmission inside an external laser source (ELS) that 'contains up to eight ultra-high-power CW lasers'; each laser 'can typically feed multiple links, usually around four', supplying the photons for silicon photonic modulators co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged (NPO) with the XPU or switch chip. It is designed for high output power (one laser split and shared across several links, lowering cost), high power-conversion efficiency (lower system power dissipation) and very low phase and amplitude noise (better bit error rate), and he said these lasers 'exceed all of our customer requirements'. On this platform Coherent has 'two long-term agreements signed with leading hyperscale AI data center customers for both CPO and NPO solutions'.
ELS holds up to eight ultra-high-power CW lasers, each usually feeding around four links; two long-term agreements with leading hyperscale AI data center customers for CPO and NPO

EVP Beck Mason said the second light source, a high-power buried heterostructure CW laser, serves NPO designs that embed the laser in the module, co-packaged with the silicon photonic modulator, instead of using a remote ELS. Its smaller size, lower power dissipation and high efficiency suit that role, he called it 'flexible and replaceable', and it is already a volume part: 'we are already shipping millions of units a month' because it is used widely in Coherent's pluggable data-center transceivers, with proven field reliability - 'It is production-ready now.' He added that Coherent has 'shipped over 300 million indium phosphide lasers to the field so far, and the pace of that is only ramping up'.
already shipping millions of units a month; over 300 million indium phosphide lasers shipped to the field so far

CTO Julie Eng said Coherent is introducing two products at ECOC 2026: a Mode-Matched Fiber that improves coupling efficiency to edge-coupled silicon photonics, and a detachable FAU (fiber attach unit) connector that helps with serviceability and installation.

CTO Julie Eng walked through the parts Coherent makes to couple light from the fiber into silicon photonics: microlens arrays lithographically formed in silicon (precisely uniform from one lens to the next), Prism Micro Lens Arrays that also turn the light for grating-coupled silicon photonics, and precisely V-groove-etched fiber guides that hold the fiber. It integrates these with its polarization-maintaining fiber into a fiber attach unit (FAU), and can integrate all the FAUs into a precision fiber assembly that routes and protects the fibers for ease of deployment and less fiber damage. She said all of these are either in production now, by the end of this year or early next year.
either in production now, by the end of this year or early next year

CTO Julie Eng said Coherent has an in-house silicon photonics design team, uses multiple foundries (as is common in the silicon industry) and does assembly and test in-house; it has demonstrated 200G-per-lane silicon photonics and is shipping it in production in its transceivers today. At OFC in March of this year it demonstrated a 400 gigabit link based on silicon photonics, on the show floor and in a post-deadline paper, and she said Coherent is, to her knowledge, the only one in the world to have shown that.
200G per lane silicon photonics in production; 400 gigabit silicon photonics link demonstrated at OFC

CTO Julie Eng detailed Coherent's 6.4T Silicon Photonics NPO module, shown at OFC and again at ECOC: it integrates silicon photonics modulators and photodetectors with drivers, TIAs and all the optical coupling in 32 lanes of 200G, and as a socketed NPO it delivers 15 gigabits per second per millimeter. It can be fed by a remote ELS through Coherent's FAU and precision fiber assembly or have the laser integrated into the silicon photonics NPO, and the same 6.4T silicon photonics provides the modulation and detection in Coherent's end-to-end CPO solution.

Silicon photonics and indium phosphide lasers are Veeco's clearest AI-linked growth vector, with a projected $700 million SAM by 2030 for its role in InP laser manufacturing and a stated opportunity of AT LEAST $2 BILLION over the coming years across the laser manufacturing flow - epitaxy, wet processing and laser facet coating. Announced with the results: a global leader in optical and photonics technologies selected Veeco's Lumina+ MOCVD system to fabricate indium phosphide lasers for the datacom industry; Lumina+ offers the largest batch size in the MOCVD industry, best-in-class throughput, lowest cost per wafer, and can deposit high-quality epitaxial layers on InP wafers of any size. Veeco is also a market leader in WaferEtch/WaferStorm wet processing and in the SPECTOR ion beam deposition tool used for the critical laser facet coating step, where its IBD is differentiated as the industry moves to higher-power lasers with stricter film specifications. Management framed the driver as the industry 'overcoming the copper wall,' with hyperscalers advancing EML pluggables, silicon photonics pluggables and the longer-term near-package and co-packaged optics architectures - all of which rely increasingly on InP lasers.
InP laser SAM ~$700M by 2030; total laser-manufacturing opportunity at least $2B; Lumina+ MOCVD selected by a global optical/photonics leader for datacom InP lasers

Clean room typically takes two, three or four years to put in place. capacity to produce double the amount of systems each quarter; 2,000 plus suppliers on 8-quarter forecast; clean room takes two, three or four years

Services model: early this year Applied talked about services growing in low double digits (11% or 12%), then raised the longer-term growth view to mid-teens because the installed base is growing faster than expected. This year's growth of over 20% is an unusual bump from utilization - leading-edge logic and DRAM at almost 100% utilization, NAND very high, ICAPS healthier - which drives spares and component buying and cannot repeat ('We cannot go to 110% next year'). The two long-term growth drivers are an installed base growing 5%, 6%, 7% every single year plus rising average revenue per tool from new, largely AI-based, service products.
installed base growing every single year, 5%, 6%, 7% every single year; Leading-edge logic and DRAM, almost 100% utilization; earlier view 11% or 12%

GPU pricing and mix (management): CFO: very little of DigitalOcean's revenue is under long-term contract, so it raises prices on renewal - including on some of its small bare-metal base - or migrates those customers onto its inference services. CEO: spot instances launched a few weeks ago and capacity placed on demand or spot 'is gone' within the minute; on an article over the weekend saying H100 prices are going up again, the CEO said DigitalOcean saw it 3 weeks ago because its fungible on-demand H100 fleet goes 'even before we have them available'. As the year end approaches it is doing fewer and fewer GPU-as-a-service deals, shifting to what it calls elastic compute (serverless inferencing, on-demand and spot) to maximize fleet utilization and yield per megawatt. CEO: surge or scarcity-based GPU pricing 'is a temporary spike', while token flow and agent flow are the durable value streams.

Breen put GF squarely in a supply-constrained posture for the next couple of years: 'We are clearly in a chasing supply moment today'; 'for the next couple of years, we will be more in a supply-constrained than a demand-constrained environment'. Job number one is ramping technologies GF already produces to higher volumes, and capex is going up again - 'We already are increasing our CapEx this year from last year. We'll be increasing further again next year' - with tool install and qualification speed, not demand, the thing that 'will gate or accelerate our growth going into next year'. Two new-cycle features: customers are co-investing financially alongside GF in the ramps ('customer skin in the game... they are willing to put capital to work'), and government partnerships provide tools that let GF 'accelerate CapEx at significant recovery rates that were not there in the past'.
capex increasing this year versus last year and increasing further again next year; supply-constrained, not demand-constrained, for the next couple of years

Mobile mix and a new read-across on foundry tightness: GF was 'more than 50% mobile going back a couple of years', is 'down to the mid-30s today' and the long-term model takes it to 'the mid-20s', with absolute mobile revenue assumed relatively flat rather than growing. 2026 is a tough year in mobile but 'not as tough at the higher end', where GF has more of its exposure. The new behaviour is that handset customers are now booking forward supply: 'mobile companies were the first to the queue in COVID... Now they are worried about being late when the data center is the one pushing all the demand. You are seeing actually more visibility where they are actually still saying, I need my supply for 2027. I need my supply for 2028.'
mobile more than 50% of revenue a couple of years ago, mid-30s today, mid-20s in the long-term model; handset customers booking supply for 2027 and 2028

CAPACITY BUILD BEYOND THE US CLEAN ROOM: Kizner said Nova is 'doubling our production floor'; besides the US expansion it has opened 'a new clean room in Germany' and will open 'a new clean room by the end of this year for the first time in Asia', with CapEx staying focused on infrastructure into 2027 and beyond. He stressed the constraint is not only Nova's own clean-room space but the whole stretched supply chain: Nova gives its vendors forward visibility so they can ramp, and qualifies a second vendor where it identifies a bottleneck, because one crucial vendor can stop Nova meeting demand regardless of floor space.
doubling our production floor; a new clean room in Germany; a new clean room by the end of this year for the first time in Asia

MEMORY PRICING IS DESTROYING THE LOW-END HANDSET BOM: smartphone volume has gone down 'by low double digits ... low teens, over the last year', with the impact concentrated on the lowest tier and second lowest tier - 'everything below $300' - because 'memory has now become more than half of the BOM of the phone', making those device prices unsustainable. At the premium end, where Qualcomm's presence is largest, Palkhiwala says Qualcomm has 'not seen much of an impact' despite higher prices. He expects continued pressure at the low end and describes handsets as at the low point of the cycle.
smartphone volume down low double digits / low teens over the last year; impact on everything below $300; memory more than half of the BOM of the phone

Albertazzi narrows the supply-chain congestion flagged on the Q2 call: it was not a generic situation but specifically referred to the converged infrastructure products OneCore and SmartRun, where Vertiv is industrializing something that is a field project and taking construction-site complexity onto itself. The consequences are coordination across multiple factories rather than component shortage, and timing variability - is revenue recognized this day or maybe four days later because some of the components are converging in the integration factory. Integration at this scale is a different capability than the power-module integration Vertiv has done for 25, 30 years, and that integration capacity is being deployed constantly to follow demand. He adds the current outlook already incorporates wiggle room against possible hiccups. Chamberlin separately points back to the ramp in infrastructure-solutions orders (Vertiv SmartRun / Vertiv OneCore) seen in last fourth quarter as evidence of the share gain.

H1 2026: Indium Phosphide substrate supply and rare earth bottlenecks are the gating risks, and the second-half outlook already reflects them - "there is substrate supply concerns, as well as rare earth bottlenecks that are highlighted in each of the calls that you are seeing in the industry... the second half outlook already reflects these risks... not over-committing to a number that we will not be able to hit". On InP specifically: "Indium Phosphide substrates are becoming some of the bottlenecks around significant volume increases. Therefore, we are working closely with everybody in the industry and with all partners to ensure that we are locking in volume allocations to secure our demand that we are currently seeing with our customers."

H1 2026: the InP substrate diameter mix, from the epiwafer maker's own view - "3-inch is still very dominant. Then it's 4-inch with almost half of the volume driven by 4-inch, and only then comes 6-inch as the fastest-growing sort of diameter, and it's scaling right now." 6-inch maturity and line yields still need to improve and "we are not seeing truly the really demand on 6-inch yet". Management clarified that IQE's tool conversions are material conversions (Gallium Arsenide to Indium Phosphide), which "doesn't necessarily come with a dimension conversion"; IQE can support 3-inch, 4-inch and 6-inch. Tightness across the three diameters is hard to rank because "there is different types of substrates too".
InP substrate volume mix: 3-inch dominant, 4-inch almost half of volume, 6-inch fastest growing but least mature

H1 2026: capacity is being added by converting existing tooling in the second half "to increase capacity to meet the strong demand for Indium Phosphide", and every conversion is gated on a signed customer commitment - "we will also not expand capacity without a clear customer commitment and a clear visibility on what value is going to be driven with that expansion" and "we are still not converting tools without customer commitments and secured demand on these tools". Conversion cost is "definitely insignificant compared to the cost of a new reactor"; the real cost is the downtime of the tool. Customer prepayments are "definitely a mechanism for us to fund our growth", following what "some of our players in the same ecosystem" already do. Newport still has "ample clean room space to add capacity" so IQE "can scale up rather quickly compared to others because we already have the infrastructure to house these reactors".

Backlog surge in an extraordinary demand environment: Q3 book-to-bill significantly greater than one; backlog up $800 million quarter-on-quarter to $8.5 billion, and expected to grow at an even greater rate in Q4 — just one month into Q4, orders booked are approaching a level equal to the ENTIRETY of Q3, and Ciena projects exiting fiscal 2026 with over $10 billion in backlog extending well into fiscal 2028. Customer mix: about 50% of the business is now hyperscalers directly, and 'neo scaler' (neocloud) demand — MOFN deals, own fiber builds — is expected to become an increasingly important part of the business through 2027 and 2028; MOFN growth called explosive in markets like India, plus Japan and parts of the Middle East.
Backlog +$800M QoQ to $8.5B; >$10B backlog projected exiting FY2026; orders +50% 2025-to-2026 after doubling 2024-to-2025; commitments through 2029

Supply, not demand, is the binding constraint: the industry needs to add significant capacity and management does not see supply and demand getting back into balance BEFORE 2028 — a similarly constrained dynamic is expected going into 2027 and likely into 2028. In recent weeks Ciena FINALIZED LONG-TERM AGREEMENTS that secure supply of certain key components THROUGH 2029, including incremental capacity for those key components; the June five-year zero-coupon convertible (economic conversion premium of 114%, proceeds retiring the 5.5% interest term loan) partly provided the capital to help secure supply over the next three years, and cash from operations will step down in Q4 as those investments are dispersed. Ciena is also qualifying additional suppliers — expanding both the number of suppliers and alternative technologies for the same functionality. Capital investments this year increased capacity sufficient to support RLS, plug and Waveserver revenue growth all over 60% year to date; capex expected at the high end of the $250 million-$275 million range; $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents. Value exchange with customers: price increases from high single digits up to high teens/low 20s depending on customer and product line, some of it selectively hitting backlog, alongside payment-terms and fill-rate discussions; possible new Canadian tariff impact of ~$10 million a quarter being mitigated.
Key-component supply secured through 2029; supply/demand balance not before 2028; price increases high single digits to high teens/low 20s; capex high end of $250M-$275M

inventory purchase commitments $17,165 million (+126%); inventories $5,694 million (+80%); inventory deposits and prepayments $1,104 million vs $825 million

Mechanism behind the better-than-expected July quarter, which the Q3 call did not spell out. April-quarter push-outs came from customers being unable to capture memory and from Asian fabs at unusually high utilization telling chip designs 'You have to delay your design because we don't have the capacity for it'. Through the July quarter those designs started to be released because the same fabs 'added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range', and in some cases told a customer with a 40 nanometer design 'if you move that chip design to 28 nanometers or 22 nanometers, I will then manufacture it for you' - i.e. the capacity shortage is actively forcing node migration, which is the ASP-positive trend Photronics benefits from. On the display side Korea is strong on high-end consumer electronics launching this fall while China has pulled back because low-end consumer electronics cannot capture memory; Moreau relayed that the memory companies are talking about 'another 2, 3, 4 years before supply and demand comes into equilibrium'.
fabs added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range and pushed 40 nanometer designs to 28 or 22 nanometers; memory supply and demand equilibrium another 2, 3, 4 years away

Named the biggest headwind of the last couple of years as geopolitics rather than demand: Photronics lost China-market customers it had good business with after 'We were told by the U.S. government, You have to stop shipping to that customer', and in another case Taiwan put a customer on its restricted list, forcing Photronics to move that production out of its Taiwan facility into its China facility, which has less capacity - so revenue with that customer fell as well. Offsetting structural positive: regionalization and reshoring, with TSMC expanding very aggressively in Arizona and GlobalFoundries and Samsung also expanding in the U.S.; the more locations that manufacture chips, the more mask business spreads out, which is why Photronics is expanding in the U.S. and Korea.

CFO put boundaries on capacity and inventory. CapEx stays in mid-single-digit percentage intensity 'for several years': 'Our revenue has to get to about 30% higher than where it is today for us even to think about adding capacity,' and about 35% of production is managed outside, which onsemi loads last. 'We're not breaking ground on a new fab anytime soon.'

AGENTIC WORKLOADS ARE THE CPU DEMAND DRIVER, AND IRELAND IS THE SUPPLY ANSWER: CFO David Zinsner quantified the workload shift for the first time - comparing a regular training data center with an agentic-like activity, 'it's like a 4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements'. Server CPU units, which used to decline low single digits, are now growing double digits with core counts growing at multiples of that, and ASP per core - which fell almost 20% in some years - has at least stabilized and in some like-for-like cases is going up, so core-count growth now flows straight through to revenue. The constraint is supply, not competitive performance: 'as we look at this year, next year, probably even into 2028, this is going to be less about competitive performance of CPUs and more about can you get the CPUs to the customer', and share will follow whoever can supply. Granite Rapids, the data-center flagship, is built in Ireland on Intel 3; part of next year's CapEx is to ramp Ireland where Intel wants to 'more than double the output there next year'. Even so Intel will 'under-supply for sure this year', 'probably under-supply next year', and hopes to be in a good position by 2028.
4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements; more than double the output there next year

MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

THE CAPITAL RAISE IS A SUBSTRATE-AND-FAB SPENDING EVENT: Zinsner explained the August equity raise as 'the capital raise precedes capital investment' - 2026 CapEx has already been upticked 'by a couple of billion dollars from $18 billion to $20 billion', next year's will be significantly higher, and 'substrates are really constrained and we're going to need to make investments associated with substrates as well next year, given the significant demand.' Committing to 14A high-volume manufacturing in 2028 means placing long-lead supplier orders now, which was one of the biggest drivers of the raise. On footprint: Ireland's shell is being equipped now; Fab 52 in Arizona is running Intel 18A and Fab 62 is almost ready, with next year's investment accelerating its equipping; Oregon stays the pilot line but will also run volume Intel 14A as 18A is pushed into Arizona; Ohio shells are in progress with the ability to have 'eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio', mod one being built as fast as possible. Zinsner said 2027 CapEx is not locked - the businesses gave him a number and 'I've told them no', sending them back for more efficiency before he guides.
from $18 billion to $20 billion; eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio

AI / HBM framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the memory market is leading semiconductor growth on AI and big-data demand, and the equipment market is expected to keep growing over the medium-to-long term on the aggressive DRAM-centric investment memory makers are making to break the HBM SHORTAGE caused by the explosive expansion of AI end-markets. 2022-2024 is described as a harsh down-cycle (memory price collapse, utilisation drop); 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase driven by generative-AI infrastructure build-out, led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than commodity products. The AI-accelerator and HBM demand surge is forcing the equipment market onto a single high-end track where marginal technology or adequate tools have no place; foreign vendors from the US, Japan and Netherlands still hold the largest shares but Korean localisation is rising and the company's tools are now in mass-production lines of major customers at home and abroad, with overseas sales rising (China semiconductor revenue KRW 63,346M in H1 2026 vs KRW 42,017M in H1 2025). Company cannot estimate market share because device makers' total orders are not observable.
HBM shortage-driven DRAM capex cited as multi-year equipment driver; 2025-2030 structural growth phase (HBM, sub-2nm foundry)

On NAND supply: 'we still able to get supply, but unfortunately supply not enough to what we need... We have supply, but supply still not enough what we need.' Phison met every NAND supplier at FMS last week and pitched that its purchases feed its own AI data-platform systems, not just module resale; it will not disclose how many LTAs it holds so competitors cannot ask for the same amounts. CEO expects the NAND shortage to continue into next year and beyond ('many year'); a top NAND-maker executive told him a new fab takes 4 years from investment to production, not 2. Downgrade-grade NAND supply is also shrinking structurally: 3D NAND yields now run 90-plus percent, with some wafers at 95% good die, so the cheap downgrade bin that used to feed consumer products is disappearing.
new NAND fab: 4 years investment-to-production; 3D NAND yields 90%+ (some wafers 95%)

NAND pricing/margin view: back in March the CEO said NAND makers' gross margin reaching a floor of 80% was easy and 85% might happen; now he says 90% gross margin may happen in 2026, but warns that is unhealthy for the industry ('if you ask component for 90% gross margin, industry potentially will be killed - you can see the IoT, you can see the consumer die'). Demand is too strong, so price will keep rising but at a decelerating rate toward saturation, at which point suppliers start choosing whom to ship. On demand structure: systems have cut DRAM content ('a lot of systems, they cut half of the DRAM') but nobody cuts storage - inference needs storage, 'storage is money' - and aiDAPTIV uses flash to complement DRAM.
NAND-maker gross margin: 80% floor easy, 85% may happen, 90% possible in 2026 (CEO view)

Inventory and funding: in June-July Phison spent more than $450 million of cash buying NAND wafers from Shenzhen module houses that were dumping consumer-heavy inventory at prices well below NAND-maker contract prices ('don't take this as price decrease - the NAND guys are not going to decline their price'). Inventory of roughly 90 billion (NT$, book value) is carried at cost and never revalued upward, only written down. Balance sheet: the large bank debt outstanding at end-March was almost fully repaid by July ('now we have no debt'); the $800 million ECB raised earlier has already been deployed into NAND ('already turned one and a half times'); if business keeps growing strongly, new fundraising may be needed in the second half of next year.
$450M+ NAND wafer purchases in June-July; inventory ~90 billion NT (book value); $800M ECB deployed

Notebook shipments were 11.5M units, up 15% QoQ (well above the flat-to-slightly-up guide) but down 5% YoY, as brand customers pulled orders forward on expectations that notebook memory supply will keep being crowded out by AI server memory demand and that memory prices keep rising; notebook gross margin stayed suppressed by memory and CPU shortages and price hikes. Chromebooks face the most severe component shortage and unfavourable supply terms because of their low ASP, staying below 10% of notebook shipments even in the seasonal education peak; brand customers are raising retail prices, further weakening demand, so H2 shipments will be below H1.
notebook shipments 1,150 ten-thousand units (+15% QoQ, -5% YoY); Chromebook below one-tenth of notebook shipments

Memory shortage impact on PCs, graphics and smartphones (CEO Stephen Chang): standard PCs grew modestly in the June quarter from March, but AOS expects an adjustment in the September quarter as end customers face memory and CPU shortages; 'We mainly see September as the main correction. The December quarter is still unclear, and we're not expecting a correction at this point, but we will need to see how the memory situation evolves.' In graphics there are no major platform releases this year; AOS expects the next platform release sometime next year and will prioritize it for growth. In smartphones, AOS is focused on premium platforms with its Tier 1 U.S. customer, where battery protection solutions and support for higher charging currents are increasing BOM content; outside the premium tier, elevated memory pricing and supply constraints are pushing some OEMs toward lower performance components in certain platforms, and AOS is 'preparing for a growth season for our battery PCM business'. He said he believes the Computing and Communications businesses are outperforming their respective end markets.
Alpha and Omega Semiconductor Q4 FY2026 (08-12-2026)

manufacturing capacity 4 times above 1H 2025; more than 10x increase in 2026

CEO on the market: AI-driven demand has pushed load growth to the highest levels in over 50 years; 'Supply chain constraints have extended gas turbine lead times to over four years' and interconnection queues 'can extend to over seven years', accelerating speed-to-power needs for hyperscalers, utilities and C&I customers. gas turbine lead times over four years; interconnection queues over seven years (CEO)

electrical equipment 'a little bit more stressed'; ORC turbine and drilling supply robust

Materials: memory and CPU have been severely short for over half a year; more recently PCB and power-related components turned very tight - PCB traced upstream to CCL and glass fibre (Pegatron is chasing material all the way to upstream suppliers in Japan), and in power not just MOSFET/PMIC but power-module supplier capacity is strained, while high-capacitance/high-voltage MLCC shows serious shortage in H2. Purchasing staff are stationed at supplier factories to secure allocations, and some material is brought in early at good prices since failing to pull material forward would delay later deliveries. In PC, customers have already secured H2 key components (CPU, memory, SSD).

Pegatron's CEO flagged high-capacitance, high-voltage MLCC as showing a fairly serious shortage in H2 2026 on server demand, alongside tight PCB (upstream CCL/glass fibre) and power components (MOSFET/PMIC and power-module capacity); memory and CPU have been severely short for over half a year. Pegatron is pre-buying and stationing purchasing staff at supplier factories to secure allocations for its ramping AI server business.

Build-cost economics disclosed for the first time at this level of detail. Abdel gave an 'indicative range' of build cost of '$10,000-$20,000' depending on geography and project type, and said power connection has gone from free to a major line item: 'Costs us tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site now. It used to cost us nothing.' He is seeing cost inflation in heavily built markets - electricians 'are making $150 an hour these days' - while cost 'definitely moderated on the manufacturing side of the equation'. The response is to shift work offsite: more prefabrication to minimise onsite labour.
build cost indicative range $10,000-$20,000; tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site; electricians making $150 an hour

The two binding bottlenecks are energy and trades labour, not demand. Abdel: 'Electricians in many locations are very constrained. There's not enough of them' - electricians and plumbers are 'probably being the most acute' trades. Example given: the greater Chicago metro area has '15 gigawatt' of planned data-center expansions on the docket 'with another 15 that's at least marketed to be planned', and 'there is just not enough electricians'. On power he said generation is 'the tertiary issue' - distribution and transmission are the bottlenecks - and that a site requested the old way 'could be 8 years before you get that power'; Equinix therefore now secures the utility conversation and line of sight to power BEFORE taking down land.
Chicago metro 15 gigawatt of planned expansions plus another 15 marketed; up to 8 years for power under the old approach

CFO on supply and visibility: as demand rose earlier this year lead times increased, 'in some cases it got over a year', and have been managed 'back down to the in the 40s'. 'The pinch point is assembly test or packaging'; the fab side is comfortable because Lattice uses older nodes; Lattice has 'invested a lot in... tester capacity, for the final test and ship out to the customer' (visible in its capex) and is expanding its supply chain. Confirming visibility to the end of 2027: 'we have bookings out through Q4 of next year. We are not booked out in the sense that we can't support more demand. We can support more demand.'
lead times over a year at peak, now in the 40s; bookings out through Q4 of next year

→ CoreWeave: CEO Mike Intrator cited CoreWeave's 'recent long-term agreement with Solidigm' as an illustration of how it is derisking access to the critical inputs needed to serve customers, alongside its close partnerships with NVIDIA and its OEM and ODM partners. He described a supply chain spanning land, power and shell through GPUs, networking and MEMORY, all of it being challenged by the growth of AI, and CFO Nitin Agrawal named Solidigm again as a new partner relationship used to strategically source required inputs amid a complex global supply chain.

$5.6B raise; net debt $1.2B; inventory $12.9B; CCC 149 days

Component procurement scaled ahead of the FY2027 ramp: closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built in anticipation of higher revenue; the $5.6B June equity raise is described as fully supporting component supply and business needs. Generation-transition risk on memory and other components is managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems that stay compatible across product lines and generations - with management noting that with prices rising so fast, older inventory has often been resold favorably.

Record demand and de-concentrating customer base: over $60B of NEW ORDERS booked in Q4 FY2026 (~70% pure AI, ~30% CPU / CPU-based AI / edge AI), taking order book and backlog to record levels entering FY2027. NINE customers exceeded $1B of revenue in FY2026 versus four in FY2025, and the largest datacenter/CSP customer was 28% of FY2026 revenue. $60B+ new orders in Q4 (70% pure AI); 9 customers >$1B vs 4; top customer 28%

Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. September and December quarter order/shipment activity described as quite strong. On the ODM-disintermediation concern, management positions Supermicro as running BOTH an OEM and an ODM model and says it will keep growing in both. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).
Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

Materials supply: T-glass is currently in shortage; Zhen Ding says it keeps long-term strategic partnerships with upstream material makers, has signed strategic-cooperation / supply-guarantee agreements with suppliers, and is qualifying second sources to diversify. Whether next-generation glass-core substrates relieve the glass supply-demand balance is 'not yet knowable' given long certification. CCL price increases are being passed through to customers smoothly with small impact on gross margin; across AI and non-AI products management says most raw-material increases can be passed on.

Optical boards and capacity (results deck): for optical modules, 1.6T and subsequent generations require mSAP technology; the company says demand for high-end optical-module PCBs continues to outstrip supply globally and it is expanding related capacity. Thailand: Fab 1 (high-end HDI, HLC and optical-module products, mass production since 3Q25); three additional fabs and one mechanical drilling center are under construction, with trial production expected to start progressively from 4Q26. Shenzhen Campus III smart manufacturing base (broke ground July 2026) will comprise three plants focused on high-end substrate-like PCBs for AI servers and optical modules, plus advanced FPCs for AI devices. New capacity comes online in phases from 2026 to 2030 in line with customer qualification and mass-production schedules.
Thailand: three more fabs and a drilling center, trial production from 4Q26; Shenzhen Campus III: three plants; capacity phased in 2026-2030

Supply chain: data-center HVAC players face constraints sourcing fans; BASX has manufactured its own fans from the day the business started and AAON insourced plenum fans a couple of years ago, which management calls a competitive benefit, though AAON still buys some fans and sees capacity constraints in the fan market. Management embeds some potential supply-chain impact into the back-half BASX outlook.

CEO on labor: availability of highly skilled labor, especially in the U.S., is in short supply; it hurt efficiencies and raised direct costs on a specific construction project in Q2. B&W is working with unions on incentives, rehires and delayed retirements and does not expect labor shortages to be persistent, as its construction focus has shifted toward variable price projects.

Memory shortage. CFO: low-end smartphones need much less memory than high-end devices, so CEVA has not seen significant issues in the last couple of quarters; the constraint hurts margins in the supply chain and bites more at the $1,000-phone end. CEO: 'the memory shortage has an impact on the wireless handset industry, and it's hard to quantify exactly how that will impact the second half'; the mobile outlook assumes typical seasonality with the caveat of memory allocation challenges.

Camtek says it is successfully managing the operational challenge of unprecedented demand: it expanded production capacity and strengthened its supply chain well in advance, has all subcontractors and supply chain in place, and COO Ramy Langer said there are no issues or obstacles regarding capacity and the company is confident of shipping machines on time. It is now further expanding manufacturing capacity, system integration capability, the sales organisation and customer support infrastructure to support substantially higher annual revenue levels. Inventory was flat in Q2 but is expected to grow in coming quarters to support forecast revenue growth.

Supply build-up: inventory RMB 8,247,509,484.00 at June 30, 2026 (+66.83% vs end-2025; 45.32% of total assets), mainly more raw materials and materials in outsourced processing; prepayments RMB 2,913,927,071.43 (+291.37%), mainly prepaid purchases, with the two largest prepayment counterparties at 47.23% and 41.91% of the balance; notes payable RMB 3,085,487,067.78 (+779.25%) from more bank-acceptance bills used for purchases. The company says upstream semiconductor raw-material prices are rising overall and it will respond through strategic stockpiling and product iteration.

Component supply is tight industry-wide: key components from Japan and Korea (mechanical parts, sliders, even robots) that used to be available in four months now take about six months; key suppliers have not raised prices, ACM stocked raw materials at the end of last year, and the 42%-48% gross margin target is unchanged. Managing supply is the one factor that could affect full-year shipments.
component lead times ~four months -> six months

Capacity: the company says semiconductor-related sales increased on steady production of wafer transfer systems and concentrated customer acceptances, and that production capacity is being expanded amid sustained high utilization; its capital expenditure aims to expand production capacity through factory expansion and renovation and the purchase of processing machinery.
Hirata Corporation results presentation: FY2026 Q1 Financial Results Explanatory Materials (08-07-2026)

Kurita Water Industries results briefing Q&A: Summary of the Q&A Session for 1Q of FY ending March 2027 (08-07-2026)

Centrus HALEU for up to five Aurora powerhouses from 2029; plutonium bridge fuel up to ~2 GW

Optorun press release: Consolidated Financial Results Briefing for FY12/2026 Q2 (08-07-2026)

IoTRAM product line update: very strong market demand and IoTRAM adoption - standard DRAM pricing continues to push customers to IoTRAM, with higher volume and higher pricing; ApSRAM mass production continues, wearables leading and global MCU vendors widely adopting ApSRAM. Long term, the company says IoTRAM's market position is stronger but moderated by capacity limitation: conversion from standard DRAM to IoTRAM is generally sticky, market demand exceeds current manufacturing capacity, and AP Memory continues to seek more capacity resources.

Per SoftBank's Q1 review and Arm CFO Jason Child: Arm Q1 revenue hit a record $1.3 billion, +22% YoY, with fully diluted EPS +29% YoY (record for a first quarter); Q2 guidance midpoints $1.38 billion revenue and $0.47 EPS, both above analyst consensus. Arm AGI CPU: starts shipping in Q4 of this fiscal year; initial guide was roughly $1 billion of revenue across this fiscal year and next combined, and confirmed orders have now grown to MORE than $2 billion - revenue guidance not yet updated because of supply-chain constraints primarily around wafer capacity, with clarity on how much of the incremental billion-plus can ship expected in another quarter or two; demand expected to DOUBLE the year after (Arm fiscal 2029) as the order pipeline keeps growing. Arm-based AGI CPU saves up to $10 billion of capex per 1 gigawatt of data center capacity vs x86; Arm IP-based CPU chips are used by about 50% of leading hyperscalers (Graviton, Axion, Cobalt, Grace), and NVIDIA's agentic PC chip carries an Arm-based Grace CPU.
Arm Q1 revenue record $1.3 billion +22% YoY; EPS +29%; Q2 guide $1.38 billion / $0.47; AGI CPU orders more than $2 billion vs ~$1 billion initial guide

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manufacturing sites missed: (1) Houston, USA — a fully automated enclosure plant with 15 GWh/year capacity that Fluence off-takes, run by the SAME contract manufacturer that operates its main Vietnam enclosure facility. Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a utility-interconnection delay (the plant has been running on generators, preventing parallel commissioning work); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected within weeks, FULL production in fiscal Q1 2027. (2) One of two new facilities in China — initial production of Smartstack components (the 'pods' that sit on the skids) failed Fluence's testing and required rework; corrections are implemented, shipping has resumed and the site reached full production in Q4. Management put a hedge and a contingency in the plan and blew through both. Organizational response: Roman Loosen (Chief Enterprise Operations Officer, 20+ years at Siemens) takes over supply chain and manufacturing and Peter Williams moves to product, both reporting to the CEO; framed as an EXECUTION/process-scaling fix, not a change of suppliers. Once Houston is fully ramped, Fluence expects domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog.
Houston 15 GWh/yr, full production fiscal Q1 2027; China site reworked, full production in Q4; ~$400M of FY26 revenue pushed to FY27

SOURCING: Fluence signed a long-term battery-cell agreement with an INTERNATIONAL supplier that covers not just supply but technology-roadmap alignment on how cells behave inside Fluence's modules — securing long-term volume and attractive pricing for FY2027-28 and letting it price future orders with more confidence, at the cost of a $15M charge on one in-flight project supplied by the same counterparty. Explicitly NOT related to AESC (the AESC review, run earlier in the year, drove some strategic expense but produced no announcement); Fluence says it is spending a lot of time talking to battery capacity across the market and sees an opportunity to work more closely with U.S. battery manufacturers. On inverters: Fluence uses ONLY non-Chinese inverters in the U.S. — mostly U.S.-made, some imported from Europe — so it expects zero impact from the FCC's inverter restrictions; in Europe it still uses a mix of Chinese and non-Chinese and is working toward a fully European solution ahead of expected European restrictions.
Long-term cell supply + tech-roadmap agreement (int'l supplier, not AESC), $15M charge; 100% non-Chinese inverters in the U.S.

In response to increased orders from Q3 onward it is expanding production capacity at the Sri Lanka plant and preparing to add semi-automated equipment; it will launch its third semi-automatic machine in 2027, is investing in front-end processing capacity for optical components, expects further sales growth in 2027 and is considering further capacity-building investments for 2027.
Kohoku Kogyo results presentation: Financial Results Materials Semi-annual FY12/2026 (08-06-2026)

Capacity utilization is expected at an average of 70%-80% in the first half and over 80% in the second half of March 2027, higher next fiscal year; production lead time is currently around eight months. Current capacity secures the JPY 340 billion revenue forecast, and capacity is being expanded for March 2028 and beyond: warehouse space at the Tonami plant is being converted to clean room, newly acquired land next to Tonami is being evaluated for rapid expansion, production engineer recruitment is ramping, and shifts (currently 1.5) can be increased. Utilization 70%-80% H1, over 80% H2; lead time around eight months; monthly unit capacity targeted at 2.5 times the March 2025 level in 10 years

Indium phosphide is the key medium-term lever. 200-GIG PHOTODETECTORS are ramping in volume production and becoming a meaningful contributor to Data Center growth; 400-gig photodetectors are in the hands of perhaps a dozen customers with very positive feedback. The 75-MILLIWATT CW LASER qualification continues: MACOM is well into HTOL testing (typically 5,000 hours) with data described as exceptional, is gaining confidence but cannot yet declare success, and is developing plans for a POTENTIAL START TO PRODUCTION IN LATE CALENDAR 2027, scoping modest capex and fab space for a rapid high-volume ramp for a few strategic customers. CEO Steve Daly called bringing a CW laser into production in 2028 'a watershed moment' that could be a very large revenue contributor. Separately, demand for MACOM's 25G DFB lasers (100G QSFP, CWDM4, LR4) is rising with urgency because of a GENERAL SUPPLY SHORTAGE OF INDIUM PHOSPHIDE DFB LASERS. MACOM expects to gain meaningful indium phosphide market share over the next three years; its Ann Arbor, Michigan facility has built photodiodes for over a decade and grows its own epitaxy by MBE.
200G PDs ramping in volume; 400G PDs at ~a dozen customers; 75mW CW laser potential production start late calendar 2027

Capacity and lead times: utilisation at the RTP, North Carolina and Lowell, Massachusetts fabs continues to increase even as capacity is added, and utilisation rates are now IMPACTING LEAD TIMES - MACOM is quoting LONGER LEAD TIMES for internally manufactured products. New capacity is being added across operations through the remainder of fiscal 2026 and into fiscal 2027, and management notes new-capacity capex is typically installed and online in less than one year per project. Fiscal 2026 capex is estimated at $60-65 million (versus $22.4 million in fiscal 2024 and $42.6 million in fiscal 2025), with fiscal 2027 capex expected to be similar at roughly $60 million including infrastructure to support a laser ramp. The Massachusetts fab mix is now a combination of Telecom, Defense and Data Center as indium phosphide ramps.
FY2026 capex $60M-$65M, FY2027 similar ~$60M; longer lead times being quoted on internally manufactured products

On the proposed U.S. ban on Chinese transceiver module makers, CEO Steve Daly said MACOM's Data Center growth is driven by U.S. hyperscalers plus U.S. enterprise and compute OEMs, and that those end users are typically directly involved in selecting chips for their hardware. If hyperscalers have to shift share between transceiver companies because of new regulations, 'we would expect to follow that business to those other manufacturers' - a customer mix shift rather than a demand loss, since MACOM has relationships with most transceiver companies in the industry. MACOM has NO MANUFACTURING IN CHINA, only about 85 employees there in application sales and logistics supporting Scandinavian telecom design centres and the optical industry, and the vast majority of what it sells into China is exported back out inside systems typically headed to the U.S.
No manufacturing in China; ~85 employees there in sales/logistics

CEO: power is becoming the central infrastructure challenge of the AI era; the market lacks enough energized, permitted capacity on a timeline customers can use, increasing the value of already-energized infrastructure. MARA can deploy mining quickly on a newly energized site and transition it to AI or HPC when customer demand is ready; Vertebra AI (power management, with TAE Power Solutions battery technology) can serve as a load bank for data center startup.

Lead times are stretching beyond the prior four-to-eight-week range as constraints spread across substrates, foundry nodes, subcontracted assembly and test. Expedite requests increased sharply and many orders placed inside lead time could not be supported; management said AI demand is crowding out advanced packaging and substrate capacity.
foundry, substrate, advanced-packaging and OSAT constraints; unsupported expedite demand

Nikon (company Q&A summary): the impact of rising memory prices on this year's operating profit, expected at the start of the year to be in the high single-digit billions of yen, is progressing in line with assumptions; Nikon has secured prospects for procuring the memory volume it needs this fiscal year but is monitoring the risk of additional impact.
Nikon results briefing Q&A: Q&A of Financial Results for the 1st Quarter of the Year Ending March 31, 2027 (08-06-2026)

CEO John Kibarian on eProbe supply: capacity is not yet a limit and suppliers can build at a higher level than this; the biggest issue has been timeline and the supply chain, and costs keep rising for the computing element of the system given where memory prices are going, so PDF is working to make its costs more effective. CFO: higher component costs to meet DirectScan demand are part of the higher year-over-year capex.

Metrology lines full for H1 2027; new capacity live by year-end; first orders for 2028; visibility partly into 2029; current capacity roughly EUR 100 million annual sales (CEO confirmation)

Pacific Biosciences' 10-Q: cost of product revenue rose $0.9 million (5%) in Q2 2026, primarily from exit costs associated with a contract manufacturer, increased memory costs, product transition costs tied to the short-read asset disposition and amortization of the patent license from the PGI settlement. cost of product revenue +$0.9 million (5%) in Q2 2026

Capacity (CEO): total secured AI factory capacity is now 212 MW across Australia and New Zealand, up 80 MW from the prior guidance of 132 MW (54 MW at the start of the year), for deployment by the end of 2027; 120 MW are contracted, leaving 92 MW of secured capacity available to sell heading into the back half of the year. The additional 80 MW in Australia comes from a new partner, with some early megawatts potentially as early as late this year, definitely in Q1 next year, and delivery through 2027. SharonAI extended its footprint with its first New Zealand facility; it co-locates in partners' Tier 3 and Tier 4 data centers rather than greenfield builds.
212 MW secured (from 132 MW); 120 MW contracted; 92 MW available

Market (CEO): the entire market is constrained; timely access to NVIDIA GPUs remains one of the most critical constraints, with manufacturing constraints and hyperscaler demand limiting supply and emerging providers facing long lead times, while ready data-center sites with power are increasingly scarce. Customer demand on the AICP program is for hundreds of thousands of GB300s against the 40,000 available; most AI-native customers (model builders, inference providers) want three- to five-year take-or-pay terms, and demand from the U.S. and Asia is equally strong. Capacity was sold this week at record prices for both B300 and GB300.
demand for hundreds of thousands of GB300s vs 40,000 available

On overinvestment concerns in AI data centers: 'we do have a very clear view on demand and supply imbalance. The supply is very much short, and that is why this project is announced one after another, which I believe is a healthy situation' - without securing computing power, AI technology and services would slow; SoftBank sees the Stargate Project as having set the fire in the market and does not view it as a bubble.

Capacity and demand: approximately 800 MW of open capacity with nearer-term delivery timelines plus line of sight to more via OEM channels and the secondary market (Amanda Brock); active negotiations for multiple gigawatts of additional demand with multiple hyperscalers and AI compute companies (Bill Zartler). Bill Zartler: demand for islanded behind-the-meter power remains exceptionally strong, driven by grid interconnection delays, speed to compute and regulatory focus on consumer prices, and there is more demand for compute than there is compute and power; the logistics business is effectively sold out of its top-fill equipment.
~800 MW open capacity; multiple GW in negotiation

NEW-BUILD ECONOMICS GAP: ERCOT year-to-date wholesale power has averaged $30/MWh (same as last year) versus the ~$90/MWh area cited for new-build contracting — '30 is not going to get new stuff built.' The price of generation EQUIPMENT 'has doubled, if not tripled' in some cases, so what was an acceptable build price a year or two ago no longer is. In PJM the $555/MW-day RPB cap 'might get some things built' but a spread around it will be needed for certain projects. Large-load customers are willing to contract with EXISTING assets at a PREMIUM because it is still a discount to new build; co-location can beat even an islanded new build on speed.
ERCOT YTD $30/MWh vs ~$90 new build; equipment costs 2-3x; PJM RPB cap $555/MW-day

Company outlook (deck): demand for high-density NOR continues to outpace supply, supporting a sustained pricing uptrend through 2026 and beyond; SLC NAND supply remains tight, with strong design-ins underpinning the upward pricing trend into 2H26; global DRAM supply remains constrained while major memory suppliers continue to scale back DDR4 bit shipments, with further upside potential in 3Q contract pricing and AI-driven demand reinforcing a positive outlook into 2H26 and 2027. Strong demand cited from AI server, data center, infrastructure, edge AI and automotive. Memory capacity utilization ~100% in 2Q26 (~100% in 1Q26, ~90% in 2Q25); increasing LTA penetration enhances long-term supply resilience and order visibility.

CEO: current capacity is about $1 billion a year of revenue and is about to triple to about $3 billion a year, 'and we're still worried about back orders'; near-term Caris Detect demand may run ahead of the rollout. Inventory increased $47 million from Q1 to Q2, built on purpose ahead of expected Detect volume, and Q2 capex of $22.1 million went to ramping capacity for the new product launches. President: capacity is being expanded aggressively, and it is quite likely it will not stay above demand.
capacity ~$1B a year of revenue, tripling to ~$3B; inventory +$47M QoQ; Q2 capex $22.1M

Mayumi: production issues at some indium phosphide substrate suppliers have led to a temporary supply shortage, which the company expects to catch up with in its annual plan, while moving to a multi-source approach. Washimori: the tight substrate procurement may become more pronounced in Q2, a temporary impact on the 100 Gbps per lane product.

Supply and channel (Emily Yang, CFO Brett Whitmire): channel inventory decreased in dollars and weeks again, below the normal range of 11 weeks to 14 weeks, and management sees no double booking; 'the supply disruption I've mentioned on previous calls continues', and with demand so strong 'definitely there are pockets where supply is a little bit constrained'. Total inventory rose to $504.6 million while inventory days fell to approximately 152 from 157; the CFO said the build supports customers, expected growth and 'longer wafer manufacturing lead times'.
channel inventory below normal 11 to 14 weeks; inventory $504.6 million; inventory days approximately 152 (157 prior quarter)

On our remaining 830 MW of approved capacity at Helios Two (energization slated for late 2028), conversations continue to advance across hyperscalers, Neoclouds, some of the labs themselves, and some new entrants; new guarantee and lease wrap structures are being formalized. We've already placed deposits and issued purchase orders on more than $180 million of long-lead electrical equipment, including main power transformers and switchgear. West's Pitchfork switching station is under construction to support energization of this 830 MW.
830 MW approved at Helios Two unleased, late-2028 energization; >$180M long-lead electrical equipment ordered

Governor Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to conduct a comprehensive audit of all data center projects seeking grid interconnection; we no longer expect communication on Batch Zero classification in the coming days. Forward market demand for power and compute is stronger today than it's ever been, while forward market supply of new projects is very quickly being constrained by both physical delivery and political headwinds. Leases for power at this scale are increasingly being signed well ahead of energization.

Full-year FY2026 forecast raised: revenue from JPY 500 billion to JPY 550 billion (+10%), electronics from JPY 350 billion to JPY 375 billion (+14%); operating profit from JPY 90 billion to JPY 127 billion (+41%, operating margin expectation raised from 18% to 23%), electronics OP from JPY 75 billion to JPY 110 billion; net profit raised to JPY 84 billion. Biggest driver: ASP and product mix with a positive impact of JPY 26.5 billion (majority is ASP - the planned quarterly price-reduction curve became less steep or prices were not reduced at all, plus general substrate price increases in an industry-wide supply shortage; not concentrated in a particular customer - GPU, CPU, switching IC and PC ASPs rising across the board). Revenue growth expected in all sub-segments: AI server, switching IC, and general-purpose server/PC.
FY revenue guide JPY 550 billion (from JPY 500 billion); OP JPY 127 billion (from JPY 90 billion, +41%); ASP/mix impact +JPY 26.5 billion

Supply-demand: 'The situation where demand exceeds the industry supply capacity is expected to continue' - substrates are getting larger and more difficult toward next fiscal year and the one after, AI server demand keeps rising, and current selling prices are expected to at least hold at present levels. Customers accepted fewer price cuts, and in some cases none, because of industry-wide shortages. Glass cloth and CCL cost increases are passed through to ASP in a timely manner. Utilization: apart from Intel Cell 5, almost everything was at full capacity utilization; sourcing for the revised FY2026 plan is already secured, though industry-wide competition for materials and equipment could constrain material supply in coming years.
Demand exceeds industry supply capacity; near-full utilization except Intel Cell 5; prices expected to at least hold

Glass cloth: procurement risks flagged at the beginning of the year have been mitigated. The number of glass cloth suppliers has increased - previously two companies in Japan and Taiwan, now a third and fourth supplier are visible, giving four glass cloth suppliers with visibility for use in mass production; the Japanese glass cloth supplier is increasing capacity, and the tight glass cloth supply situation is expected to simmer down. Ibiden believes it is in an advantageous position in the industry for glass cloth supply. Glass core substrate: joint development continuing (glass core and component-embedding structures pursued as two separate options with their own roadmaps, possibly narrowing to one later).
Four glass cloth suppliers now visible for mass production (was two); Japanese supplier adding capacity
