CFO Ankit Kumar Singhal: inventory days rose from 86 days in March to 110 days in June 2026, primarily from building raw-material stock 'to secure adequate inventory of key inputs in light of surging global demand for AI compute infrastructure'; given 'shortage shocks' across the industry the higher inventory is a deliberate decision, and he does not see memory prices softening in the next couple of quarters, 'maybe a year or so'. CMD Sanjay Lodha: component scarcity has been increasing over the last few quarters; direct relationships with technology providers and in-house manufacturing put Netweb 'in a better supply situation than others'; price increases are passed through on new orders and margins have not been impacted. CMD: 'more than the compute, the data center equipment is under shortage' - racks, chillers and other mechanical equipment.

Utilisation and supply: ABF substrate utilisation held above 90%, BT at 80% to 85%, HDI and PCB at 85% to 90% in Q2. Raw-material cost increases are being passed through via product price adjustments negotiated with customers, with further selective price rises planned in Q3. Optical-module PCB demand is described as in severe shortage; Unimicron is re-routing existing capacity and will bring the additional optical-module board capacity online in Q4 2026.
utilisation: ABF above 90%, BT 80-85%, HDI/PCB 85-90%; optical-module PCB capacity from re-routed lines opens Q4 2026

Labor constraint: WEC reduced 2026 spending on the Peoples Gas PIPE retirement program in Chicago because getting a labor force has been more challenging amid economic development 'from data centers to generation'; CEO expects to ramp the workforce up in 2027.

Book-to-bill improved month by month through Q2 and reached 2.2 by end of June (from roughly 1.3-1.5 last quarter). Customers - mostly the high-growth AI-driven names in computing and enterprise whose programs involve memory/SSDs - are increasingly asking for long-term agreements and are even willing to pay a premium to secure passive-component supply for the next 6 months, a year, in some cases multi-year baselines; some have already placed orders under these talks. The conversations typically start with capacitors (across dielectrics, not just MLCC or tantalum) and extend across resistors, circuit protection, inductors and sensors. LTA interest currently comes mostly from direct end customers (fulfillment can still run through distribution/EMS), and management noted demand acceleration in certain areas - 'memory, solid state drive is a good example'.
book-to-bill 2.2 by end of June, improving month by month

Capacity is tight: Q3 utilization rates will be raised above 90% for BOTH commodity and specialty (from about 85% blended / 80% commodity in Q2) to meet demand and rebuild healthy inventory. Capacity is being expanded across the board - Kaohsiung (the large purpose-built MLCC fab, running tight), Vietnam, Suzhou and Mexico - led by tantalum and MLCC; only less than NT$3 billion of capex was spent in H1 with larger increments planned for H2, and equipment lead times are long so expansion is planned ahead, adding capacity quarter by quarter. Channel inventory is lean and healthier than a year ago: Greater China distribution about 2 months on hand (about five to six turns, versus 3 months a year ago), global distribution about 4 months, high-service channel 5-6 months (from 7-8 a year ago).
Q3 utilization >90% (commodity and specialty), up from ~85%/80%; H1 capex <NT$3B; Greater China channel ~2 months on hand

Management endorsed as 'a fair characterization' the view that high-capacitance MLCC demand ramping alongside next-generation AI servers will force conversion of mid/low-end capacity and put shortage pressure on the rest of the portfolio - part of its customer conversations already cover securing that non-AI piece too, with peers also raising MLCC utilization. Adjacent driver: the whole AI power chain 'from the grid down to the rack of the server' has many voltage step-down/conversion stages needing filtering and ripple-current management, driving strong growth in film capacitors and aluminum electrolytic capacitors plus the magnetics (inductors) and connector lines - embedded across computing, industrial and telecom segments. In notebooks, new tantalum packaging offering higher capacitance in a smaller package positions a laptop recovery as more of a 2027 story.

CFO: the global helium supply chain remains a point of attention; Qatar production restarted at limited/reduced capacity and Air Liquide secured some volume, while Q2 also saw restrictions on Russian product to China and out of China. The helium shortage weighed on merchant volumes. CFO: electronics customers are supplied under long-term contracts and helium is 'in no means a limitation' to the electronics business; the company uses its storage cavern and multiple other sources, but stays 'extremely cautious' as the situation is fluid.

Carrier is fully booked for the second half; customers are pushing to accelerate deliveries rather than push them into 2027, and management sees no double-ordering risk because it is delivering into a rotable pool under strategic relationships in which hyperscalers and colos have established the share they expect to give Carrier. Additional resources have been moved into supply chain, supplier quality and factory quality to execute the ramp.

Cost per megawatt has risen versus the CoreWeave sites, where labour and equipment were secured starting in early 2024. Equipment costs are up year over year, partly on tariffs and partly on supply-chain constraints and availability, but 'the thing that's primarily driving the cost of construction today is labour' - large general contractors, electrical subcontractors and mechanical trades are saturated with work and scarce across a number of competitive U.S. geographies. On demand, management says data center capacity is still in very short supply and that large-scale GPU contracts are being signed today whose GPUs 'do not have a home yet', with a lot of GPUs sitting on the ground after late deliveries across the industry, which should tighten data-center supply further.

Power development at Pecos: an analyst noted an ERCOT update due August 7 covering roughly 815 MW, and management confirmed about 300 MW of that is the on-grid load study for Pecos with the rest behind-the-meter; given the uncertainty on the timing of that next 300 MW of on-grid power, the next megawatts at Pecos will be driven by the behind-the-meter strategy. Core Scientific is in advanced conversations with natural gas suppliers, has done preliminary planning on lateral pipeline development to the Pecos and Muskogee sites, and has held integrated conversations with on-site generation equipment providers - evaluating turbines, reciprocating engines, linear generators and fuel cells, with the technology choice varying by site geography, environmental conditions and supply-chain availability. The critical path per site is either the time to build the lateral pipeline or generation equipment manufacturing and production capacity. Capital was released for substation construction earlier this year across multiple sites, other sites are pad-ready for utility energization, and the full shell for the first 185 MW at Pecos will be complete within weeks.
~815 MW pending the ERCOT update (~300 MW on-grid load study at Pecos); 185 MW first shell at Pecos

Capacity: capex $28 million in the quarter, over $50 million year-to-date, now roughly $100 million for the year (under 3% of sales), accelerating investment in Cuprion and thermal interface materials for hyperscale customers plus plant consolidation. Element is not capacity constrained in semi by and large, but is capacity constrained in TIMs and other engineered materials and is adding capacity as fast as it can; it is taking sticky share where it is first to market or where under-capitalized local competitors cannot float metal at current prices.

Across electronics customers capacity is being added: device assemblers and EMS shops, printed circuit board fabs in and outside China, huge investments in Taiwan and Korea, and semi fabs expanding at the leading edge; utilization is very high at the advanced end, supporting substantial capacity additions at leading-edge circuit board fabs, semi foundries and device assemblers. Management does not see this abating in the near term.

CEO: mature-node supply has moved from cyclical swings to an irreversible structural tightening - 8-inch and 12-inch mature capacity has become a strategic resource, global capacity expansion lags demand, and shortages of labour, materials or capacity are the new normal, so foundry pricing has long-term support rather than being a short-lived phenomenon. Faraday's value is shifting from design technology (now only the entry ticket) to full value-chain management: capacity booking, wafer allocation, packaging and test capacity coordination and cost management. On 2027: mature-node capacity for Q4 2026 is already very full and will squeeze into Q1 2027 for both 8-inch and 12-inch; management expects next year to be as tight as this year and, given the UMC relationship, sees Faraday benefiting as it did during the pandemic, with a higher chance of securing capacity - calling it the best timing for Faraday.
mature-node 8-inch and 12-inch capacity full in Q4 2026, squeezing into Q1 2027; no specific figure

Macronix business update: NOR is under strong demand in all segments, with prices also reflecting market trends, and high-density NOR remains in undersupply with demand increasing. In NAND, the SLC NAND and eMMC structural shortage remains, and the company says capacity will be expanded to meet demand.

Demand visibility improved into Q4 and Q1: backlog is growing across quarter-plus-one through quarter-plus-three, providing an 18-month signal; book-to-bill is above 1 and above last quarter, customer escalations doubled sequentially, and lead times above 16 weeks now cover a large part of the portfolio.
book-to-bill >1; 18-month backlog signal; escalations doubled QoQ; broad lead times >16 weeks

Memory market: AI servers keep driving HBM demand and high-end memory packaging demand stays very strong; DRAM and NAND market demand and prices are rising together, with customers maximising output of committed capacity - customer revenue gains are mostly price-driven as supply is limited, but PTI's packaging volumes are still growing and utilisation keeps improving. Packaging material costs keep rising and PTI is passing them through to customers gradually (its customers are large long-term partners, so price adjustments are made carefully each quarter). AI-server eSSD demand keeps rising with shipments expanding QoQ and YoY.

Demand for the Wi-Fi, data-center and automotive growth engines is running well ahead of supply; data-center demand accelerated above 50%, book-to-bill remained above 1 and channel inventories were lean. Management characterized the shortages as broad-based across faster-growing products.
data-center demand >50% growth and supply-constrained; book-to-bill >1

Demand across Skyworks' data-center, automotive and Wi-Fi growth engines is ahead of available supply. Management said data-center demand accelerated above the prior greater-than-50% outlook while shortages remained broad-based across the faster-growing products.
data-center demand above >50% outlook and constrained by supply

→ Faraday Technology: CEO: with 8-inch and 12-inch mature-node capacity tight into Q1 2027, Faraday's relationship with UMC gives it a higher chance of securing capacity, as during the pandemic; MCU subsidiary Artery's capacity access was backed by strong UMC support. Android -20% QoQ on memory supply; Vietnam adding SiP + NAND memory capacity

Android -20% QoQ on memory supply; Q3 comms -high-single-digits (atypical); SiP drag into 1H27

Constraints and execution: CEO says managing supply chain and power are 'probably the two biggest constraints at the moment'. Applied Digital has contracted 2.1 GW of utility power over the past year and times building starts to when power becomes available. On supply chain, it locked in large mechanical, electrical and plumbing capacity a few years ago - about 700 MW per year of critical IT load - and has contracted to build 1.5 GW over the next couple of years, 'definitely exceeding that a little bit'; it has kept expanding that limit. Construction pace: the first Polaris Forge 1 building took about 24 months from start of construction to RFS, the second under 12 months. It previously said it could work on seven campuses simultaneously (five today); the CEO thinks it can go higher but does not want to overextend. Labor rates have been fairly steady over the past six months; the company avoids crowded markets (the CEO says it is the only one really building in North Dakota) and trains workers with local technical and vocational colleges. New-campus builds run toward the high end of its cost band because the first buildings carry all campus costs (new substations and on-campus transmission, land, the power site); one southern site will be slightly higher because of additional dirt work and site prep.

2.1 GW utility power contracted over the past year; about 700 MW per year supply chain capacity vs 1.5 GW contracted to build; about 24 months to RFS for the first building, under 12 months for the second

demand > guided revenue; lead times >52 wks; capex $1B FY26 / ~$1.5B FY27

multiple next-gen AI/ML compute programs ramping 2027; demand > guided revenue

CPS revenue $546 million (+29.2% YoY); capex $100.9 million (Q4: $135 million)

AI & cloud sales 2x YoY to EUR 446M; order intake EUR 2.8B; ~half converts within 12 months

MEMORY-RELATED NET SYSTEM SALES NOW GUIDED TO GROW OVER 75% IN 2026 — memory was 49% of Q2 net system sales (EUR 6.6B total). Driver per CEO Christophe Fouquet: 'the supply challenges driving up both DDR AND HBM PRICES have prompted significant investments in fab expansion', with customers adding meaningful capacity this year AND planning MULTIPLE MEGA FABS that come online in phases over the coming years. Ordering and backlog turned up in Q4 2025: management 'saw a good step up in the ordering patterns', the book-to-bill ratio 'was well in excess of one', and backlog is 'starting to extend out into Q2 2026'; channel inventory stayed at the low end of MPS's range. book-to-bill well in excess of one; backlog extending into Q2 2026

more than $4 billion of geographically balanced capacity secured

Capacity ramp: around $1.5 billion of announced investments across around two dozen (24) projects to expand Electrical Americas capacity. Half finished construction by mid-2025 and started ramping in the second half (mostly Q4), continuing to ramp in 2026; construction of half of the remaining projects will be largely done by the first half of 2026 with ramp starting at the end of the first half; the last quarter of projects continues through 2026 with production ramp in 2027. $1.5 billion across 24 projects; ramp margin impact about 100 basis points (2025) and about 130 basis points (2026); last projects ramp in 2027

CALL-ONLY: HYPERSCALER DEMAND AND BUILD SPEED. Asked whether customers could pause builds over bubble concerns, management said: 'Hyperscalers are not talking about a bubble. They are talking about they don't have enough fast enough', and 'many of our contracts have performance bonuses in them for us to go faster'. Capacity for the applied ramp (CEO Dave Regnery / CFO Chris Kuehn): 'our chiller capacity over the last, you know, two or three years is up over four x', through new builds, lean work and new lines. Management also works with supply-chain partners on their capacity because 'their ability could hinder us if we're not careful' - 'we're in good shape there'. Trane commissions its applied systems with its own field force of over 7,500 technicians globally. Asked about capex, the CFO confirmed the analyst's capex-to-revenue range for the last few years ('You're right, Jeff') and said 'it's been able to support all the capacity expansions we needed to do', and that 'we brought in businesses on air handling or industrial process cooling capacity for data centers' via M&A, which adds capacity inside Trane's four walls. chiller capacity up over four x (last two or three years); over 7,500 technicians

PRODUCTION TEST IS THE FASTER GROWER; REPURPOSED PRODUCTION CAPACITY IS A FRACTION OF WHAT IS NEEDED. Node cadence has compressed: 'We now see the new each technology notes turning over. Every two years. So no longer, let's say, between between a 100 gig and a 400 gig you have six years. technology nodes turning over every two years (vs six years between a 100 gig and a 400 gig); significant growth over the next two years

Legrand unveils its data-center roadmap, including its vision of the transition to Low Voltage Direct Current (LVDC) architectures and a full roadmap designed to enable next-generation gigawatt-scale AI data centers; 'chip to grid' solutions and numerous innovations to be commercialized over the coming quarters. Market drivers cited: AI workloads, rising rack density, faster time to operation and new power-distribution architectures. A Malaysia case study (with Linkk Busway Systems) presents a regional data-center platform combining local production, engineering, project execution and recent acquisitions.

HIGH BANDWIDTH COMPUTE MOVES FROM THE DATA CENTER TO THE SMARTPHONE. CEO Cristiano Amon: HBC, the engine that 'connects memory and the accelerator' introduced with Qualcomm's data-center entry, 'is now scaled all the way into the smartphone' - 'we developed HBC for Snapdragon as a co-processor to Snapdragon that is going to bring memory and AI processing closer together'. He expects it in laptops, smart glasses and cars as well, and said the HBC-for-Snapdragon announcement will come at Mobile World Congress. Rationale: future agentic AI devices 'may process up to 1 million tokens per day on device'.
up to 1 million tokens per day on device (future agentic devices)

PhotonLink formally launched at ECOC (pre-announced on the August earnings call). CMO Sanjai Parthasarathi introduced it as 'our integrated optics platform, purpose-built for AI data center connectivity', and CEO Jim Anderson set out its scope and rationale: it is a single integrated platform that is 'architecture agnostic, that works across CPO, NPO, chip-to-chip as well', and it exists because a number of customers 'came to us and asked' for 'the complete optical solution, the complete assembly' rather than components, since pulling together laser sources, fiber optic cable, complex optical assemblies and passive optics is the hard part of moving to optics. Anderson framed the transition it targets: telecom, scale-across and scale-out networks were long ago converted from electrical to optical, and over the coming years 'the only remaining electrical portions of the network' - the scale-up network and even chip-to-chip links - will become photonic. His end-to-end example for a switch or compute chip fed by an external laser source: Coherent supplies the complete ELS, the complete optical assembly from the ELS to the chip, and the complete optical assembly back out to the faceplate for photonic I/O. He argued only Coherent has the whole generate/shape/guide/detect technology set in-house, and cited 'hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies' delivered as evidence it can ramp at data-center scale.
architecture agnostic across CPO, NPO and chip-to-chip; hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies delivered

CEO Jim Anderson laid out production timing by architecture. CPO (unchanged from the August call): 'our first production will start to ramp in our December quarter, this Q4 of this calendar year', initially for scale-out, then 'About a year later, in the second half of 2027, we'll start ramping CPO for scale-up applications.' New at the launch: NPO is expected 'to start to ramp in the second half of next calendar year' (calendar 2027), 'primarily for scale-up applications', and chip-to-chip optical links are 'a little further out', expected 'in the 2029, 2030 timeline', although customer design activity on chip-to-chip photonic connections is already intense.
CPO scale-out ramp in the December quarter (Q4 of this calendar year); CPO scale-up in the second half of 2027; NPO in the second half of next calendar year; chip-to-chip in the 2029, 2030 timeline

CTO Julie Eng laid out the CPO vs NPO trade-off: CPO puts the optical engine literally on the package of the switch or XPU chip and offers the lowest power consumption and, in many cases, the highest density, while NPO moves the optics off the package onto the board right next to it - easier to deploy and more serviceable, but moving it away from the chip costs power and the socket impacts signal integrity. NPO is also an architectural platform: a common form factor and socket can accommodate either silicon photonics or VCSELs, and Coherent is a founder of the Open CPX MSA, helping develop an open ecosystem for a common connector among vendors to give customers architectural flexibility.

CTO Julie Eng said interest in chip-to-chip optical interconnect has grown a lot in the last 3-9 months (this calendar year): as bandwidth between compute and memory scales, the optical link moves from the edge of the package to the interior of the package - after the intercontinental, terrestrial, data-center and now in-rack shifts from electronics to photonics, 'the next frontier, inside the chip package'. Customers are looking at multiple architectures, including an ELS with ultra-high-power lasers, integrated lasers and high-density VCSEL solutions, and with so many lanes there is a lot of discussion of WDM, making circulators and WDM multiplexers 'a very important architectural tool'.
interest up over the last 3-9 months

Arteris launched FlexGen Multi-Die, a NoC IP for non-coherent AI and HPC chiplet architectures that complements Ncore Multi-Die (cache-coherent), Magillem integration automation and Cycuity hardware security assurance. FlexGen Multi-Die supports bidirectional transactions over a single UCIe PHY, reducing PHY area, power and I/O requirements by up to 50% (company claim), with virtual-channel link technology and QoS across die-to-die links. The expanded multi-die solution is available today to early access partners and strategic customers; the company says customers are already using its technology to move from single-die to multi-die products. The release carries supporting statements from AMD (the multi-die portfolio 'supports the flexibility and productivity required for our next generation of data center, client, gaming, and embedded compute products'), Socionext (collaborating with Arteris on its UCIe-based multi-die solution, with early access), Synopsys (validated interoperability of its UCIe IP with Arteris Ncore), UniVista (UCIe interoperability with Ncore Multi-Die), Cadence (physical-AI collaboration) and Silitronics (plans to use FlexGen in an OCP-derived chiplet architecture).
PHY area, power and I/O reduced by up to 50%; available today to early access partners and strategic customers
Arteris press release: Arteris Accelerates Industry Transition to Multi-Die (09-15-2026)

He said interest from KV cache and compute is so strong that the company does not need to focus as much on QLC pure-storage drives.
16 terabyte NAND flash drive for KV cache (Rubin); multibillion-dollar market
Silicon Motion Piper Sandler growth frontiers conference 2026 (09-15-2026)

Deal size and density are stepping up. Shaw: 'Whereas a 250 kVA deal was a large deal for us, a megawatt is kind of the going thing now.' That is denser than we have ever gone'. He added that Equinix does 'not build gigawatt data centers to perform training'. Instead, xScale is meant to bring the clouds closer to the dense metro ecosystems. The moderator named the Hertfordshire campus and the Osaka site, and Shaw said 'those are the two right now that we are looking at. They are on track.'
250 kVA deal was a large deal; a megawatt is kind of the going thing now; DA12 about 67 megawatts at about 18 kVA per cabinet

Liquid-cooling strategy is to build it into new sites, not to retrofit old ones. Shaw: 'When we think about new builds, we think about liquid cooling. We're less prone to retrofitting a building for liquid cooling' and 'We're not going back and retrofitting a bunch of buildings for liquid cooling.' He said enterprise demand has changed: liquid-cooled space used to sit empty because customers found it 'really expensive', but 'Now it's a requirement'. The optional design means Equinix is 'not stuck with liquid cooling that we're not utilizing'. CFO Ryan Burke compared the in-cage deployment to 'a NASCAR pit crew': customers who want liquid cooling pay for it, and Equinix can pull it out and deploy it elsewhere when they no longer need it.

CEO Fred Thiel: Bitcoin mining infrastructure and compute typically cost somewhere around $1 million, $1.5 million a megawatt, very different from AI HPC, where revenue and asset value per megawatt provide a considerable step-up. MARA's model converts Bitcoin mining sites to AI: mining is load it can turn on immediately while waiting for energization, and as an AI tenant moves into the data center MARA deprecates mining there and moves it to another acquired site. Because the cost of Bitcoin mining ASICs has never been as low on a per terahash basis, MARA's exahash capacity does not have to shrink as the megawatt capacity allocated to Bitcoin shrinks.
Bitcoin mining build cost around $1 million, $1.5 million a megawatt
MARA Holdings h.c. wainwright global investment conference 2026 (09-14-2026)

Matt Ramsay: 'We haven’t been super specific on the gigawatt comments in terms of CPU.'
CPU to GPU: started at one to four; today one to one sort of ratio, going to continue to grow
AMD Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-11-2026)

SHARE INSIDE BUMP-PACKAGING INSPECTION, AND HYBRID BONDING AS THE NEXT STEP: Ahmad Khan (President of Semiconductor Products and Customers) says KLA entered advanced packaging about five, six years ago with 10% share and is 'Now we are above 50%, 56%, 57% share in advanced packaging', driven by capability requirements; he notes this is still bump packaging. Hybrid bonding / die-to-wafer bonding in logic (SOIC) brings 'a 10x change in specifications of defects that kill the die', pulling KLA's most advanced front-end systems into packaging, and the introduction of hybrid bonding in memory will tighten specs significantly as well. Economics: a logic wafer out of the front-end fab is worth '$30,000, $40,000, $50,000' and a memory wafer '$50,000, $60,000, $70,000', so a loss in packaging also loses that wafer's value and customers 'want to inspect every step'.

a little over one-fourth of the total business

Mechanism behind the better-than-expected July quarter, which the Q3 call did not spell out. April-quarter push-outs came from customers being unable to capture memory and from Asian fabs at unusually high utilization telling chip designs 'You have to delay your design because we don't have the capacity for it'. Through the July quarter those designs started to be released because the same fabs 'added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range', and in some cases told a customer with a 40 nanometer design 'if you move that chip design to 28 nanometers or 22 nanometers, I will then manufacture it for you' - i.e. the capacity shortage is actively forcing node migration, which is the ASP-positive trend Photronics benefits from. On the display side Korea is strong on high-end consumer electronics launching this fall while China has pulled back because low-end consumer electronics cannot capture memory; Moreau relayed that the memory companies are talking about 'another 2, 3, 4 years before supply and demand comes into equilibrium'.
fabs added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range and pushed 40 nanometer designs to 28 or 22 nanometers; memory supply and demand equilibrium another 2, 3, 4 years away

MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

INTEL 14A: 0.9 PDK IN OCTOBER, RISK PRODUCTION 2027, HIGH-VOLUME 2028: Zinsner said Intel is within two months of the 14A 0.9 PDK, so 'you can pretty much now expect us to land in October with that 0.9 PDK', and the remaining step from 0.9 to 1.0 is much smaller than 0.5 to 0.9. Defect density on Intel 14A is tracking better than the target curve and is coming down faster than any previous node - 'we haven't seen this performance since 22 nanometer, which is arguably one of the best nodes Intel's ever put out' - while 18A yields are beating internal milestones. Demand side: internal product teams, 'probably the most cynical bunch out of anybody', are now designing products on Intel 14A, and external foundry engagements have increased enough that Lip-Bu Tan and the team meet customers weekly and the conversation has moved from data to 'how much capacity can I get? What does that supply look like?'. That sequence forces risk production in 2027 ahead of high-volume manufacturing in 2028.
0.9 PDK in October; risk production in 2027; high volume production in 2028; 22 nanometer

DATA-CENTER VOLTAGE STEP-UP IN ONE YEAR - CONTENT MIX MOVING TO POWELL'S HIGH END: 'If I was sitting here last year talking specifically about data centers, it was 5,000 and 15,000 volt. 1.6T TEST ECONOMICS THE CALL DID NOT SIZE: CEO Oleg Khaykin said a 1.6T tester carries 'about 50% price increase' over an 800G box, 'because the components are much more expensive', comparing it to TSMC raising price per wafer 'about 1.5x' each node. → NVIDIA: Siemens developed a reference architecture together with NVIDIA, nVent and Fluence across compute, cooling, power and control systems for the latest NVIDIA DGX Vera Rubin platform — goal: maximizing tokens per watt and ensuring predictable, scalable operations; Siemens built a modular, scalable automation framework on it with ready-to-use Simatic libraries.

BOYD RAISED AND THE 800V PLAYBOOK: Boyd (liquid cooling — COLD PLATES + CDUs) raised to $1.8B FY2026 revenue, up from the ~$1.7B+ trajectory flagged in Q1 ($1.5B lands in Eaton's books; Boyd did $1.1B in 2025); Q2 $432M was 20% ABOVE plan; wins on being the DESIGN PARTNER embedded in chip providers' roadmaps (first look/first bid), aerospace-grade quality at scale (smaller rivals showing 'quality issues from the get-go'), and it hands Eaton an early strategic read into chip development; joins organic growth in 2027. 800V DC: content ~$3.4M PER MW CONFIRMED 'the right number'; the customer objective is TOKENS PER MEGAWATT (~5% efficiency gain from DC conversion — 'when there's so much money involved, this is going to happen'). Eaton frames FOUR technical blocks required to win 800V — (1) medium-voltage SOLID-STATE TRANSFORMER (Resilient Power, 'clearly ahead' per hyperscaler and chip-maker feedback), (2) DC BREAKER technology, (3) power electronics/power quality (UPS), (4) COOLING (Boyd) — plus a service network that arrives 'in an hour, not days'; players missing blocks 'will have a really hard time.' Prefab/modular (Fibrebond): electrician/plumber scarcity pushes modular builds, and 800V's simpler architecture INCREASES the modular opportunity, extending Eaton from gray space into white space.
Boyd raised to $1.8B FY26 (Q2 +20% vs plan); $3.4M/MW confirmed; 800V = 4 blocks (SST/DC breaker/UPS/cooling) + service; modular expands with 800V

Advanced Solutions, which includes the Fluxless Thermo-Compression (FTC) bonding platform, recognised revenue 20% ABOVE last quarter's record. K&S is maintaining its target of OVER $100 MILLION in Advanced Solutions revenue for fiscal 2026, and for fiscal 2027 Lester Wong guided TCB revenue to a range of $150 MILLION TO $200 MILLION - significant sequential growth. The company remains closely engaged with a broad base of IDM, OSAT and foundry customers as heterogeneous packaging goes mainstream, with particular confidence in heterogeneous integration around logic for Fluxless TCB.
Advanced Solutions revenue 20% above prior record; >$100M Advanced Solutions target for FY2026; TCB guided to $150M-$200M in FY2027

Beyond thermocompression, K&S accelerated its HYBRID BONDING program over the last year and says its hybrid bonder has unique features not currently in the market; it PLANS TO DELIVER A HYBRID BONDING TOOL TO A CUSTOMER IN THE FIRST HALF OF FISCAL 2027. It is also investing significantly in a PANEL-level project, seeing a lot of interest from IDMs, foundries and OSATs because panel geometry allows many more dies on a rectangle than a circle; specific panel applications are still being scoped with customers. Management frames FTC, vertical wire, direct copper-to-copper, hybrid and panel-based architectures as the emerging packaging set that will be critically necessary across a much wider array of semiconductor production, and stresses the industry is still in the relatively early stages of this More-than-Moore advanced packaging transition.
Hybrid bonding tool to be delivered to a customer in H1 FY2027

NAND is turning: MKS saw increased momentum in NAND UPGRADE activity in Q2 and expects it to continue, possibly better. RF power is the LARGEST PART OF THE BILL OF MATERIALS in such an upgrade, which is why MKS benefits disproportionately from upgrades. Announced NAND GREENFIELD fabs are expected to come in towards the END OF 2027 AND BEGINNING OF 2028, which would be even better because MKS would supply the rest of its semiconductor portfolio around a brand-new tool; NAND should become a bigger percentage of semi revenue in 2028. Until then the mix stays largely logic and DRAM driven.
NAND greenfield fabs expected end-2027 into 2028; NAND to become a bigger share of semi revenue in 2028

Demonstrated 2,200 volt PowiGaN technology, extending PowiGaN into application spaces traditionally served by silicon carbide and using the same proven architecture as the prior 750, 900, 1,250 and 1,700 volt nodes, with eight years of demonstrated field reliability and 1,500 volt architectures already in view. Positioned as a single-platform alternative to complex stacked-device approaches so data-center customers can adopt GaN today without being forced to change technologies on next-gen designs. Timing: it is a technology demonstration, not a launched product; data-center products would sit on the 1,500 volt roadmap, 'several years' out — 'the next couple of years before we see anything meaningful there', not the next couple of quarters.
2,200 volt PowiGaN demonstrated; products several years out (1,500 volt roadmap)

Data-center engagement runs on two tracks. (1) Main power path to the GPU — the biggest component of the projected billion-dollar data-center SAM — being developed with customers around Power Integrations' 1,250 volt GaN as a high-density alternative to stacked 650 volt designs; this track is earlier, still requires work with customers, and depends on when the 800 volt systems deploy. (2) Auxiliary power in and around the rack — switch trays, power sidecars and other high-voltage sockets — where there is 'a healthy roster of design-ins and a strong pipeline of ongoing design activity' with 1,700 volt products for 800 volt data centers, addressable with products in hand today and pointing to revenue in 2028. Broad range of ongoing customer engagements addressing 800 volt data centers; recent hyperscaler discussions confirm power remains a major challenge.
Aux-power design-ins could be revenue in 2028; main GPU power path further out

Battery energy storage: already shipping SCALE-2 gate-driver boards into battery storage systems used alongside renewable installations, and won an important new customer in Q2 — a utility-scale design at a top supplier of batteries for energy storage systems and EVs (customer not named). Rising power demands are pushing storage toward higher-voltage architectures and greater silicon-carbide adoption, which requires more advanced gate drivers. A number of customer engagements are underway for battery storage specifically targeting AI data centers, described as another element of the projected billion-dollar data-center SAM in 2030. Deployments of battery storage are expected to grow at a double-digit CAGR through 2035.
One new utility-scale gate-driver design win; billion-dollar data-center SAM in 2030

→ NVIDIA: In June, Power Integrations published two reference designs targeting NVIDIA 800 volt racks using its 1,700 volt InnoMux products. These auxiliary supplies sit on the compute tray in a native 800 volt system, powering components such as MCUs, gate drivers and op-amps, and deliver space savings of about 30% compared to discrete silicon carbide designs. Alongside the aux track, the main power path to the GPU is being developed with 1,250 volt GaN as a high-density alternative to stacked 650 volt designs. Aux-power design-ins point to revenue in 2028; the main power path depends on when the 800 volt systems deploy.
units: two reference designs; 1,700 volt InnoMux aux supplies on the compute tray; about 30% space saving vs discrete silicon carbide

Drug-design efficiency: candidates are being advanced with roughly 330 synthesized compounds over about 1.5 years versus an industry benchmark of roughly 2,500 compounds over four years. REC-7735 was designed in 10 months using 242 compounds across 13 cycles and is nearly 130x selective over wild type.
~330 compounds / 1.5 years vs ~2,500 / 4 years; REC-7735: 242 compounds, 13 cycles, 10 months

Advanced nodes portfolio grew more than 20% in Q2 (Investor Day plan was ~7%): continued growth at three nanometer, emerging activity at two nanometer, really strong pull for 2 nm and 18A, and successful scale-up of HBM3/HBM4 on the memory side; advanced nodes were about 40% of the portfolio exiting the first half versus the 45%-50% Investor Day target, which Qnity expects to reach early.
advanced nodes +20% YoY; ~40% of portfolio vs 45%-50% target

New advanced packaging architectures (panel-level packaging, larger package formats, tighter lines and spaces on high-layer-count boards and IC substrates) all mean more material complexity and more material intensity, with fewer suppliers able to qualify; Qnity has incumbency with the same customers that commercialized the existing advanced packaging formats and expects more content per package as formats grow. Customer capacity expansions in advanced packaging underpin the durability of ICS growth.

AMD's new MI450 series is on schedule and Wistron, as AMD's main component-level supporter, sees AMD's customer forecasts growing (citing Lisa Su's optimism). Beyond components, Wistron has already taken rack/system orders for MI450 from customers ('yes'), on schedule to ship together with AMD's product ramp in H2 2026; whether Wistron builds components or full AMD systems is decided by the customer, across enterprise and CSP.

VR (Vera Rubin) is already in mass production - management confirmed it, citing Jensen - and the generation handover has caused no Q3 air pocket: some customers still prefer GB300 so GB300 volume persists, while others are moving to VR, leaving Q3 looking quite good. Wistron expects to keep a reasonable margin after the VR launch despite the higher rack price, with OP margin 'no worse than GB300' and the trend holding into H1 2027 when VR volume ramps; some new customers are starting directly on VR. Wistron is also working on the pure Vera CPU racks and switch/storage racks NVIDIA announced alongside VR, has already received orders for the new products, and will ship them in H2 2026.
→ AMD: MI450 series is on schedule; Wistron is AMD's main component-level supporter and has additionally received customer orders for MI450 rack systems, shipping when AMD's product ramps in H2 2026.

→ NVIDIA: Vera Rubin is already in mass production and Wistron ships as NVIDIA's component-level partner; Wistron has also received orders for NVIDIA's new Vera-based products (pure Vera CPU racks, switch and storage racks), shipping in H2 2026, and NVIDIA develops these new products with its small set of ODM partners.

Long-term targets raised: the annual revenue target goes to $600 million from $500 million, driven by the semiconductor market. The long-term semiconductor opportunity is raised to $200 million annually from the previously estimated $100 million, on broader and faster adoption of hybrid bonding; CEO: achievable in about five years (the long-range planning horizon). The long-term media target is unchanged at $400 million annually. CEO: e-commerce licensing could grow over the long term to a size similar to consumer electronics, which has been approximately 10% of total revenue.
long-term revenue target $600 million (from $500 million); semiconductor $200 million annually (from $100 million) in about five years; media $400 million

CEO view on hybrid-bonding adoption: hybrid bonding has become a critical enabler of next-generation chip architectures (density, performance, thermal management). AMD started shipping hybrid-bonded logic devices in 2022; Apple, Intel and Broadcom all have products ramping into production using hybrid bonding. He believes hybrid bonding will be a requirement in HBM with 20 or more layers, if not sooner, and in NAND as layer counts approach 400, with the big three memory players all ramping to get there. Leading foundries, memory companies and OSATs are planning to spend approximately $125 billion in the near term on advanced packaging including hybrid bonding — 'we know broad adoption of hybrid bonding is coming because the capital equipment required is being ordered.' Hyperscalers 'are semiconductor companies now', differentiating with their own chips, which he expects to create additional opportunity. He puts the semiconductor market at over $1.5 trillion this year.
HBM with 20 or more layers; NAND approaching 400 layers; ~$125 billion near-term advanced-packaging spend; semiconductor market over $1.5 trillion

The new Turing design center began trial operation in Q2 running small and mid-size projects and is expected to be in full use in H2; it adds some depreciation/R&D cost but is aimed squarely at 3nm, 2nm and even more advanced process work plus advanced packaging. The R&D roadmap already includes CPO, IVR (integrated voltage regulator), next-generation UCIe die-to-die, and N2-on-N2 advanced-process development; opex should grow only modestly versus a clearly larger revenue increase next year.

Capacity and technology roadmap: multi-site production at Yokkaichi (one of the world's largest flash memory bases, leading-edge R&D) and Kitakami; the K2 fab at Kitakami began operation in September 2025 and began production of the 10th generation BiCS FLASH this year. Capex plan: average JPY 470 billion annually from FY2026 to FY2028 (JPY 450 billion this year), flexible to market change and fully covered by cash flow. R&D about JPY 200 billion for the full year, concentrated on BiCS 10/BiCS 11 and AI inference SSDs (super high IOPS SSD for inference servers); UFS 5.0 new high-speed standard for edge AI / on-device AI announced. Strategy: not pursuing market share through aggressive investment - pursuing quality and profitability via higher sequential speed, energy efficiency and product quality.
Capex average JPY 470 billion/year FY2026-FY2028 (JPY 450 billion this year); R&D ~JPY 200 billion; BiCS10 in production at Kitakami K2, BiCS11 and AI inference SSD in development

AI data center applications drive the WFE market: sales to AI data center are expected to grow by five times or more in the five years from calendar 2023 through calendar 2027, spanning not only GPU and HBM but also DDR, CPU and 3D NAND. Technology transitions expected within two years: logic scaling from the 3 nanometer mainstream toward 2 nanometer with backside PDN adoption, DRAM evolving to the 1D node (1C to 1D transition), HBM stacked DRAM count rising from 12 to 16, and NAND evolving to 300 layers and further to 400 layers. Agentic AI is the driver of the overall WFE market; CY2026 WFE application mix is about 60% logic and 40% memory, versus 65%/35% last year.
AI data center WFE sales to grow five times or more CY2023-CY2027; HBM stacks from 12 to 16; NAND to 300 then 400 layers; logic mainstream 3 nanometer moving to 2 nanometer

Power electronics stable at a low level: SiC installed base underutilized, GaN utilization around 60%-70% and gradually increasing; GaN has a strong opportunity in AI data centers for 800-volt DC to DC conversion, with SiC coming first at the high-voltage entry point and GaN following with a delay; mid-term view of a GaN market 3X-ing to around EUR 450 million of tool revenue fully holds; AIXTRON systems (G5+ and G10-GaN) are the tools of record across the GaN power market, so customers are expected to arrive with multi-dozen tool orders when the wave starts
GaN installed-base utilization around 60%-70%; mid-term GaN tool revenue view around EUR 450 million

HVDC ramp: plus/minus 400V and 800V systems start mass production in Q3 2026, but Q4 shipments and full-year volume stay limited - larger volume comes next year. The plus/minus 400V architecture is being pushed more aggressively and ships more this year; 800V is driven mainly by NVIDIA and depends on when data-center operators adopt that power architecture - NVIDIA's Blackwell shipments are still much larger than Rubin, and part of the Rubin lineup can still run on low voltage. On the 110kW power shelf and other new product cycles Delta believes its market share remains high because it engages customers earliest, and the fast generational churn of AI power architecture favors its engineering resources; it declined to quantify share for the Rubin-linked 110kW PSU but asserts market leadership. A solid-state transformer (an energy gateway, not a one-for-one transformer replacement) has its first trial customers in smaller data centers, and a first small fuel-cell line starts by year-end with the first volume line planned next year, with units at Taipower and another test site performing well.
HVDC plus/minus 400V and 800V mass production from Q3, limited volume this year, ramp next year; 110kW power shelf share seen high

Liquid cooling keeps scaling: liquid-cooling products were about 10% of group revenue last year and will exceed 12% this year (an analyst cited about US$1.6 billion of Liquid-to-Air contribution last year). Management expects Liquid-to-Air to persist considerably longer than the market's assumption that Liquid-to-Liquid fully takes over around 2028.
liquid cooling about 10% of revenue last year, above 12% this year; Liquid-to-Air about US$1.6B contribution last year

Technology read-through on evolving cooling architectures: asked whether higher inlet fluid temperature specs for future GPU designs reduce chiller demand, management said demand is improving and increasing for Modine because of its free-cooling technology — a higher inlet temperature lets the unit run in free-cooling mode more of the time, driving further efficiency and reducing data-center power consumption, while the chiller and refrigerant cycle stay in place as the 'insurance policy' for temperatures above that band. Chillers support both facility cooling and incorporation into direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems — similar models and SKUs sit on the same data-center rooftop doing both — so Modine cannot split its order book between the two. The enhanced three-megawatt chiller is being introduced to customers and will raise output per line versus the 2 MW unit.
3 MW chiller launching (vs 2 MW today); higher GPU inlet temperatures increase free-cooling/chiller demand

BBU content growth with next-generation accelerators: asked about NVIDIA Rubin production starting and per-rack battery cell capacity possibly rising from 80 W to 120 W, management said the Rubin percentage will not be so high yet but Panasonic's portion will increase including capacity, and as the BBU solution evolves the unit price would go up - required output changes and the total solution expands ('it's not replacing PBU, but it's PBU plus CPU'); non-GPU demand (TPU, ASIC, including CPU racks for inference) is also expanding and is part of the JPY 550 billion full-year picture.
Per-rack battery cell capacity discussion 80 W to 120 W with Rubin; unit price to rise as BBU solution evolves

Management on Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi 7 notebook penetration is estimated to reach approximately 30% this year; broadband upgrades are constrained by higher DDR capacity requirements and system costs, and FTTR rollouts remain based on Wi-Fi 6. Wi-Fi 8 is expected to become a key technology focus from next year (plugfests underway), with commercial adoption first in PCs and routers, the earliest TV models around the first quarter of 2028, and tier 1 operators in Europe and North America expected to begin deploying Wi-Fi 8 routers in 2028. Management says Realtek's Wi-Fi development is on track and competitive. On broadband, 10G PON / XGS-PON is the baseline and tier 1 operators have begun testing 25G PON.
Wi-Fi 7 notebook penetration approximately 30% this year; Wi-Fi 8 routers in 2028

Market shift toward SPX solutions: as more liquid cooling goes under the roof, dry cooling appears to be the most favored heat-rejection solution, with adiabatic and cooling towers also in demand; SPX sees significantly increasing demand from existing hyperscalers and had nice wins with colos and neoclouds. Hyperscalers give visibility several years forward because they need SPX's product to turn the data center on and send teams of 10 people into SPX facilities for two weeks at a time.

Data center architecture roadmap (CEO): rising GPU power density per rack will require alternative power architectures - not overnight and not everything will switch. After the power rack, the priority over the next two years is an industrialized 'power center' with a new SST (solid-state transformer) solution, already prototyped and being tested with a couple of customers, to be ready when market demand accelerates. Motivair liquid cooling: 95% of Motivair sales were in North America at the acquisition; Schneider is now ready to manufacture liquid cooling equipment and CDUs in Conselve, Italy and in Bangalore, India to serve the rest of the world. New AVEVA DSX portfolio for the design stage and EcoCare condition-based maintenance services for data centers.

Data center: CEO said data center remained a leading contributor to growth in the computing, communications and diversified industrial (CCDI) market, and the CFO said it was the fastest-growing market in the quarter and the first half; management expects it to keep growing through the second half of 2026. CEO: this year's data center revenue is largely from low-voltage architectures; high-voltage architectures are expected 'probably in 2027 and beyond', with very low volume proof-of-concept shipments today that will ramp later.
high-voltage data center architectures expected probably in 2027 and beyond; very low volume proof-of-concept shipments today

High-voltage data center content: CEO said data center design wins more than doubled compared with a year before, heavily focused on the higher-voltage architectures, and the pipeline has heavy strength there. CFO: the content opportunity is two to four times higher in high voltage versus low voltage today in terms of revenue, and management is 'pretty confident' in the 25% to 30% CAGR over the next five years laid out for its data center markets.
data center design wins more than doubled YoY; high-voltage content two to four times low-voltage; 25% to 30% data center CAGR over five years

EMIB-T advanced packaging: Unimicron is one of three substrate makers (alongside two Japanese peers) qualified on the EMIB-T platform; first-phase yield target is 50%, with the customer contractually protecting supplier profitability below that yield and volume production starting next year (2027). Key EMIB-T equipment is centrally allocated among the three suppliers and second/third equipment sources are being qualified; EMIB-T-related investment is less than 10% of the raised capex and platform-dedicated equipment only 10% to 15% to 20% of that, since much of the new capacity is general FC-BGA for CPU-based inference designs that need no interposer. Management notes hyperscaler customers moving toward chiplet-style in-house designs are qualifying substrate suppliers directly and pre-booking capacity. Glass-core substrates: no volume production expected before 2029-2030, though R&D programs run with three customers, each customised. Mid-to-long-term gross-margin ambition is 50 to 60%.
EMIB-T first-phase yield target 50%, volume production 2027; EMIB-T investment under 10% of capex (dedicated equipment 10-15-20% of that); glass-core substrate volume not before 2029-2030

Ahead of schedule and currently billing for 437 MW of capacity. Billing began on 437 MW in mid-July, nearly 200 MW more than at the end of the first quarter, after substantially completing four of the five CoreWeave campuses ahead of the end-of-summer target. Management stresses that delivering hundreds of megawatts of high-density infrastructure 'requires far more than access to power' - it requires an integrated development and operating platform - and that the AMD sites are not greenfield: equipment is secured, contractors are on site across the five campuses, and at Pecos the building shell is essentially complete.
437 MW billable, nearly 200 MW more than at the end of Q1

The Bitcoin-mining-to-AI conversion is nearly complete: Core Scientific ended June with nearly 30% fewer miners online than at the end of the first quarter and is now self-mining at only two sites, running that business primarily to offset contractual power costs during the wind-down, which continues over the remainder of the year so that 2027 starts with a clean sheet of paper. Having spent the past year converting existing power capacity from Bitcoin mining to high-density colocation, the next phase complements that with selective acquisition of powered land and development of new sites: a new site pipeline of more than 2 GW of potential incremental power has been identified, with initial capacity potentially available from late 2028 through 2030, and management hopes to bring a new site to market by year-end. The Hunt County, Texas acquisition earlier this year is representative of that pipeline.
nearly 30% fewer miners online QoQ, self-mining at two sites; >2 GW new-site pipeline (late 2028-2030)

→ CoreWeave: Four of the five CoreWeave campuses were substantially completed ahead of the end-of-summer target, taking the program to 437 billable megawatts - nearly 200 MW more than at the end of the first quarter - and driving GAAP colocation revenue to $137 million. Dalton Phase II, the fifth and final campus and the last 150 MW of the CoreWeave build-out, begins delivering at the end of 2026 and is on track for full completion in early 2027. The relationship began as a 16 MW lease at the Auburn campus in 2024 and has since expanded to 590 MW of total contracted capacity; revenue is recognized straight-line over the 12-year lease terms, pulling contractual escalators forward. Auburn and Dalton become fully leased once the AMD-credit-supported neocloud leases are added.
units: 437 MW billable of 590 MW contracted; 150 MW remaining at Dalton Phase II; value: $137 million GAAP colocation revenue in the quarter

Advanced packaging (quantified as several hundred million dollars of revenue) is performing quite well with share gain in the IC substrate / package substrate part of circuitry, strong high-end paste and wafer-level packaging; Element is establishing processes of record for the transition from CoWoS to CoPoS and other emerging technologies expected to ramp about 18 months from now, and expects the advanced packaging business to accelerate into 2027 and 2028.
advanced packaging several hundred million dollars of revenue; CoWoS-to-CoPoS ramp ~18 months out

Product content for higher-capacity data centers: 'We're adapting some of our products for those applications ... our new Pin & Sleeve devices that are going to higher amperage to the 800 volt infrastructure.' Modular/factory-built trend: PCX power skids for data centers and System Control substation control houses built in a factory setting, DMC crimp connectors replacing field welds on busbar.
new Pin & Sleeve devices for 800 V data-center infrastructure

The next product wave is not yet in revenue: NXP's S32N 5-nanometer processor and S32K5 16-nanometer zonal-controller products remain in the design-win phase, while management said physical-AI deployments have not begun in earnest. Their future ramps underpin management's constructive 2027 outlook.
S32N 5nm and S32K5 16nm not yet ramping; physical-AI deployments still early

Fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) for AI: chairman confirms PTI is an AMD AI-chip supply-chain partner providing fan-out PLP solutions and is actively pursuing more AMD AI-chip applications; despite equipment-delivery delays, installation issues and doing new-product qualification in parallel, the program is on schedule and PTI is confident of volume production before the middle of next year, which would make it the world's first company to mass-produce fan-out PLP for AI applications. The former-AUO fab conversion is going smoothly: floor 1 for middle-end/RDL processing, floor 2 for chip-on-panel and mounting packages onto ABF substrates; the G7 panel equipment supporting the AMD program is fully installed and in qualification, with automation being added. PTI showed an engineering sample of a 5x-reticle-size AI package (one reticle = 26x33mm) - it says only TSMC otherwise has this capability - and notes a G7 panel fits about 45 such large AI packages versus 8 to 9 on a wafer, positioning panel output as a complement to foundry wafer-based advanced packaging. FOPLP equipment lead times run about a year plus installation; management estimates a new entrant would need roughly three years from ordering to customer qualification (PTI started fan-out panel work in 2015). In high-end flip-chip BGA, PTI already mass-produces large FC-BGA/MCM and will move a large one-reticle-size chip package into volume production in Q3.
AMD fan-out PLP volume production before mid-2027 (target: world's first FOPLP for AI); 5x reticle-size panel packages, ~45 per G7 panel vs 8-9 per wafer; FOPLP equipment lead time ~1 year

Optical/CPO roadmap: the Broadcom cooperation has brought PTI into optical communications - it will build Optical Engines using its panel fan-out technology, with small-volume production of the first OBO and OSFP versions starting around end-2026; integrating the Optical Engine into a switch (a CPO switch) is targeted to start shipping in H2 2027, and integration of the Optical Engine into AI chips is expected around 2028 or later once designs mature (engineering simulations already completed). Separately, TSV interconnection for DRAM co-developed with a partner has completed DDR-5 trial production and moves to volume production and shipments in Q4 2026 - a foundation for future HBM manufacturing that management expects to start shifting DRAM packaging from 30-year-old wire-bond formats toward advanced packaging, with a meaningful revenue and margin contribution from next year.
Optical Engine small-volume production from end-2026 (OBO, OSFP); CPO switch shipments from H2 2027; AI-chip integration ~2028; TSV-based DDR-5 DRAM volume production from Q4 2026

→ AMD: Chairman: PTI has become a supply-chain partner for AMD AI chips and will provide AMD fan-out PLP (panel-level packaging) solutions, and is actively pursuing additional AMD AI-chip applications. Despite equipment-delivery delays and parallel qualification, the AMD program is on schedule; PTI is confident of volume production before the middle of next year at the converted former-AUO fab, where the G7 panel equipment supporting AMD is installed and in qualification - which would make PTI the first company globally to mass-produce fan-out PLP for AI applications.

→ Broadcom: PTI and Broadcom will form a joint venture in Singapore - a major milestone making PTI a strategic and preferred partner of Broadcom. Built on PTI's fan-out PLP AI packaging experience, the JV will co-develop and produce additive-process fine-line-width redistribution-layer (RDL) packaging directly on advanced substrates (fan-out based), and will serve Broadcom exclusively without affecting PTI's fan-out PLP work for existing and future customers. An NDA is signed and the deal awaits Taiwan investment-authority approval, after which details will be disclosed; the JV funding goes in staged installments and does not raise PTI's NT$500 hundred million capex. The cooperation also brought PTI into the optical-communications field (Optical Engine, CPO switch roadmap).

Skyworks is engaged with leading data-center customers on the transition to 400V and 800V HVDC architectures. Rising rack density is driving demand for its advanced power-delivery solutions alongside its precision timing portfolio, and AI data center is the company's fastest-growing business at more than 50% annual growth.
400V/800V HVDC power transition; AI data-center growth >50%

Bookings in the third quarter were strong with book-to-bill better than 1.1; Sanmina continued to secure more customer orders for the next-generation accelerated compute business in Q3 (after securing orders with both hyperscale and OEM customers last quarter), expanding its overall customer base, while the legacy accelerated compute platform at ZT Systems has gone to zero.

Sanmina's ZT Systems business (the acquisition announced in May 2025 that created its partnership with AMD) is working in very close collaboration with AMD and joint customers to support almost all pre-production activities for the next-generation accelerated compute program; these non-recurring engineering services carry little revenue but a lot of labor charges and drove the non-GAAP operating margin beat to 8.0%, though longer-term margin is still expected in the 6%-7% range.
non-GAAP operating margin 8.0% (+230 bps YoY); long-term 6%-7%

Q4 FY2026 outlook: revenue $3.3 billion-$3.6 billion (core Sanmina $2.5 billion-$2.6 billion, ZT Systems $0.8 billion-$1.0 billion) and non-GAAP operating margin 7.5%-8.0%; the ZT range is below the prior implied guidance entirely because of a few legacy programs, and the new next-generation accelerated compute program is not included in the Q4 outlook due to revenue recognition timing — it is expected to begin contributing revenue in Q1 fiscal 2027 and ramp over time.
Q4 revenue $3.3 billion-$3.6 billion; ZT Systems $0.8 billion-$1.0 billion; op margin 7.5%-8.0%

→ AMD: ZT Systems is working in very close collaboration with AMD and joint customers to support almost all pre-production activities for the next-generation accelerated compute program; orders have been secured with both hyperscale and OEM customers, with more added in Q3; production revenue is expected to begin in Q1 fiscal 2027 and ramp over time through fiscal 2027 into fiscal 2028.

→ AMD: The ZT Systems partnership with AMD dates from the ZT Systems deal announced in May 2025; the business was expected at a $5 billion-$6 billion annualized run rate in its first year, and AMD 'continues to add more customers', which management says broadens Sanmina's addressable market for AMD Helios production even though share is hard to gauge.
value: ZT Systems run rate $5 billion-$6 billion (FY2026)

HBM hybrid bonding at a decision point: evaluations ongoing at one of the three memory companies with another starting its evaluation; all three are preparing to adopt hybrid bonding at some point because the device performs significantly better and produces far less heat; H2 2026 will clarify which HBM applications (HBM4E or even HBM3) adopt the technology and at what scale; the JEDEC height relaxation does not change that characteristic

Photonic SOI addresses pluggable transceivers, near package optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO); most current revenue and growth comes from scale-out, mostly pluggables, with NPO taking share and CPO expected to ramp on scale-out at the end of the year; scale-up is starting with pluggables and will move to CPO; roughly the same Photonic SOI content in all these architectures

MD: the next lot of B200 is expected in the next couple of months; E2E also plans to build more Blackwell capacity, including non-flagship Blackwell, and to expand into Vera Rubin, and will announce GPU counts when available; capacity expansion will be 'aggressive as well as judicious'.
