OFC demos: 1.6T ACCs running live traffic to NVIDIA's 224G SerDes and next-generation 448G per-channel CopperEdge chips.
ACC MSA with 12 founding members; 1.6T ACC shipments start in the April time frame; next-gen 448G per-channel CopperEdge

CEO VIEW ON COPPER VS CPO: 'Copper scale-up is always going to be there, and CPO scale-up is only going to make more sense in multirack systems' (e.g. NVL576 across eight racks, NVL1152); copper scale-up stays mainstream within a rack — 'do not put a terminal value on copper yet'. NPO is a complement to CPO that leverages the whole ecosystem: 'In CPO, we may not have much content in there except for lasers. But in NPO, we will be all over the place—with laser drivers, TIAs, and lasers, and even silicon photonics modulators'.

Media-mix response to NAND inflation: after the price increases, customers are having more discussions about hybrid flash arrays (HFA), Keystone and cloud alternatives; Kurian said it is 'too early' to call it a trend but 'HFAs are starting to see a lot of interest from customers', and NetApp's broad portfolio (unlike all-flash-only competitors) lets it serve price-sensitive workloads.

NVIDIA still leads the GPU market and will remain the larger share of Wiwynn's GPU business, but AMD is re-entering the fight with its next generation and more than one customer has approached Wiwynn about AMD GPU projects; Wiwynn will co-work with AMD from the pilot-build stage, leveraging a similar rack design across customers. The AMD rack is double-wide, also a 72-GPU configuration but with more memory content, so its price should be higher than the GB rack: against an analyst's roughly US$3.58M per GB rack reference, management indicated around US$5M for the AMD rack (with margin rate expected similar to GPU projects). Customers are still deciding how to portfolio their data centres across NVIDIA, AMD and their own ASICs.
GB rack about 358 ten-thousand US dollars per rack (analyst reference); AMD next-gen rack seen around 500 ten-thousand US dollars; 72-GPU double-wide with more memory

2026 outlook: demand remains strong for both AI and general-compute servers, with good growth expected for the full year but the momentum weighted to H2 because of the AI platform transition. AI stays above 50% of revenue (slightly above 2025's roughly half), with ASIC projects still the main AI contributor at roughly nine-tenths of AI volume. General server growth is driven by AI itself - CSPs split workloads such as agentic AI front/back-end services and part of inference onto general compute for TCO - and 2026 general server revenue and shipment units will both exceed 2025 (management suggested roughly 20-30% growth as a reference), with every quarter growing versus last year's H1-weighted pattern. Q1 2026 will certainly grow YoY, while QoQ growth off the record Q4 is challenging.
AI above 50% of 2026 revenue; ASIC about nine-tenths of AI volume; general server revenue and units both above 2025

The previous-generation GB200 GPU project has concluded - its cost structure drove the Q4 gross margin decline - and 2026 GPU efforts shift to developing the new-generation platform with customers and technology partners, with new ASIC and new GPU products both starting to ship in H2 2026. Wiwynn has been pushing customers toward a consignment model for GPU components since GPU projects began and hopes to have a definite answer by the next-generation ramp; it mostly builds to L11 for CSP customers (who handle their own integration), with L12 opportunities limited to sovereign-AI style tenders it pursues selectively after last year's project.

Interconnect IP: more than 40 PCIe design wins in the quarter with HPC and automotive customers, an industry-first demonstration of PCIe 8.0, and a first-to-market 224 gig SerDes on advanced nodes and leading foundries with 10 lifetime wins. Interconnect standards now turn over in about half the historical 3-to-4-year life. Hyperscalers, which lack their own IP teams, want customized IP delivered 'one generation ahead'; Synopsys is in active talks and expects several to become actual business in FY26, with the upside arriving after customer tape-outs.
more than 40 PCIe design wins; 224 gig SerDes 10 lifetime wins

Logic/foundry annealing: LSA is production tool of record at all 3 Tier 1 logic customers; the next-generation NSA (nanosecond annealing) system has 2 evaluations at Tier 1 logic customers, an evaluation system is planned to ship to the third in 2026, and 2 evaluation sign-offs are expected during 2026 with potential pilot line orders shortly after (low thermal budget uses such as contact annealing and 3D device stacking). Annealing SAM is projected at $1.3 billion by 2029 as devices shrink and shallower, more precise anneals are required, and the IBD300 low-resistance metals platform plus ion beam EUV mask blank and pellicle deposition SAM at $500 million by 2029; management expects the semiconductor SAM to expand on investment in gate-all-around, high-bandwidth memory and 3D packaging, with IBD a key enabler of high-NA EUV adoption. In 2026 logic, foundry and memory customers are all increasing capacity for annealing tools.
LSA tool of record at all 3 Tier 1 logic customers; NSA 2 evaluations; annealing SAM $1.3 billion by 2029; ion beam SAM $500 million by 2029

Technology drivers (CEO): industry projections suggest semiconductors could reach $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2027, possibly earlier. Leading-edge fabs are deploying new materials like molybdenum and new structures such as gate-all-around and high-bandwidth memory, raising deposition/etch capex intensity. UCT expects strength around etch and deposition, especially ALD and high-precision etch, to support gate-all-around and backside power distribution logic transitions as well as high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging and greater than 300-layer NAND. A multiyear WFE upturn should follow once wafer fabs address their near-term clean room constraints.
semiconductor market $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2027 (industry projection); greater than 300-layer NAND

Wafer-size transition: Tim Bettles says 'there's already been a big move from 3-inch to 4-inch' and AXT has scaled up its 4-inch business; 'we all know one customer that's really driving 6-inch demand' (customer not named), so AXT is 'looking at adding significant 6-inch capacity' as it doubles capacity through 2026 and beyond. CEO: a major focus of the expansion is more investment in 6-inch InP for 'next-generation EML and silicon photonic-based devices', and customers are deciding how much to switch 'from 3 to 4 and 4 to 6'. Larger sizes normally bring better margins, but 6-inch is 'still a little bit in development stage', with lower margins at first; the product mix is still 'very much geared towards 3-inch and 4-inch'.
big move from 3-inch to 4-inch already made; significant 6-inch capacity to be added as capacity doubles through 2026 and beyond

Asked about possible changes to cooling requirements for next-generation chips, the CFO said the impact on Comfort is 'not at all': 'the new chip stuff—they said, okay, we can use 45-degree water. Still needs pipe. Still needs water.' He added that 45-degree water is not naturally occurring for 99% of the year in 99% of places, and that as long as servers run on electricity they produce heat, so customers will keep needing electricians and pipe fitters; the CEO said the change is 'Far more impactful for the OEMs than for us.'
45-degree water (next-generation chip cooling requirement cited by management)

VPD lead customer (not named on this call) is ramping a Gen 4 factorized power system before transitioning to a Gen 5-based solution with higher current density and performance. The transition is expected to start in the second half of 2026, while Gen 4 production continues to 'ramp at a steep rate to the end of 2026'. According to the CEO, the Gen 4 system is mature, but the customer's next-generation system as a whole 'isn't quite there yet'. By year-end the lead customer will be using 'a significant share of our capacity' on the earlier generation, and the next-generation system adds 'an additional layer of use of capacity' into next year. Other Gen 5 (second-gen) VPD engagements will be selective: over the next couple of weeks, the global FAE team is being trained on Gen 5 VPD demo boards before engaging target hyperscalers and OEM chip companies. One prospect 'alone fill 2 fabs', and an automotive customer has shown interest. The VP of Sales says one very, very large company uses vertical power delivery in very high volume today (increasing year on year); high-volume use by anyone else is 'fairly limited', with others 'all trying to get Gen 1 VPD to work' and none he knows of deploying it in volume yet. The CEO says second-gen VPD with fifth-generation modules has much higher density, needs no stacking and is more efficient.
lead customer Gen 4 -> Gen 5 VPD transition to start in second half of 2026; Gen 4 ramping steeply to end of 2026

Content per accelerator: the VP of Sales puts Vicor's second-gen VPD opportunity at 'somewhere between $200 to $400 per XPU', depending on the XPU's current and number of rails. The CEO added 'Take that with a grain of salt' and clarified it is 'about like a 2,000 amp up to a 4,000 amp type of product'. For context, the CEO said a GPU power-system opportunity a number of years ago was 'about $100 million per year'. 'We are locking into an opportunity that will double that', he said, and a hyperscaler opportunity 'could be another'.
$200 to $400 per XPU; 2,000 amp up to a 4,000 amp product

DC power architecture for data centers (an analyst asked about the shift from 54-volt to 800-volt DC): Duke Austin - 'voltage going to DC, some of the architecture that NVIDIA has put out ... I believe we're in front of that I don't see it changing our TAM at all. You might get more medium voltage type arrangements in there. Still a lot of low voltage type things.' 'We work with NVIDIA and others to make sure that we see where they're going and make sure we have the craft necessary.' Older architecture will still be used and 'both are growing significantly'. Front vs behind the meter: it is better to let the utility take the chips' intermittency, but 'People are trying to go behind the meter simply because you can't get to the meter' because of queue constraints; he expects much off-grid generation to become backup power ('you'll start with 100, 200 max and then back up for a bit and then come on with utility type solutions'). Quanta never left natural gas and is getting involved in plants 'backing up some of the hyperscalers and data centers'.
no specific figure (DC power architecture not expected to change Quanta's TAM; more medium voltage arrangements possible)

2026 logic and industry outlook: management expects Entegris to benefit from node transitions in both logic and memory. Rising demand for two-nanometer devices should meaningfully lift wafer output through 2026, and that node carries both higher content per wafer and strong share for Entegris. Advanced logic fab utilization is already near 100%, and customers are investing aggressively in more capacity. At the most advanced logic node, Entegris has secured strong POR (position of record) positions in CMP consumables, advanced deposition and implant materials, liquid purification and filtration, and wafer handling. The team is now focused on winning incremental share and PORs at subsequent advanced nodes. Separately, the CEO said it takes time to grow two-nanometer and to transition to new nodes such as 1.4 nanometer. Management expects 'middish single-digit' industry MSI (wafer starts) growth in 2026 and strong WFE growth. Fab construction CapEx should grow modestly after last year's high single-digit decline, weighted to the second half, with a bigger acceleration in 2027 as work starts on new fabs. Management flagged ongoing memory shortages as a possible second-half 2026 risk for mainstream end markets; guidance assumes no impact.
middish single-digit industry MSI growth expected in 2026; advanced logic utilization near 100%

NAND: the move from roughly 250 layers to approximately 300 layers is under way. Management expects more than 20% NAND bit growth in 2026, driven mainly by higher-layer, higher-capacity NAND rather than a big increase in wafer starts. Entegris expects a double-digit increase in its NAND content per wafer as customers move to higher layer counts and adopt new materials such as moly and selective etch. It has won strong POR positions in NAND deposition materials, CMP and selective etch. NAND utilization is around 85%, and layer-count increases are absorbing most of the remaining 15% of capacity, with fewer new wafer starts. If demand stays strong, flash makers will likely need to add significant fab capacity, setting up higher NAND MSI growth in 2027. The CEO said Entegris gains from both layer growth and wafer growth, with slightly more from a full wafer start.
more than 20% NAND bit growth expected in 2026; double-digit increase in NAND content per wafer; NAND utilization around 85%

Technology roadmap. PANEL: ASE will have a FULLY AUTOMATED 310x310 panel line in production by the end of this year (manual today, which management says 'doesn't count'), for chiplet sizes too large for the 300-millimeter wafer form; a move to 620x620 depends on volume and technology requirements. FULL PROCESS 2.5D is not new for ASE; management frames it as second-source capacity next to the foundry partner ('We're not competing'), with configurations evolving as the HBM and TPU size grows. CPO / SILICON PHOTONICS: ASE is working with its foundry partner and the end customer on the silicon photonics (CPO) part, managing PIC and EIC together or separately across chip-to-chip, chip-to-packaging and chip-to-rack configurations, and expects 'some early volume on the silicon and the CPO part of it'. The EMS subsidiary USI made a fiberoptic acquisition, EugenLight, as part of piecing together early deployment for the future optical road map ('There is no conflict' with ASE), and EMS is extending into AI server, optical and power solutions. The packaging toolbox also includes next-generation power delivery for the VRM.
fully automated 310x310 panel in production by the end of this year (2026); CPO early volume expected

CEO Andrew Jassy: Trainium3 was recently launched and has just started shipping, with up to 40% more price performance than Trainium2. Demand is very strong, and Amazon expects nearly all of its Trainium3 chip supply to be committed by mid-2026. Trainium4 is still being built and is coming in 2027, with very substantial interest already, and Amazon is already having conversations about Trainium5.
up to 40% more price performance than Trainium2; nearly all supply expected to be committed by mid-2026; Trainium4 coming in 2027

800V DC transition: KR says AI racks will need 800 volts DC ('This switch to 800 volts DC is a necessity and not a choice') because upcoming AI racks will consume almost 100 times more power than traditional CPU racks. Grid, turbine or engine-powered sites will need transformers, rectifiers and power-conditioning gear to convert high-voltage AC, while 'Bloom, and only Bloom, natively produces 800 volts DC today.' 'Starting now, every Bloom server we ship will be 800 volts DC ready', with a removable adapter for legacy AC environments, and Bloom offers to convert previously shipped servers with simple modifications. KR says it also cuts copper use (copper is short in transformers) and efficiency losses.
every Bloom server shipped from now is 800 volts DC ready; AI racks almost 100 times the power of traditional CPU racks

800V data-center power: in 2025 MPS positioned for a further shift to solutions by sampling its 800-volt power solution for data centers. Asked whether 800-volt racks will use GaN or silicon carbide, Michael Hsing said MPS is developing silicon carbide and in the last few years developed its own GaN devices (he mentioned '100 volts'); 'that revenue is not for this year, not for even for next year. So, okay, maybe end of the next year. However, we're the first company to sample it.' Tony Balow: whether GaN or silicon carbide is what is demanded, MPS expects to be well-positioned.
800-volt power solution sampling; revenue 'maybe end of the next year'

Modules and vertical power: MPS had record module revenue in 2025 and is migrating 'from silicon to systems', with customers changing from silicon to modules on MPS's power density. On the packaging innovation to double module current density (raised by an analyst), Michael Hsing said 'We start to sampling those products' and 'expect to have a shipping in this quarter and next quarter', with customers having gone through qualification. On vertical power delivery: 'everybody is going to a vertical power'; Bernie Blegen called it 'the only energy-efficient solution' at high current. On server CPUs, the majority still use 12 volts while some models use 48 volts, and modules are 'the way to go'. Michael Hsing also said MPS is moving into MCUs, data converters and high-speed products.
record module revenue in 2025; higher-density modules shipping this quarter and next quarter

AGENTIC INFERENCE RAISES CPU CONTENT: AI is shifting from training to inference, and that inference is increasingly agent-based: 'persistent, always on, and power constrained'. Agent coordination runs on CPUs, so customers want higher core counts and better power efficiency. Haas said the latest hyperscaler and NVIDIA CPU generations 'have increased the number of cores. And we think that only continues.' He cited four examples. AWS's fifth-generation Graviton has 192 cores, double Graviton4. NVIDIA's Vera has 88 Arm-based cores, up from 72 cores in the 'gray CPU generation' (as transcribed). Microsoft's Cobalt 200 has 132 cores on Neoverse CSS V3, up from 128 in Cobalt 100 on Neoverse N2. Google previewed its second Arm server processor (Axion-powered m4a instances). Integrated platforms raise output per watt: AWS pairs Graviton with Arm-based Nitro DPUs and training accelerators, and NVIDIA pairs GPUs with Arm-based CPUs and BlueField. Over the next three years Haas expects CPUs to take on work GPUs used to do and more custom CPU-based chips to appear. He also sees specific prefill/decode inference solutions continuing to extend.
Graviton 192 cores; Vera 88 cores (vs 72); Cobalt 200 132 cores (vs 128)

→ NVIDIA: NVIDIA's next-generation Vera CPU has 88 Arm-based cores, up from 72 cores in the 'gray CPU generation' (as transcribed). Arm cited it as evidence that agentic inference is pushing CPU core counts higher. Haas said NVIDIA pairs its GPUs with Arm-based 'gray CPUs' (as transcribed) and Arm-based BlueField parts (printed 'blue field GPUs'), 'which has transitioned to Vera, delivering a 6x increase in GPU compute capability over the prior generation' (quoted as transcribed; the sentence is ambiguous).

Data center chiller launches introduced 'earlier this week', at 'the big show that's ongoing as we speak'. The YDAM 'delivers up to 3.5 megawatts of cooling in a compact footprint, providing approximately 20% higher capacity density than competing options and enabling warm water cooling for advanced GPUs'. The YKHT offers 'the industry's widest operating range and supports waterless heat reduction, which can eliminate up to 9 million gallons of cooling tower water annually in typical deployments'. The Smart Ready Chiller provides '10 times the insights over a standard remote connected chiller', which management expects to move more customers into recurring service. JCI also released a new reference guide that 'maps the full thermal chain and outlines scalable high-performance cooling architectures for an emerging class of AI factories'. CEO Joakim Weidemanis said 'We continue to work closely with NVIDIA' and that some of the guides 'is in collaboration with NVIDIA'. An analyst asked about the technology path, noting investor worry over NVIDIA and warm water cooling. The CEO would not comment on future launches but said there is 'a significant roadmap behind that'. He said the new products' effect on orders so far is 'very minor' ('it's more about what's to come') and that he expects them to start lifting orders in the current quarter.
YDAM up to 3.5 megawatts of cooling with approximately 20% higher capacity density; YKHT can eliminate up to 9 million gallons of cooling tower water annually

Data center thermal portfolio, per CEO Joakim Weidemanis. JCI plays in three categories plus controls: chillers; CRAHs (transcribed as 'craws') and air handling units 'through our silent air franchise, which is the leading franchise in air handling'; and CDUs. JCI entered the CDU space 'a couple of quarters ago' and is 'now starting to grow nicely here on the CDU side'. CDU sales today are 'a mix': plenty of business is CDUs only, but JCI sees 'plenty of opportunity for combined offers' with key accounts. As data center thermal architecture evolves, 'the roles that certain devices play today might evolve', which is why JCI added CDUs. Customer mix: JCI historically had a good position with hyperscalers and many large colos in the United States. Growth in Europe and Asia has now become 'very meaningful', and more future growth will come from Asia Pac and Europe, where the mix of hyperscalers and local colos is a little different, so 'our data center business is gonna broaden'. Countries in Southeast Asia and India are looking at data centers, with several emerging players. The CEO saw no material change in how the big hyperscaler and colo players behave. Every other week, large engineering teams from JCI's largest customers, colos and hyperscalers, work with JCI engineers at its JADEC innovation center in Pennsylvania on next-generation designs, and that work feeds the product roadmap.

AI data center: 'we have doubled our data center revenue in the last three quarters, with 50% quarter-over-quarter growth from Q1 to Q2'; Wolfspeed devices are 'already embedded in critical AI data center power systems'. The company is 'actively collaborating with a broad ecosystem of partners to support the industry transition from legacy 400-volt architectures to next-generation 800-volt AI platforms'. AI data centers operate at significantly higher voltages than legacy data centers, and as voltages rise management expects a growing share of the addressable market 'from grid to rack' to be better served by SiC than by silicon.
data center revenue doubled in the last three quarters; 50% quarter-over-quarter growth from Q1 to Q2

DDR5 RCD SHARE AND GENERATION MIX (CEO): Rambus believes it ended 2025 at mid-40% share for DDR5 RCDs, up from the early forties in 2024, the result of a larger design-win footprint at every DDR5 generation; the market grew mid-single digit from 2024 to 2025 while the DDR5 portion rose and DDR4 kept shrinking. DDR5 is still early in its cycle, leaving room to gain share: 'We always said we could be between forty and fifty.' Mix: in Q4 Gen 2 was predominant and Gen 3 was starting to ramp (growing vs Q3); in 2026 Gen 3 is expected to be the predominant version of DDR5; Gen 4 will contribute but with more limited adoption because it is on a different type of core; the big next step is Gen 5, which depends on the introduction of next-generation Intel and AMD platforms. As DIMM speeds rise, customers increasingly want all module chips from the same supplier for interoperability, an indirect positive for Rambus's companion chips.
mid-40% DDR5 RCD share in 2025 (early forties in 2024)

MRDIMM AND SOCAMM2 TIMING (CEO): MRDIMM timing unchanged; the rollout depends on the Intel and AMD platform rollouts (the analyst cited Intel Diamond Rapids and AMD Venice). Rambus expects MRDIMM to ramp towards the very end of 2026, with only the very initial contribution towards the end of the year and the main contribution happening in 2027: 'As far as we're concerned, we are ready.' SOCAMM2: 'On SOCAM two, we have an opportunity for the SPD hub'; Rambus is taking part in defining next-generation SOCAMM chips, where power management could open further opportunities, in line with its strategy of having solutions for every JEDEC standard module on the client and data center side.

New networking win (CEO): Celestica 'secured the design and manufacturing award for the 1.6T networking switch platform with a third hyperscaler customer'; this HPS engagement is expected to ramp production beginning in 2027, with design work already underway. With this hyperscaler Celestica held predominant share on 400G and on 800G; the 1.6T engagement started with a design win and Celestica was also awarded the mass production for the switch. Separately, mass production for the first 1.6T switching programs is expected to begin ramping in the latter part of 2026.
1.6T switch design and manufacturing award with a third hyperscaler; production ramp beginning in 2027

Switch generation cadence (management): Celestica has '10 active 1.6T programs in the pipeline right now'; about five of them start ramping in the back half of 2026 and into 2027, and several of the rest are in development and ramp later in '27 into '28. The gating factor is completing the development cycle as planned, and silicon is on track. 400G remains highly resilient and a strong 2026 contributor, 800G continues to grow, and 1.6T comes on toward the end of 2026: 'the next-generation technology is not necessarily cannibalizing the previous generation.' The 1.6T wins to date are used for both scale-up and scale-in. At 1.6T and 3.2T the engineering complexity is moving engagements toward HPS (design-led) work, and the CFO expects 1.6T programs to be as profitable as past switching programs. Some business Celestica declined to chase on price in 2025 came back in 2026 'because others could not execute on it.'
10 active 1.6T programs; about five ramp in the back half of 2026; 400G, 800G and 1.6T running concurrently

Co-packaged optics and 3.2T (management): customer conversations on co-packaged optics are increasing, but 'in terms of mass adoption, it's going to be more towards 3.2T, which are programs that we're working on in our R&D group. But we haven't seen customers looking for mass adoption of CPO as of yet.' 3.2T switch samples are due probably towards the end of 2026 and work has already started; Celestica has proof-of-concept work on co-packaged optics so it is ready when CPO hits the 3.2T cycle. On scale-up, management sees increasing R&D activity toward fully integrated AI/ML and networking systems supporting both scale-up and scale-out fabrics: 'scale-up will be as much of an opportunity as scale-out.'
3.2T samples towards the end of 2026; CPO mass adoption expected at 3.2T

Next-generation compute (management): Celestica has 'already won the next generation of that program' (the hyperscaler AI/ML compute program ramping through 2026) and expects those programs 'to actually ramp into 2027'. Looking towards 2027, management anticipates strong demand from hyperscaler and digital native customers driven by ramps in next-gen AI/ML compute programs; on the compute side Celestica focuses on HPS and JDM design-oriented work and has 'several projects in the pipeline to improve those engagements on the HPS side'.
next-generation program already won; ramp into 2027

Scale-across and speed transitions (CEO): scale-across data center interconnect is 'one of the most significant near term' drivers of optical demand. 'We've gone through the 400- and 800-gig transition very quickly.' 'we expect that 1.6 and 3.2 will come. And when you look at that scale across is the tailwind for both the technology transitions and the demand. And then, of course, over time, we see scale out increasingly be an opportunity for coherent optics.' Scale-across is also a tailwind for routing ('switching is much more about the data center racks, the spine-leaf architecture'). Later: 'Scale across is an emerging opportunity' and 'over time, as speeds continue to ramp within the data center, there will be more opportunity for coherent optics within the data center.' He described 'a much more mature and larger optical market, driven by the AI infrastructure build-out than we've seen in the past.'
400- and 800-gig transition passed very quickly; 1.6 and 3.2 will come; coherent optics moving toward scale out / inside the data center over time

Data-center architecture and future designs (CEO Dave Regnery, answering analyst questions on recent comments from a data-center partner about chillers and liquid cooling): 'we're working very closely with many influencers in the data center vertical. So think of hyperscalers, think of chip manufacturers, like Nvidia and others. We're helping them design data centers of the future. Or you may have heard them referred to as reference design data centers' - data centers to be built 'maybe two to four years out'. 'I have not seen a reference design or data center of the future that does not include chillers, just to be very clear', with 'a lot of innovation around the thermal management system, specifically around the chiller' in Trane's pipeline. Future data-center farms will build in free cooling: fans keep running through the free-cooling cycle while the compressor side runs less often; because chillers are sized to the thermal load, 'you're still gonna have the same number'. Asked whether HVAC's share of data-center spend is higher or lower two to four years out: 'I'm gonna err on the side of saying it's probably about the same', while 'the amount of power that is being consumed by the thermal management system may be less', letting operators redirect power to computing.

CALL - THE AI INTERCONNECT CONTENT THESIS ENTERING 2026: the CEO stressed breadth 'up and down the stack of AI' - 'the big web scale folks', 'the cloud, the Neo cloud', equipment manufacturers, and 'companies who are designing the chips and the architecture around those chips'. Customers' 'investment plans are all going up', and 'upgrades of the technology embedded in those data centers' require 'a higher technology, more complex, higher content degree of interconnect.' Amphenol participates in 'bringing the power in, power to the racks', in 'the data communication within racks, within adjacent racks', and now, with CommScope, in 'the broader fiber optic opportunity' - 'getting a signal from a GPU to a GPU or from a central office home somewhere'. Asked about an eventual move to 800-volt data-center power (the analyst's framing), the CEO answered: 'what we care about, Joe, is that there's more of everything... they go to different voltages. They go to different speeds... The ultimate what comes out of that is more complexity', adding that with CommScope Amphenol is 'even stronger than we were before' to help customers with these trade-offs.

Scale-up optics timing (CEO, answering a CPO/scale-up question): 'we do not have a significant revenue amount for scale-up included in this most recent SpringBoard upgrade', so it would be on top. Photons use 'greater than three times lower power' than electrons even over very short links, and the advantage 'can be 20 times or more' at longer reach or higher bit rate. There is a broad effort to bring optics into scale-up, closer to the GPUs and switch ASICs; he believes those links going to photons, with Corning's innovations playing a significant role, is inevitable. On timing, some scenarios fall between now and 2028 and others start 'primarily starting immediately in 2028 and beyond', so the plan treats timing conservatively.
no significant scale-up revenue in the upgraded plan; photons greater than three times lower power, 20 times or more at longer reach/higher bit rate; timing between now and 2028 or 2028 and beyond
